00

Experiment record and image guide

The experiments and their record

This is a set of in-depth SRv6 experiments. This page records the process of each experiment, and uses AI to make the experiments into videos.

This is a real test of SRv6 on a lab network, not only from books. Each experiment: first a question, then a test, and last the answer.

You can repeat the experiments in your own lab. The slides and the text version record the detailed process. They include commands, device configurations, and experiment outputs.

The text version records the experiment process with screenshots. Each step includes its commands, outputs, and interpretation. Each chapter separates observation, inference, and the next useful check.

Starting knowledge and lab topology

You need basic knowledge of IPv6, IS-IS, BGP, and MPLS VPN. Basic routing tables and VRFs are also necessary. Appendix A defines SRv6 terms. Command examples use Cisco IOS XR.

A PE is a provider edge router between customers and the core. A P router operates in the core. A CE is a customer device. PE1 and PE6 are the two service ends. P2–P5 are core nodes. BLUE, RED, and GREEN identify services; they are not fixed packet-header fields.

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

Experiment sequence

Stage Chapters Question to answer
Establish the model 1–3 Which node executes each SID, and how does the destination change?
Connect routing and services 4–5 Where does the locator route come from, and how does the SID select a VRF?
Calculate encapsulation 6–7 What does the core carry, and why does the size limit change?
Verify paths and protection 8–10 Where does traffic go after failure, and does a node list specify each link?
Diagnose and migrate 11–12 Which evidence identifies the cause, and when can the previous transport be removed?

Both language editions use this chapter and laboratory order. A video episode, figure number, and chapter number are different references. Captions retain the original episode numbers.

Predict, observe, explain

  1. Predict: record the expected packet header, table, path, or size before the test.
  2. Observe: compare the commands, outputs, and screenshots with that prediction.
  3. Explain: record what changed, what stayed correct, and which evidence supports the cause.

Use the worked examples and Appendix B to compare explanations. Read each step and its starting conditions before changes.

Without a laboratory, complete the field-reading exercises, path calculations, and size calculations. L1 needs a working L3VPN. From an empty environment, read Chapter 1 first, then return to L1 after Chapter 5.

Read the experiment images

Each image has an F number, episode number, and timestamp. Identify the device and state first. Then find the field discussed in the text. Decide what that field proves. Select an image in the HTML edition to enlarge it.

For example, F06 shows a working state and F07 shows a locator fault. Compare locator reachability and BGP resolution. Do not look only for error messages. F08 shows a separate allocation fault; it does not have the same cause as F07.

Scope of the evidence

The main laboratory uses six XRd vRouter nodes with IOS XR 26.2.2 on CML 2.10.0. Additional tests use XRv9000 with IOS XR 26.1.1. These results do not prove physical hardware performance, capacity, or support on every release.

A measured result describes an observed test. A calculated example follows from stated conditions. An unmeasured item has no completed lab test. Worked examples explain this evidence; they are not new experiment runs.

Before changes, save the baseline and verify management access and the restoration procedure. Introduce faults only in an isolated laboratory. If a prerequisite fails, stop at that step and record the difference. Do not hide it with later changes. Restore and accept the baseline after each run.

The explanations, tables, and images support study without the internal files. Paths in Appendices C and D are local references, not public download links. A laboratory rebuild still needs matching images, node definitions, and configurations.

01

State, packets, and the five questions

Experiment focus: Separate the destination from the action

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

Follow one customer packet through three roles. PE1 selects the service and adds encapsulation. The core forwards on the outer IPv6 destination. PE6 executes the service SID and delivers the inner packet. Each role needs different state.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter identifies the state on PE1, P2, and PE6. It explains why the core does not need the customer VRF.

Starting state: Read the explanation first. If the laboratory starts empty, complete the L3VPN in Chapter 5 before you do L1.

Why a route is not sufficient for SRv6

A customer packet arrives at PE1. Its destination is a customer address. PE1 must first identify the customer table. Then PE1 must select the remote service and the transport path.

SRv6 uses an IPv6 destination address to identify a segment. A segment can identify a node, an adjacency, or a service function. The ingress router can put multiple compressed segments in one destination address.

The destination address is not general executable code. The router applies an installed behavior to a matching local SID. An ordinary transit router uses IPv6 forwarding.

Five questions connect the experiments:

Question Necessary information First evidence to examine
Which node receives the packet? Reachable locator IPv6 RIB and CEF
Which action occurs there? Local SID behavior Egress SID table
Which customer receives the payload? Service context BGP attributes and VRF
Which path stays after a failure? Repair path CEF and a failure capture
Which mechanism selects the path? Policy or algorithm Policy state and actual path

Where the state stays

With LDP, core routers keep label bindings and neighbor sessions. With RSVP-TE, midpoint routers also keep tunnel state. The recorded lab did not configure RSVP-TE.

With SRv6, PE1 keeps customer routes and the instructions for encapsulation. PE6 keeps local service SIDs and customer tables. Core routers keep locator routes, local SIDs, and protection state.

Thus, the core is not stateless. The design removes the need for customer routes and individual SR Policy state on ordinary midpoint routers. Resource use increases with topology and local features.

“Transit” gives information about a role for a specified packet. P4 is a transit router when the destination belongs to PE6. P4 becomes a segment endpoint when the destination matches its own SID.

One packet, three transports

The following example has a 100-byte customer IP packet. Ethernet headers have 14 bytes. The calculation excludes VLAN tags and FCS.

Transport Added transport bytes Core frame bytes
MPLS with two labels 8 122
SR-MPLS with two labels 8 122
SRv6 with one outer IPv6 header 40 154

The SRv6 example uses 32 more bytes than the two-label examples. This difference applies only to these encapsulations. More labels, an SRH, or other headers change the calculation.

Worked example: Follow one BLUE packet

CE-A sends a packet to PE1. PE1 looks up the destination in the customer VRF and selects the remote service. P2 forwards on the outer destination through the PE6 locator. PE6 removes the outer encapsulation and looks up the inner destination in BLUE.

Read the figures: Read F01 for the core state on P2. Compare it with the customer state on PE1 in F02. The core lacks this customer VRF, but it still has forwarding state.

Think first: P2 has a PE6 locator route, but PE6 lacks the customer route. Which lookup prevents delivery?

Reason from the evidence: What must change when you add a customer?

Add a VRF on PE1 and PE6. Keep the core topology and locator plan unchanged. Which routers need new customer routes?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

The PEs need customer routes and service SIDs. A transit P router still forwards toward locators. Its lack of customer BGP does not mean it has no state.

Separate transport state from service state. A new core adjacency can add local SIDs even when the customer count stays constant.

L1 — Make a state record

Starting state: Use the completed L3VPN state from lab L5. This first exercise reads state without changing it.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

Stage · Ep01 — Commands and results
1.1 · What P2 actually holds

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show bgp summary

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show route vrf all summary
VRF: **iid
connected                        0          0          0           0
Total                            0          0          0           0

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show segment-routing srv6 locator
Name                  ID       Algo  Prefix                    Status   Flags
FA128                 1        128   fcbb:bb01:2::/48          Up       U

  • Now we examine P2 in the finished lab. All the services in this lab go through it.
  • BGP does not run on P2.
  • There is no customer VRF. The only entry is an internal entry with no routes.
  • P2 has two locators. MAIN is the locator that we use most. The second locator is for Flex-Algo. Episode 11 explains it.
  • P2 has 12 local SIDs: its node and adjacency SIDs. With three customers or three thousand customers, P2 keeps the same state.
1.2 · And what PE1 holds
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 sid
fcbb:bb00:1:e004::          uDT4              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e005::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e006::          uDT6              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e007::          uDT6              'RED'                             bgp-65000           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e00a::          uDT4              'GREEN'                           bgp-65000           InUse  Y

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route vrf all summary
VRF: RED     ...  bgp 65000      2
VRF: BLUE    ...  bgp 65000      2
VRF: GREEN   ...  bgp 65000      1
  • Now the edge. This is PE1 in the same finished lab.
  • PE1 has a service SID for each customer and address family: two for BLUE, two for RED and one for GREEN.
  • PE1 also keeps the remote routes of each customer, from BGP. The per-customer state is on the edge, and only on the edge.
1.3 · What the customer sees

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo traceroute -n -s 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2 -w 1 -q 1 -m 8
traceroute to 10.1.6.2 (10.1.6.2) from 10.1.1.2, 8 hops max, 46 byte packets
 1  10.1.1.1  1.259 ms
 2  10.1.6.1  2.902 ms
 3  10.1.6.2  1.610 ms
  • We examine the same fact from the customer side, with a traceroute from CE-A to CE-B.
  • The first hop is PE1, the gateway of the customer.
  • The next hop is PE6, then CE-B. The four core routers do not appear. They do not touch the customer packet. They touch only the outer header.

Acceptance: Compare each result with its interpretation. Record missing checks as Not verified. Restore the stated baseline before another experiment.

Questions:

  1. Which state stays on a P router?
  2. Can one router be a transit router and a segment endpoint?

Next: Chapter 2. Keep the accepted state and observations before adding the next mechanism.

02

Build and accept the laboratory

Experiment focus: Establish a known working state

A fault becomes easier to identify when a working record is available for comparison. First fix the topology, addresses, and initial configuration. Then check adjacency, local SID installation, and remote locator reachability separately. A successful commit does not prove service delivery.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter checks the sixteen directed adjacencies and the route from PE1 to the PE6 locator.

Starting state: Complete this acceptance check before fault experiments. Without CML, use F03–F05 to practice reading the results.

The fixed topology

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

The eight core links have sixteen directed IS-IS adjacencies. Each PE has two neighbors. Each P router has three neighbors. The shortest PE1-to-PE6 path is PE1–P2–P4–PE6, with cost 30.

Item Value
Loopback of node n 2001:db8:100::n/128
MAIN locator fcbb:bb00:n::/48
FA128 locator fcbb:bb01:n::/48
Core subnet for nodes a and b 2001:db8:200:ab::/127
IS-IS level Level 2
BLUE route target 65000:100
RED route target 65000:200

The loopback is outside the locator. With different prefixes, you can do the two reachability checks independently. The block and address plan are design choices.

Minimal PE1 example

This excerpt supplies the core baseline for PE1. It does not include management access, other routers, customer services, or protection. Interface names must match the imported node.

interface Loopback0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:100::1/128
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:200:12::/127
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:200:13::/127
!
segment-routing
 srv6
  encapsulation
   source-address 2001:db8:100::1
  locators
   locator MAIN
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fcbb:bb00:1::/48
!
router isis CORE
 is-type level-2-only
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  metric-style wide
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
 interface Loopback0
  passive
  address-family ipv6 unicast
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  point-to-point
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   metric 10
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
  point-to-point
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   metric 40

Worked example: Count before you inspect

The eight core links have two ends each. Thus, the network has sixteen directed adjacencies. One router shows only its own neighbors. The PE1–P2–P4–PE6 link costs total 30. Use this path as the initial comparison.

Read the figures: Use F03 for neighbors, F04 for local locator and SID installation, and F05 for the remote locator route. These are separate checks.

Think first: F03 is correct, but PE1 lacks the PE6 locator in F05. Which advertisement should be examined next?

Reason from the evidence: Can a successful ping accept the underlay?

PE1 can ping PE6. One expected P2 adjacency is missing. Can you continue to the protection experiment?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

The ping proves one working path. It does not prove the complete topology. An alternate path can hide a missing link.

Compare each neighbor with the diagram first. Then check the local SID, remote locator route, and CEF. Protection needs the intended topology.

L2 — Accept the baseline

Starting state: Start with six running routers and the links shown above. Configure both ends of every link.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

Stage · Ep02 — Commands and results
2.1 · Know what you are running
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show version
Cisco IOS XR Software, Version 26.2.2 LNT
Copyright (c) 2013-2026 by Cisco Systems, Inc.

Build Information:
 Built By     : cisco
 Built On     : Thu Sep 10 00:39:05 UTC 2026
 Workspace    : /auto/srcarchive13/prod/26.2.2/xrd-vrouter/ws/
 Version      : 26.2.2
 Label        : 26.2.2

cisco XRd vRouter
cisco XRd-vRouter-C-01 processor with 9GB of memory
XRd vRouter Container
  • Before you configure anything, record the software that you use. This is the first line of every lab report.
  • The version is IOS XR 26.2.2.
  • The platform is XRd vRouter, a container. Most output uses this platform and release. XRv9000 comparisons identify their platform separately.
2.2 · Step 1: addresses
interface Loopback0
 description router-id and SRv6 encapsulation source
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:100::1/128
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
 description TO-P2 cost 10
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:200:12::/127
 no shutdown
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
 description TO-P3 cost 40
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:200:13::/127
 no shutdown
  • The configuration has three steps. This is PE1. The other five nodes use the same pattern.
  • Step 1 is the addresses. Loopback0 gets the /128 from our plan. It is the router ID and the source of every encapsulated packet.
  • The two core interfaces get their /127 addresses. There is no IPv4 address, no MPLS and no LDP.
2.3 · Step 2: SRv6 and the locator
segment-routing
 srv6
  encapsulation
   source-address 2001:db8:100::1
  !
  locators
   locator MAIN
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fcbb:bb00:1::/48
   !
  !
 !
  • Step 2 enables SRv6. Only four lines are important.
  • The encapsulation source address is the loopback. When this router encapsulates a customer packet, this address is the outer source.
  • The locator has the name MAIN. Its prefix is the /48 of this node.
  • This line makes it a micro-SID locator. The node SID is a uN with the PSP and USD flavors. Episode 4 explains these flavors.
  • On hardware platforms, you can also need a hardware profile and a reload. This virtual router needs neither.
2.4 · Step 3: IS-IS carries the locator
router isis CORE
 is-type level-2-only
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  metric-style wide
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
 !
 interface Loopback0
  passive
  address-family ipv6 unicast
 !
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  point-to-point
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   metric 10
  • Step 3 is IS-IS. Most of this configuration is normal IS-IS.
  • We enable the IPv6 address family with wide metrics.
  • These two lines are the SRv6 part. They attach the locator to IS-IS. Then IS-IS advertises the locator and creates the adjacency SIDs.
  • If you do not include them, the commit is still successful. The locator is on this router, but no other router can reach it.
  • Each core interface is point-to-point, with the metric from our plan.
2.5 · Check 1: IS-IS neighbors

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show isis neighbors

IS-IS CORE neighbors:
System Id      Interface        SNPA           State Holdtime Type IETF-NSF
PE1            Gi0/0/0/0        *PtoP*         Up    28       L2   Capable
P3             Gi0/0/0/2        *PtoP*         Up    23       L2   Capable
P4             Gi0/0/0/1        *PtoP*         Up    28       L2   Capable

Total neighbor count: 3
  • Check 1, on P2. First, count the neighbors and compare them with the diagram.
  • P2 has three neighbors: PE1, P3 and P4. All are up, level 2 and point-to-point.
  • The diagram also shows three. Each PE has two neighbors, and each P router has three.
2.6 · Check 2: what the router says it can do
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 manager
Parameters:
  SRv6 Enabled: Yes
  SRv6 Operational Mode:
    Micro-segment:
      SID Base Block: fcbb:bb00::/24
  Encapsulation:
    Source Address:
      Default: 2001:db8:100::1
      Configured: 2001:db8:100::1
  SID Formats:
    f3216 <32B/16NFA> (2)
      uSID LIB Range:
        LIB Start   : 0xe000
        ELIB Start  : 0xfe00
      uSID WLIB Range:
        EWLIB Start : 0xfff7
  • Check 2 is one command: show segment-routing srv6 manager. The output is long, so we read it in three parts.
  • SRv6 is enabled, and the operational mode is micro-segment.
  • The encapsulation source is the loopback that we configured.
  • The SID format is f3216. This is a 32-bit block, then 16-bit node and function IDs.
  • Local functions start at hexadecimal e000. Remember this number. You will see it in every SID table in this series.
2.7 · Check 2, continued: behaviors
Platform Capabilities:
  SRv6: Yes
  TILFA: Yes
  Microloop-Avoidance: Yes
  Endpoint behaviors:
    uN (PSP/USD)
    uA (PSP/USD)
    uDT6
    uDT4
    uDT46
    uDX2
    uDT2U
    uDT2M
    uB6 (Insert.Red)
  Headend behaviors:
    T
    H.Insert.Red
    H.Encaps.Red
    H.Encaps.L2.Red
  • The second part lists the behaviors that this router supports.
  • uN and uA are the node and adjacency behaviors. Every path uses them.
  • The uDT and uDX entries are service behaviors. They are for Layer 3 VPN and for point-to-point Ethernet.
  • uB6 is the Binding SID. A behavior in this list does not prove that every related feature works. For example, this platform rejects bridge domains.
  • The headend list has H.Insert.Red and H.Encaps.Red, the reduced forms. It does not have plain H.Encaps.
  • This missing line changes the packets in all later episodes. Read this output before you design anything.
2.8 · Check 2, continued: depth
  Signaled parameters:
    Max-SL          : 3
    Max-End-Pop-SRH : 3
    Max-H-Insert    : 3 sids
    Max-H-Encap     : 3 sids
    Max-End-D       : 4
  Default parameters (under srv6):
    Encapsulation:
      Hop-Limit     : value=0, propagate=No
      Traffic-class : value=0, propagate=No
  Max Locators: 16
  Max SIDs: 64000
  • The third part is about limits.
  • The router signals these depths to its neighbors. It can insert or encapsulate 3 SIDs.
  • Here, a SID is a full 128-bit container. One container holds several micro-SIDs. Thus the limit of 3 is larger than it looks.
  • By default, the router does not copy the hop limit and the traffic class from the customer packet to the outer header. Episode 13 checks this on the wire.
  • The limits are 16 locators and 64000 SIDs. These are the limits of a virtual router. Do not use them for hardware.
2.9 · Check 3: the locator and the local SIDs
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 locator
Name                  ID       Algo  Prefix                    Status   Flags
--------------------  -------  ----  ------------------------  -------  --------
MAIN                  1        0     fcbb:bb00:1::/48          Up       U

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 sid

*** Locator: 'MAIN' ***

SID                         Behavior          Identification                    Owner               State  RW
--------------------------  ----------------  --------------------------------  ------------------  -----  --
fcbb:bb00:1::               uN (PSP/USD)      'default':1                       sidmgr              InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e000::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/0, Link-Local]:0         isis-CORE           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e001::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/1, Link-Local]:0         isis-CORE           InUse  Y
  • Check 3 uses two commands. You will use them more than any other commands in this series.
  • The locator MAIN is up, in algorithm 0, with the prefix that we configured.
  • The first SID is the node SID, a uN. The SID manager owns it. It is available when the locator is up.
  • The next two SIDs are adjacency SIDs, one for each core interface. IS-IS owns them. That is why step 3 is important.
  • Their functions are e000 and e001. These are the first two values of the local range.
2.10 · The remote locator, as PE1 sees it
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 isis

i L2 2001:db8:100::6/128
      [115/30] via fe80::5454:ff:fe9b:6d1f, 01:12:13, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
i L2 fcbb:bb00:2::/48
      [115/11] via fe80::5454:ff:fe9b:6d1f, 01:12:32, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
i L2 fcbb:bb00:4::/48
      [115/21] via fe80::5454:ff:fe9b:6d1f, 01:12:13, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
i L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
      [115/31] via fe80::5454:ff:fe9b:6d1f, 01:12:13, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  • A local SID is useful only when other routers can reach it. Thus, on PE1, we examine the routes from IS-IS.
  • PE6's loopback has metric 30, through GigabitEthernet 0. This is the upper path, as we predicted.
  • PE6's locator is a different route, with metric 31. On this release, the router adds 1 to the path cost for the locator.
  • The locators of P2 and P4 are also here, with metric 11 and 21. The locator of each node is a normal IPv6 route.
  • This is an important property of SRv6. A router in the middle needs no new function to forward a packet to a SID. It needs only a route.
2.11 · Check 4: ping the node SID
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 2
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 2, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!
Success rate is 100 percent (2/2), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms
  • This is the ping command on PE1. The destination is the node SID of PE6, fcbb:bb00:6::.
  • The source option sets the source address. We use the loopback of PE1, because every router can reach it. The reply needs this address to come back. The count option sends two packets.
  • The router sends two echo requests, each with 100 bytes.
  • Each exclamation mark is one reply that came back.
  • The success rate is 100 percent: 2 of 2. The ping works. But the ping alone does not show the path. For this, we need the captures.

Router / tool: tcpdump

  • This is the output of tcpdump. Each line is one packet. The first part of each line shows the hop limit. Then we see the source address, the destination address, and the packet type. We show the first echo request of each capture.

  • On the second link, the destination is the same, and the hop limit is 59.

Acceptance: Compare each result with its interpretation. Record missing checks as Not verified. Restore the stated baseline before another experiment.

Questions:

  1. Why does the laboratory keep loopbacks outside the locator block?
  2. Why is the final PE1 configuration incorrect for a VPWS test?

03

Read a SID and follow the packet

Experiment focus: Follow each SID operation

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

The previous chapter checked reachability. This chapter separates forwarding toward a locator from execution of a local SID. Then it follows each uSID shift. Identify the changed field and the address used for the next lookup.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter traces the destination at each stage. It compares uN node instructions with uA adjacency instructions.

Starting state: Start with the three-node example. Add service functions, multiple blocks, and repair paths only after the shift is clear.

Two different matches

A locator is a routable prefix. It directs a packet to a node. A local SID entry tells that node which behavior to apply.

For example, P2 can forward fcbb:bb00:6:e004:: through a route to fcbb:bb00:6::/48. The BLUE VRF is not necessary on P2. At PE6, the more specific local service SID selects BLUE.

After decapsulation, PE6 does one more lookup for the inner destination in BLUE. A reachable locator cannot replace this lookup. A local SID cannot replace the route to the customer.

f3216 and the six positions

fcbb:bb00 : 0006 : e004 : 0000 : 0000 : 0000 : 0000
<32 bits>   <16>   <16>   <16>   <16>   <16>   <16>
  block     node  function       remaining positions

The format uses a 32-bit block and 16-bit compressed identifiers. Six positions stay after the block. These positions can contain node instructions and local function instructions.

The positions do not always mean six different routers. A service function consumes a position. An adjacency function can consume one more position. A change to a different block makes one more container necessary.

The recorded IS-IS structure for uN is 32/16/0/80. The uN has no different function field in that advertisement. Its argument can hold five more 16-bit identifiers.

The recorded uA structure is 32/16/16/64. The service BGP attribute in Chapter 5 reports a different structure. Those advertisements give information about different objects.

Behaviors and flavors

IOS XR name Main operation Service context
uN Advance to the next compressed instruction Node
uA Use the specified adjacency Link
uDT4 Remove encapsulation and use an IPv4 table VRF
uDT6 Remove encapsulation and use an IPv6 table VRF
uDT46 Use an IPv4 or IPv6 table VRF, if supported
uDX2 Remove encapsulation and deliver an Ethernet frame Attachment circuit
uDT2U / uDT2M Use a bridge table or BUM delivery function E-LAN, not measured here
uB6 Apply an associated policy SR Policy

Cisco uN and uA use NEXT-CSID behavior. The service names identify the associated endpoint functions. The recorded uB6 uses an insertion form. Its name alone does not show the encapsulation operation.

PSP removes the SRH at the penultimate segment endpoint. USP removes the SRH at the last endpoint. USD can remove the outer IPv6 encapsulation at the last endpoint under its specified conditions.

A uDT service does its own decapsulation. That action is not proof of USD. The lab measured PSP but did not isolate a USD experiment.

A three-node example

Captured link IPv6 destination Hop Limit
PE1–P2 fcbb:bb00:2:4:6:: 60
P2–P4 fcbb:bb00:4:6:: 59
P4–PE6 fcbb:bb00:6:: 58

At P2, the active uN identifies P2. P2 advances the remaining identifiers by 16 bits and fills the last position with zero. P2 then forwards on the new destination. P4 does the same operation.

An ordinary transit hop decreases Hop Limit without a change to the identifiers. Thus, a changed Hop Limit does not show that a segment instruction occurred.

The full endpoint procedure also examines the remaining argument, the SRH, and the payload. Segments Left = 0 alone does not show that all compressed instructions are complete.

Worked example: Calculate a uSID shift

Start with fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::. After P2 executes its uN, the destination becomes fcbb:bb00:4:6::. After P4 executes its uN, it becomes fcbb:bb00:6::. Each router forwards on the new destination. The list does not directly specify a physical output interface.

Read the figures: Read the uN entry in F09. Compare the links and destinations in F11. F12 explains the missing ping reply separately from the observed shifts.

Think first: Hop Limit decreases. Which additional field change proves that the uN instruction advanced?

Reason from the evidence: Does an address select a path or a service?

Compare a node instruction with a uDT4 service instruction. Both use IPv6 addresses. What must the receiving router do differently?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

A node instruction advances the transport program. A uDT4 instruction removes the outer encapsulation and selects an IPv4 table. The address alone does not explain the behavior.

Read the local SID behavior and its owner. Then predict the next lookup and the headers that remain. Confirm those predictions in the capture.

L3 — Observe a shift and an adjacency

Starting state: Start with working GREEN, BLUE, and the MAIN locator. Restore each fault before the next test.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

3.14 · Read the label field
Healthy:
      Received Label 0xe0080
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: 31
        T:1(Sid information), Sid:fcbb:bb00:6::(Transposed), Behavior:63
           Length [Loc-blk,Loc-node,Func,Arg]:[32,16,16,0], Tpose-len:16, Tpose-offset:48

Fault B:
      Received Label 24004
  • This is a fast method to identify the two cases. Read the received label.
  • In the healthy state, the label is a hexadecimal value, e0080. This is the SID function, e008, in the label field.
  • The next lines show the method. BGP sends the locator one time, and puts the 16-bit function in the label field. The receiver builds the full SID again.
  • RFC 9252 calls this method transposition. Episode 13 reads it field by field from a captured update.
  • In fault B, the label is a normal decimal MPLS label. In a core with only SRv6, this tells you that there is a problem.

frame 116, 154 bytes

  • Now we use that uA. You can do the same in your lab. First, in CML, start a packet capture on every link of the path. Then ping from PE1.
  • The destination is fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6::. After the block, it has three parts. 3 is the node P3, e005 is the uA of P3 toward P5, and 6 is the node PE6.
  • The ping fails: two dots, and 0 percent. This does not mean that the packet is lost. We show the reason later in this episode.
  • For comparison, we ping the node SID of PE6 in the same way.
  • This ping works: two replies, and 100 percent. A normal address gets replies. The first address gets none. The captures show the difference.
4.4 · The capture, link by link

Router / tool: tcpdump

$ tcpdump -nn -t -v -r <capture file> icmp6
# PE1 to P2
IP6 (hlim 60) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6::: [icmp6 sum ok] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P2 to P3
IP6 (hlim 59) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6::: [icmp6 sum ok] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P3 to P5
IP6 (hlim 58) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6::: [bad icmp6 cksum 0x0316 -> 0xe31e!] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P5 to P4
IP6 (hlim 57) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6::: [bad icmp6 cksum 0x0316 -> 0xe31e!] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P4 to PE6
IP6 (hlim 56) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6::: [bad icmp6 cksum 0x0316 -> 0xe31e!] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
  • Now we read the captures. We save each capture from CML, and we read it with tcpdump on our own computer. We show the first echo request of each file.
  • On the link PE1 to P2, the destination holds all three instructions. The hop limit is 60. tcpdump says that the checksum is correct.
  • On the link P2 to P3, the destination is the same. P2 has no matching SID. It routes the packet, and it lowers the hop limit by one.
  • After P3, the destination is fcbb:bb00:6::. P3 removed its node instruction and the uA, and it shifted PE6 to the front. Now tcpdump reports a bad checksum. Remember this.
  • P5 and P4 route the packet like a normal address. The packet arrives at PE6 with hop limit 56, after four routers. Each change agrees with the prediction.

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 3
Sending 3, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (3/3), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/3/3 ms

Sending 3, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
...
Success rate is 0 percent (0/3)
  • The capture showed a strange result. The shifted packet arrived at PE6, but PE6 did not reply. We compare two pings from PE1.
  • First, a ping directly to the node SID of PE6. All three packets get a reply.
  • Second, a ping to fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::. This address holds three instructions: P2, then P4, then PE6. It gets no reply. The cause is on PE6.
4.6 · PE6 counters after each ping

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show ipv6 traffic      (ICMP statistics, three times)
before the pings
  Rcvd: 23 input, 6 checksum errors, 0 too short
        13 echo request, 0 echo reply
after 3 direct pings
  Rcvd: 26 input, 6 checksum errors, 0 too short
        16 echo request, 0 echo reply
after 3 shifted pings
  Rcvd: 29 input, 9 checksum errors, 0 too short
        16 echo request, 0 echo reply
  • On PE6, we read the ICMP statistics before the pings, and after each ping. The command is show ipv6 traffic.
  • This is the starting point: 6 checksum errors, and 13 echo requests.
  • After three direct pings, the echo request counter increased by three, to 16. The checksum error counter did not change.
  • After three shifted pings, the checksum error counter increased by three, to 9. The echo request counter did not change. PE6 discarded the packets as damaged.
4.7 · Why PE6 discards the packet

Router / tool: analysis

# ICMPv6 checksum, calculated again from the capture on P4 to PE6
direct: arriving DA fcbb:bb00:6::, checksum in packet 0xfd85
   computed with the arriving DA                     0xfd85  match
   computed with the sender's DA fcbb:bb00:6::       0xfd85  match
shifted: arriving DA fcbb:bb00:6::, checksum in packet 0xfd34
   computed with the arriving DA                     0xfd3a  MISMATCH
   computed with the sender's DA fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::   0xfd34  match
  • We calculated the ICMPv6 checksum again from the capture of the link P4 to PE6.
  • For the direct ping, the packet arrives with the same address that PE1 sent to. The checksum matches.
  • For the shifted ping, the arriving destination gives 0xfd3a. The packet carries 0xfd34. They do not match.
  • The destination that PE1 sent to, fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::, gives 0xfd34. This matches. PE1 calculated the checksum with its own destination.
  • RFC 9800, section 6.5, says that the source must calculate the checksum with the final destination: the address of the packet when it arrives. Our ping used the container as a normal address.
  • This does not affect customer traffic, because its checksum is in the inner packet. The finding is for tests: use captures, not ping replies, to examine a shifted path.
4.8 · PSP: the policy that PE1 uses
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf BLUE ipv6 2001:db8:c:106::/64 detail
2001:db8:c:106::/64, version 22, SRv6 Headend
   via fcbb:bb00:1:e009::/128, 3 dependencies, recursive
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e005::}
      SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb01:3:5::}
    Hash  OK  Interface                 Address
    0     Y   GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1    fe80::5454:ff:fec1:58eb
  • Now PSP, in the lab. The route to the BLUE customer in IPv6 uses an SR policy. Episode 6 explains the policy. Here we only read the forwarding entry.
  • The first SID list is the service SID of PE6, fcbb:bb00:6:e005::. PE1 puts it in the routing header.
  • The second SID list is the policy. It is one container, fcbb:bb01:3:5::, with two instructions: P3, then P5. PE1 puts it in the destination address.
  • The packet needs both lists, so it needs a routing header. Now we ping from CE-A, and we capture on the links.
4.9 · PSP on the wire

Router / tool: tcpdump

# CE-A: sudo ping6 -c 2 2001:db8:c:106::2   (2 received, 0% packet loss)
# PE1 to P3, 182 bytes
IP6 (hlim 255, next-header Routing (43)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb01:3:5::: RT6 (segleft=1, [0]fcbb:bb00:6:e005::)
# P3 to P5, 182 bytes
IP6 (hlim 254, next-header Routing (43)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb01:5::: RT6 (segleft=1, [0]fcbb:bb00:6:e005::)
# P5 to P4, 158 bytes
IP6 (hlim 253, next-header IPv6 (41)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005:::
# P4 to PE6, 158 bytes
IP6 (hlim 252, next-header IPv6 (41)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005:::
  • In the lab, we start captures on the links of the path. Then, on CE-A, we ping the customer address on the far side. Both replies return.
  • On the link PE1 to P3, the destination is the container fcbb:bb01:3:5::. The routing header has one entry: the service SID of PE6. Segments Left is 1. The frame has 182 bytes.
  • After P3, the destination is fcbb:bb01:5::. P3 shifted out its own instruction. The routing header is still there, with one segment left.
  • P5 is the penultimate endpoint. It copies the last SID into the destination, and it removes the routing header. This is PSP. The frame is 24 bytes smaller: 158 bytes.
  • On the link P4 to PE6, there is no routing header. PE6 receives a normal encapsulated packet, and the service SID e005 does the rest.
4.10 · uDT4: a service decapsulates by itself

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6:e006::/64
fcbb:bb00:6:e006::/64, version 179, SRv6 Endpoint uDT4
    next hop VRF - 'RED', table - 0xe0000001
    0     Y   recursive                 Lookup in table
  • Do not mix up USD and service decapsulation.
  • A uDT4 is a different behavior. It does not need a flavor to remove the outer header. To remove the outer header is its function.
  • Then it looks up the inner packet in a specified VRF, here RED. Thus it is a service, not a waypoint.

$ tcpdump -nn -t -v -r shift-<link>.pcap icmp6     (eight files, merged in time order)
link        destination            hop limit
PE1 - P2    fcbb:bb00:3:5:6::      60
P2 - P3     fcbb:bb00:3:5:6::      59     toward P3

PE1 - P3, P3 - P5, P5 - PE6:  nothing
  • This is one ping. We read the capture of each core link with tcpdump, and we put the results in time sequence.

04

Verify the underlay: from IS-IS to CEF

Experiment focus: Use five separate routing checks

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

The locator must appear in an LSP before SPF can calculate its route. The RIB must select a route. CEF must then install a usable forwarding entry. An adjacency alone does not prove this complete sequence.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter traces faults from adjacency through CEF. The first failed stage determines the next check.

Starting state: Keep the Chapter 2 baseline. Restore and accept the network after each fault before you introduce another fault.

Five different results

An adjacency permits two routers to exchange link-state information. It does not prove that a specified locator is present. The locator must appear in the originating LSP.

SPF uses the link-state database to calculate a route. The RIB then selects an eligible route. CEF must install a usable forwarding entry.

Stage Question IOS XR command
Adjacency Is the neighbor available? show isis adjacency detail
LSP Did PE6 advertise the locator? show isis database verbose
SPF Did IS-IS calculate a path? show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48
RIB Is the route installed? show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
CEF Is there a usable exit? show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail

These stages can give different results. A local route filter can leave the LSP and SPF route complete but prevent RIB installation. A healthy adjacency cannot detect that filter.

In the baseline, three links cost 30 in total. The recorded locator metric is 31 because this implementation adds one for the locator. The loopback metric is 30. This additional one is not a universal SRv6 cost rule.

Capability is not service acceptance

The manager and IS-IS advertisements give different limits. Maximum SID count gives information about router resources. Maximum SID Depth gives information about supported packet operations.

The recorded manager shows Max-H-Encap 3 and Max-H-Insert 3. A 128-bit entry can carry multiple micro-SIDs. These values are not a limit of three physical hops.

A listed endpoint behavior does not show complete service support. The lab routers listed E-LAN behaviors but rejected bridge domains. Chapter 7 gives the result.

Worked example: Explain an SPF route without a RIB route

Assume that the LSP contains the locator and SPF calculates its route. A local RIB filter on PE1 can prevent route installation. The LSP and SPF information can remain. This does not mean that PE6 stopped advertising the locator.

Read the figures: F18 is the working reference. F19 shows an alternate path after an interface fault. F20 shows different SPF and RIB results. Find the first changed stage.

Think first: Which LSP observation separates a missing locator advertisement from a local RIB filter?

Fault 2: find the first failed stage

The neighbors remain Up. PE6 still advertises FA128, but MAIN is absent. Thus SPF, RIB, and CEF cannot resolve MAIN.

Do not conclude that IS-IS is down. Restore the MAIN locator attachment on PE6, then repeat all five checks.

Reason from the evidence: Two missing routes, two different causes

Case A: the LSP lacks MAIN. Case B: the LSP and SPF contain MAIN, but the RIB does not. Should both repairs change PE6?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

No. Case A points toward advertisement or its prerequisites. Case B points toward local route installation. Changing the remote locator can obscure the second cause.

Find the first changed stage. Keep the successful earlier stages as evidence. Choose a repair that explains both the failed and working observations.

L4 — Isolate three failures

Starting state: Start with working MAIN and FA128 locators. Test the three faults separately.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

Stage · Ep08 — Commands and results
8.1 · Where the LSP content comes from
! PE6 (trimmed)
router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  metric-style wide
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
   locator FA128
 flex-algo 128
  metric-type delay
  advertise-definition
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  point-to-point
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   fast-reroute per-prefix ti-lfa
   metric 10
performance-measurement
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  delay-measurement
   advertise-delay 5000
  • Before we read the LSP, we look at the configuration that creates it. This is PE6, trimmed to the lines that matter. You can copy the same structure on each router.
  • Wide metrics are necessary for segment routing. The IPv6 address family carries everything.
  • Two locators are attached to IS-IS: MAIN for algorithm 0, and FA128 for Flex-Algo 128. Each one becomes a locator in the LSP.
  • The flex-algo 128 block gives the metric type, delay, and it advertises the definition. We use it in Episode 11.
  • Each core interface is point-to-point, with a metric. The metric is the link metric that we read in the LSP.
  • The link delay of 5000 microseconds comes from the performance-measurement block. It is a static value that we configured, not a measurement.
8.2 · Layer 1: the adjacency
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis adjacency detail
P2             Gi0/0/0/0                *PtoP*         Up    25   06:50:33 Yes None Up
  Neighbor IPv6 Address:  fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1*
  END.X SID:              fcbb:bb00:1:e000::/64 uA (PSP/USD), Algorithm 0
  Non-FRR END.X SID:      fcbb:bb00:1:e001::/64 uA (PSP/USD), Algorithm 0
  END.X SID:              fcbb:bb01:1:e000::/64 uA (PSP/USD), Algorithm 128
  Non-FRR END.X SID:      fcbb:bb01:1:e001::/64 uA (PSP/USD), Algorithm 128
  Topology:               IPv6 Unicast
    Usable by Flex-algo:  128
  BFD Status:             Neighbor Useable (BFD Required)
  • Layer 1, on PE1, for the neighbor P2.
  • The adjacency is up. It uses IPv6 link-local addresses. There is no IPv4 here.
  • IS-IS allocated two adjacency SIDs for this link in algorithm 0. Fast reroute can protect one of them. The SID with the Non-FRR mark is never protected.
  • There are two more for algorithm 128, the Flex-Algo of Episode 11. One link has four adjacency SIDs.
  • The topology is IPv6 unicast, and Flex-Algo 128 can use it. BFD is necessary, and it is up. Each of these lines can be the cause of a missing path.
8.3 · Layer 2: the LSP, capabilities
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis database verbose PE6.00-00
PE6.00-00             0x00000034   0x359c        1145 /1200         0/0/0
  IPv6 Router ID: 2001:db8:100::6
  Router Cap:     0.0.0.0 D:0 S:0
    SR Algorithm:
      Algorithm: 0
      Algorithm: 1
      Algorithm: 128
    SRv6: O:0
    Node Maximum SID Depth:
      SRH Max SL:       3
      SRH Max End Pop:  3
      SRH Max T.insert: 3
      SRH Max T.encaps: 3
      SRH Max End D:    4
  • Layer 2 is PE6's link-state packet on PE1. We read it in three parts. Use verbose. The detail option does not show most of the information.
  • This is PE6's LSP, with a sequence number, a remaining lifetime and an IPv6 router ID.
  • PE6 gives the algorithms that it uses: 0 and 1, which are the defaults, and 128, which we configured.
  • RFC 9352 defines this SRv6 capability flag. It tells that PE6 can process SRv6.
  • These are the maximum SID depths. They are the same values that the manager showed in Episode 2. Each router learns the limits of the other routers from here.
8.4 · Layer 2: the LSP, locators
  SRv6 Locator:   MT (IPv6 Unicast) fcbb:bb00:6::/48 D:0 Metric: 1 Algorithm: 0
    END SID: fcbb:bb00:6:: uN (PSP/USD)
      SID Structure:
        Block Length: 32, Node-ID Length: 16, Func-Length: 0, Args-Length: 80
  SRv6 Locator:   MT (IPv6 Unicast) fcbb:bb01:6::/48 D:0 Metric: 1 Algorithm: 128
    END SID: fcbb:bb01:6:: uN (PSP/USD)

  Metric: 1          MT (IPv6 Unicast) IPv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  • Part 2: the locators.
  • The SRv6 locator TLV contains fcbb:bb00:6::/48, in algorithm 0, with a metric of 1. This is the additional 1 in the metric 31 from Episode 2.
  • Below it is the End SID, PE6's uN, with its structure: block 32, node 16, function 0, argument 80. The 80 bits of argument are the space for the next micro-SIDs.
  • This is a second locator, in algorithm 128, for Flex-Algo.
  • The same locator is here again, as a normal IPv6 prefix. RFC 9352 permits this. Then routers without SRv6 can also route to the locator.
8.5 · Loopback and locator, side by side
  Metric: 0          MT (IPv6 Unicast) IPv6 2001:db8:100::6/128
    Prefix Attribute Flags: X:0 R:0 N:1 E:0 A:0
    Source Router ID: 2001:db8:100::6
  Metric: 1          MT (IPv6 Unicast) IPv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
    Prefix Attribute Flags: X:0 R:0 N:0 E:0 A:0
  • In the LSP, compare PE6's two most important prefixes. The first fault in Episode 3 is here.
  • The loopback has metric 0 and the N flag. The N flag means that this prefix identifies the node.
  • The locator has metric 1, and it is a different prefix. These are two lines in the same LSP, from different parts of the configuration. One can disappear while the other stays.
8.6 · Layer 2: the LSP, links
  Metric: 10         MT (IPv6 Unicast) IS-Extended P4.00
    Interface IPv6 Address: 2001:db8:200:46::1
    Neighbor IPv6 Address: 2001:db8:200:46::
    Link Average Delay: 5000 us
    END.X SID: fcbb:bb01:6:e000:: B:1 S:0 P:0 uA (PSP/USD) Alg:128
    END.X SID: fcbb:bb01:6:e001:: B:0 S:0 P:0 uA (PSP/USD) Alg:128
    END.X SID: fcbb:bb00:6:e000:: B:1 S:0 P:0 uA (PSP/USD) Alg:0
    END.X SID: fcbb:bb00:6:e001:: B:0 S:0 P:0 uA (PSP/USD) Alg:0
      SID Structure:
        Block Length: 32, Node-ID Length: 16, Func-Length: 16, Args-Length: 64
  • Part 3: each link. This is PE6's link to P4.
  • The metric is 10, with the IPv6 addresses of the two ends.
  • The link delay is 5000 microseconds. This is the static value that we configured for Flex-Algo. It is not a measurement. Episode 11 uses it.
  • There are four End.X SIDs, two for each algorithm. The B flag shows the SIDs that can have protection.
  • Their structure is block 32, node 16, function 16, argument 64. Our first plan expected an argument of zero. The router shows 64, and the router is correct.
8.7 · Layers 3, 4 and 5
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [31/115]
     via fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2
    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, from 2001:db8:100::6, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, Protected

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
   via fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1/128, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  • Now the last three layers, for the same locator, on PE1.
  • Layer 3: IS-IS calculated the route, with metric 31, through P2.
  • Layer 4: the RIB installed it. It shows the route as an SRv6 locator, protected. Episode 9 explains the word protected.
  • Layer 5: CEF forwards it out of GigabitEthernet 0/0/0/0. All layers show the same next hop. When the layers do not agree, you have found the fault.
8.8 · Fault 1: the interface leaves the IPv6 topology
! PE1
router isis CORE
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  no address-family ipv6 unicast
  • Now we break the network, one layer at a time. Fault 1: on PE1, we remove the IPv6 address family from the IS-IS interface to P2.
  • The interface stays up, with its addresses. Only IS-IS stops the use of IPv6 on it. Predict the result before the next page.
8.9 · Fault 1: what changed
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis neighbors
P3             Gi0/0/0/1        *PtoP*         Up    22       L2   Capable

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 71, SRv6-locator, type level-2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1
 1  2001:db8:200:13::1
 2  2001:db8:200:23::
 3  2001:db8:200:24::1
 4  2001:db8:100::6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 2
Success rate is 100 percent (2/2), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms
  • This is PE1, twenty seconds later.
  • The adjacency to P2 is gone. When IS-IS runs only IPv6, the IPv6 topology is the only reason to keep a neighbor.
  • PE6's locator now has metric 71, not 31.
  • The traceroute shows the new path: down the expensive link to P3, back to P2, then P4 and PE6. Each packet now goes through two more hops.
  • The customer ping still works. Nobody complains. This fault is quiet, thus it is dangerous. When we restored the address family, P2 came back and the metric became 31 again.
8.10 · Fault 2: what PE1 shows
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
% Network not in table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: inaccessible

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32
    unresolved
    0     Y   recursive                 drop

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 3
Success rate is 0 percent (0/3)
  • You saw fault 2 in Episode 3: on PE6, we removed the locator from IS-IS. Here are the outputs on PE1, in the layer model.
  • Layer 4: the RIB has no route to the locator.
  • BGP still has the customer path, but the locator is inaccessible.
  • Layer 5: CEF is unresolved, and the last column shows drop.
  • The customer ping fails.
8.11 · Fault 2: layers 1 to 5 on PE1
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis adjacency
P2             Gi0/0/0/0    *PtoP*   Up
P3             Gi0/0/0/1    *PtoP*   Up

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis database verbose PE6.00-00 | include Locator
  SRv6 Locator:   MT (IPv6 Unicast) fcbb:bb01:6::/48 D:0 Metric: 1 Algorithm: 128
! before the fault: a second line, fcbb:bb00:6::/48, Algorithm: 0

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48
The requested route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 was not found in the IS-IS CORE IPv6 Unicast Routing Table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
% Network not in table
  • Now we read all five layers of fault 2. On PE6, the locator MAIN is removed from IS-IS.
  • Layer 1: the adjacencies are up. PE1 still has its neighbors P2 and P3.
  • Layer 2: the LSP of PE6 has lost the locator. Only the Flex-Algo locator remains. Before the fault, the LSP also had fcbb:bb00:6::/48 in algorithm 0.
  • Layer 3: SPF has no prefix to calculate. The IS-IS route table does not contain the route.
  • Layer 4: the RIB has no route. Layer 5 follows: CEF drops the service, as the previous page showed.
  • The fault started at layer 2, on the far router. When the locator is added back, the route returns with metric 31, and the ping succeeds.
8.12 · Fault 3: a filter on the way into the RIB
! PE1
ipv6 prefix-list BLOCK-PE6-LOCATOR
 10 deny fcbb:bb00:6::/48
 20 permit ::/0 le 128
!
router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  distribute-list prefix-list BLOCK-PE6-LOCATOR in
  • Fault 3 is the most difficult to see. On PE1, we add a filter between IS-IS and the RIB.
  • It is a prefix list. It denies only PE6's locator and permits all other prefixes.
  • We apply it with distribute-list in, under the IPv6 address family. It filters the routes that IS-IS installs. It does not stop the flooding of LSPs.
8.13 · Fault 3: the layers disagree
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis database verbose PE6.00-00 | include Locator
  SRv6 Locator:   MT (IPv6 Unicast) fcbb:bb00:6::/48 D:0 Metric: 1 Algorithm: 0

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [31/115]

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
% Network not in table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
      valid, internal, best, group-best
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: inaccessible

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 2
Success rate is 0 percent (0/2)
  • Now read the five layers on PE1, from top to bottom.
  • Layer 2: PE6's locator is in the LSP. The filter did not change the flooding.
  • Layer 3: IS-IS still calculates the route, with metric 31.
  • Layer 4: the RIB does not have it. Network not in table.
  • BGP keeps the customer path as best, with the locator inaccessible, as in Episode 3.
  • The customer has no service. Layers 2 and 3 say yes, and layer 4 says no. This difference shows that there is a filter.

Acceptance: Compare each result with its interpretation. Record missing checks as Not verified. Restore the stated baseline before another experiment.

Questions:

  1. Can an LSP contain a locator that the local RIB does not install?
  2. Which evidence distinguishes a missing advertisement from a local installation filter?

Next: Chapter 5. Keep the accepted state and observations before adding the next mechanism.

05

Build L3VPN: from BGP information to delivery

Experiment focus: Connect service information to delivery

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

The IPv6 underlay now works. PE1 must identify the remote customer service. PE6 must select the correct VRF when the packet arrives. RD, RT, and the service SID have different purposes in this sequence.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter reconstructs a service SID from BGP information. CEF and captures at both ends verify delivery.

Starting state: Follow BLUE in one direction first. Then examine the return path, RED, and customer isolation.

Three identifiers with different tasks

An RD makes a VPN prefix different in BGP. An RT controls route import into a VRF. A service SID selects an egress behavior and its service context.

The same customer address can exist in BLUE and RED. The RD keeps the BGP routes different. The RT and service SID must keep the correct customer context through delivery.

In the source design, BLUE uses RT 65000:100. RED uses RT 65000:200. BLUE RDs are 65000:101 on PE1 and 65000:106 on PE6.

Our route distinguishers

An RD only makes routes unique in BGP. It does not need to be the same on every PE. In this lab, each PE uses a different RD for the same VRF.

VRF RD on PE1 RD on PE6 Route target
BLUE 65000:101 65000:106 65000:100
RED 65000:201 65000:206 65000:200
GREEN 65000:301 65000:306 65000:300

The route target is the same on both PEs. Thus each VRF imports the routes of the other PE. The RD shows which PE sent the route.

Check this on PE1. The local VRF uses its own RD. The route from PE6 shows the RD of PE6 as its source.

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.99.0.6/32 detail
BGP routing table entry for 10.99.0.6/32, Route Distinguisher: 65000:101
      Received Label 0xe0040
      Extended community: RT:65000:100
      Source AFI: VPNv4 Unicast, Source VRF: default, Source Route Distinguisher: 65000:106

The first line shows the RD of BLUE on PE1: 65000:101. The last line shows the RD of PE6: 65000:106. The two values are different, and the route still imports into BLUE because the route target matches.

One service SID for each VRF and address family

With alloc mode per-vrf, BGP allocates one service SID for each VRF and each address family. BLUE has two SIDs: a uDT4 for IPv4 and a uDT6 for IPv6. One VRF does not mean one SID.

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 sid
fcbb:bb00:1:e004::   uDT4   'BLUE'   bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:1:e005::   uDT6   'BLUE'   bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:1:e006::   uDT6   'RED'    bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:1:e007::   uDT4   'RED'    bgp-65000

The function values e004 to e007 come from the dynamic range, in the order of allocation. PE6 has its own SIDs with different values. Do not write these values in your configuration. Read them from the router. Other allocation modes exist. We tested only per-VRF. The capacity chapter compares the modes.

The resolution chain

  1. The ingress VRF has the customer prefix.
  2. BGP supplies the RT and the remote service SID information.
  3. The ingress can resolve the service SID through a remote locator.
  4. The ingress CEF entry supplies the encapsulation action.
  5. The egress has the same service SID installed locally.
  6. The selected egress VRF has a route to the customer.
  7. The remote customer has a return path.

A BGP session in the Established state shows that the session operates. It does not prove all seven conditions. BGP next-hop resolution and SID locator resolution are different checks. The BGP next hop in this lab is the remote loopback, not the service SID.

Reconstruct the captured SID

The recorded VPNv4 update contains label value 917568. The hexadecimal value is 0xE0040. The transposition length is 16, and the offset is 48.

20-bit label value:  E0040
function:           E0040 >> 4 = E004
base SID:           fcbb:bb00:0006:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000
insert at bit 48:    fcbb:bb00:0006:e004:0000:0000:0000:0000
result:             fcbb:bb00:6:e004::

The Prefix-SID attribute supplies the base SID and the structure information. The label field supplies the transposed function bits. The receiver must have the two parts.

A label value of 917568 alone does not identify one global service. One more locator can use the same function. Different services can also use different transposition parameters. The right shift above applies only to the stated layout.

The 32/16/16/0 service structure does not contradict the 32/16/0/80 uN advertisement. One gives information about a service SID. The other gives information about a node behavior and its argument.

Configuration excerpt

This PE6 excerpt enables SRv6 allocation for BLUE IPv4. Before this step, the VRF, RT, BGP session, locator, and customer interface must be available.

router bgp 65000
 vrf BLUE
  rd 65000:106
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
    alloc mode per-vrf
   redistribute connected

The IPv6 address family must have its own configuration. The source implementation allocated different uDT4 and uDT6 SIDs. The function values depend on allocation sequence. Values such as e004 are recorded examples, not permanent assignments.

From CE-A to CE-B

For BLUE IPv4, PE1 receives a packet on the BLUE interface. PE1 adds an outer IPv6 header with the remote uDT4 destination. P2 and P4 forward through the PE6 locator. PE6 removes the outer header and uses BLUE for the inner lookup.

A recorded customer frame was 98 bytes. The related core frame was 138 bytes. The egress customer frame was 98 bytes again. Ordinary IP forwarding at the PEs can change the inner TTL.

The recorded outer Hop Limit started at 255. The inner DSCP was 46, but the outer Traffic Class was zero. The tested default did not copy the customer marking. A core queue that examines the outer header thus sees a different marking.

Worked example: Reconstruct and verify a service SID

The VPNv4 label is 917568, or 0xE0040. This example has transposition length 16 and offset 48. The chapter calculation gives function e004. Combine that function with the base SID information. The function alone does not identify a globally unique service.

Read the figures: F21 supplies the field structure. F22 shows ingress resolution. F23 shows the egress SID and customer route. Read them in this order.

Think first: The reconstructed SID is correct, but PE6 BLUE lacks a return route to CE-A. How can the forward capture and ping result differ?

Reason from the evidence: Why is a best BGP route not enough?

BGP marks the VPN route best. Its RT matches BLUE. The SID locator is inaccessible. Which part of delivery is still missing?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

BGP selected service information, but forwarding cannot reach its locator through ordinary routing. A selected route does not supply missing transport reachability.

Check the BGP next hop and SID locator separately. Then inspect CEF. If a policy supplies an explicit path, verify that path independently.

L5 — Prove service and isolation

Starting state: Start with the accepted IPv6 underlay. Configure BLUE and RED at both PEs and their CEs.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

Stage · Ep12 — Commands and results
12.1 · The VRF
vrf BLUE
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  import route-target
   65000:100
  export route-target
   65000:100
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  import route-target
   65000:100
  export route-target
   65000:100
  • This is VRF BLUE on PE1.
  • There is one VRF with the name BLUE.
  • For IPv4, it imports and exports route target 65000:100.
  • IPv6 is the same. RED uses 65000:200. In this lab, these values are examples. Compare them with your own numbering plan.
12.2 · The attachment
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
 description TO-CE BLUE
 vrf BLUE
 ipv4 address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:c:101::1/64
  • This is the attachment to CE-A.
  • First, the interface goes into VRF BLUE. Then it gets an address.
  • Then it gets an IPv4 and an IPv6 address. RED has its own port and its own addresses.
12.3 · BGP
router bgp 65000
 address-family vpnv4 unicast
 address-family vpnv6 unicast
 neighbor 2001:db8:100::6
  remote-as 65000
  update-source Loopback0
  address-family vpnv4 unicast
  address-family vpnv6 unicast
 vrf BLUE
  rd 65000:101
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
    alloc mode per-vrf
   redistribute connected
  • BGP connects all the parts.
  • One IPv6 session between the PE loopbacks carries VPNv4 and VPNv6. There is no IPv4 in this core.
  • Under the VRF, there is a route distinguisher: 65000:101 on PE1, and 65000:106 on PE6.
  • This is the SRv6 part. BGP allocates the service SID from locator MAIN, one for each VRF.
  • Redistribute connected advertises the CE subnet and the tenant loopback on the PE. In a real network, you also add static or eBGP routes to the CE.
12.4 · The service SIDs

Router / tool: PE1 and PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 sid
fcbb:bb00:1:e004::          uDT4              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:1:e005::          uDT6              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:1:e006::          uDT6              'RED'                             bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:1:e007::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 sid
fcbb:bb00:6:e004::          uDT4              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:6:e005::          uDT6              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:6:e006::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000
fcbb:bb01:6:e004::          uDT6              'RED'                             bgp-65000
  • These are the service SIDs on the two PEs.
  • On PE1, BLUE has a uDT4 and a uDT6. BGP owns both.
  • RED has its own pair. The function values, e004 to e007, come from the dynamic range, in the sequence of allocation.
  • PE6 has its own SIDs, with different values. On PE6, RED IPv6 is in the fcbb:bb01 block. This is the algorithm 128 setting from Episode 11. Do not write these values in your configuration. Read them.
12.5 · BGP and the VRF table
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast summary
Neighbor        Spk    AS MsgRcvd MsgSent       TblVer  InQ OutQ  Up/Down  St/PfxRcd
2001:db8:100::6   0 65000      31      21           70    0    0 00:02:51          5

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route vrf BLUE
C    10.1.1.0/24 is directly connected, 00:05:38, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
L    10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, 00:05:38, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
B    10.1.6.0/24 [200/0] via 2001:db8:100::6 (nexthop in vrf default), 00:01:13
L    10.100.1.1/32 is directly connected, 00:05:43, Loopback101
B    10.100.6.6/32 [200/0] via 2001:db8:100::6 (nexthop in vrf default), 00:01:13
  • Now the control plane.
  • The VPNv4 session to PE6 is up. It received five prefixes. The VPNv6 session shows four.
  • VRF BLUE on PE1 has the local CE subnet and the tenant loopback.
  • It also has two BGP routes from PE6. Their next hop is in the default table: PE6's loopback. The router resolves this next hop through PE6's locator and service SID. Episode 13 follows this chain step by step.
12.6 · Tests from CE-A

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.2.1.2 10.2.6.2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 2001:db8:c:106::2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 2001:db8:c:206::2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -W 1 -I 10.1.1.2 10.2.6.2
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss
  • Now the important tests, from the customer side. On CE-A, the option -I sets the source address, and the source address selects the BLUE or RED port.
  • BLUE IPv4, site to site: both packets are answered.
  • RED IPv4: both packets are answered.
  • BLUE and RED IPv6: the pings are successful.
  • Now the negative test: from a BLUE source to a RED address, there is no reply. A test of reachability only is half a test. Always prove the isolation too.
12.7 · Experiment: the same address in both customers
! PE6
interface Loopback199
 description BLUE overlap test
 vrf BLUE
 ipv4 address 10.99.0.6 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback299
 description RED overlap test
 vrf RED
 ipv4 address 10.99.0.6 255.255.255.255
  • Customers do not plan their addresses together. Thus we give the two customers the same address on PE6, on purpose.
  • 10.99.0.6 in BLUE.
  • 10.99.0.6 in RED. The same router has the same address two times.
12.8 · Two routes for one address
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.99.0.6/32 detail
      Received Label 0xe0040
      Extended community: RT:65000:100
      Source Route Distinguisher: 65000:106

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf RED 10.99.0.6/32 detail
      Received Label 0xe0060
      Extended community: RT:65000:200
      Source Route Distinguisher: 65000:206
  • How does BGP keep them separate?
  • The BLUE route arrived with PE6's BLUE route distinguisher. The RED route arrived with RED's. Thus BGP has two different routes.
  • Each route has its own route target. Each VRF on PE1 imports only its own route.
  • Each route has a different service SID function: e004 for BLUE and e006 for RED. They are in the label field, as Episode 3 showed.
12.9 · One address, two destinations

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.1.1.2 10.99.0.6
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.2.1.2 10.99.0.6
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss

# outer destination on PE1 to P2, from the capture
from 10.1.1.2, BLUE   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::
from 10.2.1.2, RED    fcbb:bb00:6:e006::
  • Now the wire. CE-A pings the same address, 10.99.0.6, with two different source addresses.
  • From its BLUE address, the ping is answered by the BLUE loopback.
  • From its RED address, the ping is answered by the RED loopback.
  • In the capture, PE1 sends the BLUE packet to PE6's BLUE service SID, e004. It sends the RED packet to the RED service SID, e006. The same address, two customers and two SIDs: the router does not mix them up.
12.10 · Experiment: forget one import
! PE1
vrf BLUE
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  no import route-target 65000:100
  • One more test shows the function of route targets. On PE1, we remove only BLUE's IPv4 import route target. The export and IPv6 do not change.
  • Before the next page, predict what fails, and in which direction.

2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
  • These are the results from the two ends, after we removed the import of 65000:100 for BLUE IPv4 on PE1.
  • PE1's BLUE table lost all the IPv4 routes from PE6. Only the local routes are there.
  • BGP has no path for CE-B's subnet. PE1 did not keep PE6's route, because no VRF on PE1 imported that route target.
  • PE6 does not know about the problem. It still has PE1's routes, because PE1 still exports them. The VPN is broken in one direction only.
  • BLUE IPv4 pings fail.
  • But BLUE IPv6 still works, because we did not change the IPv6 import. When we restored the line, all the routes came back in some seconds.
  • When one address family of one customer fails, first examine the route targets of that address family on the two ends.

13.10 · TTL, hop limit and DSCP

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo traceroute -n -t 184 -s 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2 -w 1 -q 1 -m 5
 1  10.1.1.1
 2  10.46.0.1
 3  10.1.6.2

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "ip.dst == 10.1.6.2 and udp" -T fields \
    -e frame.len -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.hlim -e ipv6.tclass -e ip.dsfield.dscp -e ip.ttl
# CE-A to PE1   60                                 DSCP 46   TTL 1, 2, 3
# PE1 to P2    100   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::   hop limit 255   tclass 0x0   DSCP 46   TTL 1, 2
# P4 to PE6    100   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::   hop limit 253   tclass 0x0   DSCP 46   TTL 1, 2
  • Two header fields are important: the hop limit and the quality of service marking. We send traceroute probes from CE-A, with the DSCP mark EF, which is 46.
  • The traceroute shows PE1, then PE6, then CE-B. The customer cannot see P2 and P4. RFC 2983 calls this the pipe model.
  • On the access link, the probes have DSCP 46 and the TTL 1, 2 and 3.
  • In the core, PE1 sets the outer hop limit to 255. It does not copy the customer TTL. P2 and P4 decrease only the outer hop limit: it is 253 at PE6.
  • The inner TTL did not change. The inner DSCP is still 46, but the outer traffic class is 0. A core router that queues on the outer header sends this traffic as best effort.
  • On this platform, the traffic class propagation is configurable, as the manager showed in Episode 2. If your core queues on the outer header, configure it, and verify it with a capture.
