06

Understand encapsulation: SRH, MTU, and fragmentation

Experiment focus: Calculate at the correct packet boundary

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

Chapter 5 established the customer service. Now compare the same customer data under different encapsulations. Identify each added or removed header. Distinguish IP packet size from Ethernet frame size before you calculate an MTU limit.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter calculates L3VPN limits with and without an SRH. It separates forwarding limits, reported MTUs, and source responses.

Starting state: Use the working L3VPN for L6. Complete Chapter 7 before the VPWS size tests.

When the SRH is necessary

H.Encaps.Red adds an outer IPv6 header. In the single-container examples, the destination contains all necessary instructions. No SRH is necessary for those examples.

An SRH can carry more containers. The destination can have insufficient space for the instructions. A change of block also makes an SRH necessary in this example. Optional information can also affect the header layout.

In reduced encapsulation, the initial segment is in the IPv6 destination. The SRH contains the remaining segment entries. The SRH stores the segment list in reverse processing sequence.

For an SRH without TLVs, its size is 8 + 16 × N bytes. Here, N is the number of stored 128-bit entries. Each entry can itself contain compressed instructions.

The two-block example

PE1 uses path instructions from fcbb:bb01 and a service SID from fcbb:bb00. The destination initially contains fcbb:bb01:3:5::. One SRH entry contains the PE6 service SID.

Location Destination Segments Left SRH size
PE1 to P3 fcbb:bb01:3:5:: 1 24 bytes
After P3 fcbb:bb01:5:: 1 24 bytes
After P5 PE6 service SID Not present 0 bytes

P3 advances in the destination container. Thus, Segments Left does not change there. At P5, the next container comes from the SRH. PSP then removes the SRH.

In the recorded test, the customer frame was 118 bytes. The first core frame was 182 bytes. After PSP, the core frame was 158 bytes. These are frame sizes without FCS, not customer IP sizes.

The IPv6 Next Header field is 43 when a routing header follows. The SRH Routing Type is 4. Its Next Header identifies the payload, such as 41 for IPv6.

For the 24-byte SRH, Hdr Ext Len is 2. The field counts 8-byte units after the first 8 bytes.

Calculate before the size test

Let M be the available core IPv6 MTU. Let H be the actual SRH size. These examples exclude more extension headers and VLAN tags.

Service Maximum customer IP size With M = 1500
L3VPN without SRH M − 40 1460
L3VPN with one SRH entry M − 40 − 24 1436
VPWS without SRH M − 40 − 14 1446

For VPWS, the inner Ethernet header consumes 14 bytes. The outer link Ethernet header is outside the IPv6 MTU. A 9000-byte core IPv6 MTU gives 8936 bytes for the second case.

Linux ping -s usually specifies ICMP data bytes. Add 28 bytes for IPv4 or 48 bytes for IPv6 without options. IOS XR ping size specifies the complete IP packet in this laboratory.

PMTUD can fail differently

The lab recorded three different L3 results:

Condition Observation
IPv4 with DF at ingress 1460 passed. 1461 failed without an recorded ICMP response.
IPv6 with one SRH entry 1436 passed. 1437 caused a PTB with reported MTU 1436.
IPv4 through a 1300-byte core link 1260 passed. 1261 caused ICMPv4 fragmentation needed, with reported MTU 1236.

In the third case, the ICMP message followed the service path before it returned to the source. The source subsequently used smaller fragments. Other implementations can process the error differently.

A different investigation found the condition for the 64-byte reporting difference. On the two tested virtual platforms, a destination with an installed TI-LFA repair path caused the lower PTB value. With egress IPv6 MTU 1400, the report was 1336. Actual forwarding accepted 1400-byte packets.

With no backup, or with a plain LFA backup, the report matched the configured MTU. Enabling TI-LFA alone did not show the condition. The installed repair type mattered.

The idea that the router reserves repair-header space stays an inference. The numerical equality 64 = 40 + 24 does not prove the internal cause. This result is not a universal rule for SRv6 MTU calculations.

Worked example: Test the size boundary

The core IPv6 MTU is 1500 bytes. The outer IPv6 header uses 40 bytes. An SRH with one stored entry uses 24 bytes. The customer limit is 1500 − 40 − 24 = 1436 bytes. Test 1436, then 1437, to change only the boundary condition.

Read the figures: Use F13 to check the SRH fields and F14 to compare frame sizes around PSP. F16 compares the limit and the larger packet. A smaller reported MTU does not by itself prove a smaller forwarding limit.

Think first: A core Ethernet frame measures 182 bytes. Can this value be subtracted directly from the IPv6 MTU to find the remaining capacity?

Reason from the evidence: Where did the extra bytes come from?

Compare one service SID with a policy that needs one SRH entry. The inner packet stays unchanged. What changes in the core size?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

The outer IPv6 header adds 40 bytes. A one-entry SRH adds 24 more bytes: eight fixed bytes and one 16-byte entry.

At core MTU 1500, the calculated inner IP limits are 1460 and 1436. Confirm the actual SRH before choosing a size test.

L6 — Find the actual limit

Starting state: Start with working BLUE IPv4 and IPv6. Use the stated policy and MTU for each case.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

6.2 · Configure the policy on PE1
! PE1 (trimmed)
segment-routing

    sid-format usid-f3216

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing traffic-eng policy color 300 detail
Color: 300, End-point: 2001:db8:100::6
    Admin: up  Operational: up

6.5 · What PE1 programs
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf BLUE ipv6 2001:db8:c:106::/64 detail
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e005::}
      SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb01:3:5::}
  • Now the forwarding entry for the BLUE destination. It has two important lines.
  • Line 1: H.Encaps.Red to PE6's service SID, e005. This is the VPN part. PE1 encapsulates the customer packet and sends it to the BLUE service on PE6.
  • Line 2: H.Insert.Red with the path container fcbb:bb01:3:5::. This is the policy. PE1 inserts the path in front of the service SID.
  • The third SID of the policy, PE6's node SID, is not there. The service SID already ends at PE6, so the router does not use it.
6.6 · The SRH, field by field

Router / tool: capture

$ tshark -r c300-PE1-P3.pcap -Y "ipv6.nxt == 43" -V     (first packet, trimmed)
Internet Protocol Version 6, Src: 2001:db8:100::1, Dst: fcbb:bb01:3:5::
    Payload Length: 128
    Next Header: Routing Header for IPv6 (43)
    Hop Limit: 255
    Routing Header for IPv6 (Segment Routing)
        Next Header: IPv6 (41)
        Length: 2
        [Length: 24 bytes]
        Type: Segment Routing (4)
        Segments Left: 1
        Last Entry: 0
        Address[0]: fcbb:bb00:6:e005::
Internet Protocol Version 6, Src: 2001:db8:c:101:5054:ff:fe0b:8f87, Dst: 2001:db8:c:106::2
  • Now we decode one of the 182-byte packets from the capture of the PE1 to P3 link. We use tshark with the verbose option.
  • The outer destination is the path container: P3, then P5, in the Flex-Algo block. Next header 43 means that a routing header follows.
  • This is the SRH. Type 4 means segment routing. Its next header is 41, an IPv6 packet: the customer packet. Its length is 24 bytes.
  • It has one entry: the service SID. Segments Left is 1. One more SID is in the list after the current destination.
  • Then there is the customer IPv6 header, with no change.
6.7 · Segments Left along the path

Router / tool: tcpdump

$ tcpdump -nn -t -v -r <capture file> 'ip6[6] == 43 or ip6[6] == 41'   (first packet, trimmed)
# PE1 to P3, 182 bytes
IP6 (hlim 255, next-header Routing (43)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb01:3:5::: RT6 (segleft=1, [0]fcbb:bb00:6:e005::)
# P3 to P5, 182 bytes
IP6 (hlim 254, next-header Routing (43)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb01:5::: RT6 (segleft=1, [0]fcbb:bb00:6:e005::)
# P5 to P4, 158 bytes
IP6 (hlim 253, next-header IPv6 (41)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005:::
# P4 to PE6, 158 bytes
IP6 (hlim 252, next-header IPv6 (41)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005:::
  • Follow the Segments Left field on the path. We read the capture of each link with tcpdump. The RT6 part is the routing header.
  • When the packet leaves PE1, the destination is the container fcbb:bb01:3:5::. Segments Left is 1, and the entry is the service SID of PE6.
  • After P3, the destination has shifted to fcbb:bb01:5::, and Segments Left is still 1. A shift in a container does not change the SRH.
  • At P5, the container has no more micro-SIDs. P5 decreases Segments Left to zero, and it copies the next SID into the destination. P5 is the penultimate endpoint, thus it also removes the SRH.
  • The next header is now 41, and the frame is 24 bytes smaller. This is step 2 of the procedure from Episode 4, on the wire.
6.8 · The BLUE packet, measured

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmpv6.type == 128 and icmpv6.echo.sequence_number == 0" -T fields -e frame.len
link                   small  large  what is added
CE-A to PE1            118    1062   nothing: the customer packet
PE1 to P3, P3 to P5    182    1126   + 40 outer IPv6 + 24 SRH = 64
P5 to P4, P4 to PE6    158    1102   + 40 outer IPv6 only
  • Now we count each byte. For each capture file, tshark prints the frame length of the echo requests. The small ping and the large ping give two values.
  • On the access link, the frames are 118 and 1062 bytes. This is the customer packet.
  • From PE1 to P5, each frame is 64 bytes larger: 40 for the outer IPv6 header and 24 for the SRH.
  • After P5, each frame is only 40 bytes larger. P5 was the penultimate endpoint, and PSP removed the SRH, as Episode 4 showed.
  • Thus the overhead of the same flow changes on the path: 64 bytes in the first part, 40 bytes in the second part.
6.9 · Why our lab never shows 1596
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 manager
  Headend behaviors:
    T
    H.Insert.Red
    H.Encaps.Red
    H.Encaps.L2.Red
  Signaled parameters:
    Max-H-Insert    : 3 sids
    Max-H-Encap     : 3 sids
  • Our captures do not show a 1596-byte packet. This is the reason.
  • This headend has only the reduced forms. There is no plain H.Encaps, so the first SID is never in the SRH also. In this lab, the 1596 case is only a calculation.
  • It can insert or encapsulate a maximum of 3 SIDs. Each SID can be a full container of micro-SIDs. Thus 3 is a limit on containers, not on instructions.
Stage · Ep07 — Commands and results
7.1 · Case 1: what PE1 programs
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf RED 10.2.6.0/24 detail | include SID-list
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e006::}
      SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:e004::}
  • Case 1 uses IPv4 in VRF RED. First, we check what PE1 programs for the RED prefix 10.2.6.0/24.
  • The service SID is fcbb:bb00:6:e006::. It is the uDT4 of RED on PE6.
  • The path is one container, fcbb:bb00:e004::. PE1 inserts it in front of the service SID.
  • Each list has one SID, so the packet has no routing header. The overhead is 40 bytes, and the limit is 1460.
7.2 · Case 1: the pings

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 1 -I 10.2.1.2 -s 1432 10.2.6.2
1440 bytes from 10.2.6.2: seq=0 ttl=62 time=1.495 ms
1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 -I 10.2.1.2 -s 1433 10.2.6.2
3 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss

CE-A:~$ sudo cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_no_pmtu_disc
0
  • Now CE-A sends IPv4 pings to the RED far side. The option -s is the data size, and -I sets the source address.
  • A data size of 1432 makes a 1460-byte IPv4 packet. This is the limit, and the reply returns.
  • A data size of 1433 makes a 1461-byte packet. All three pings are lost. The packet loss is 100 percent.
  • The Linux host sets the don't-fragment bit, because this kernel setting is 0.
7.3 · Case 1: the captures

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y icmp
# PE1 to CE-A, the 1460-byte ping
1474 bytes  10.2.1.2 > 10.2.6.2  echo request
1474 bytes  10.2.6.2 > 10.2.1.2  echo reply
# PE1 to CE-A, the 1461-byte ping
1475 bytes  10.2.1.2 > 10.2.6.2  echo request   (no reply follows)
# PE1 to P3, the 1460-byte ping
1514 bytes  10.2.1.2 > 10.2.6.2  echo request, inside the outer IPv6 header
# PE1 to P2, PE1 to P3, P4 to PE6, P5 to PE6, the 1461-byte ping
no echo request on any core link
  • We captured on the access link and on the core links, and we read each file with tshark. The frame length includes 14 bytes of Ethernet header.
  • On the access link, the 1460-byte packet is a 1474-byte frame. The reply returns.
  • The 1461-byte packet is a 1475-byte frame. It arrives at PE1, and no reply follows.
  • The 1460-byte packet crosses the core in a 1514-byte frame. This is the largest frame that the link carries.
  • For the 1461-byte packet, no core link carries an echo request. PE1 dropped it before the encapsulation.
7.4 · Case 2: the pings

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 1 -s 1388 2001:db8:c:106::2
1396 bytes from 2001:db8:c:106::2: seq=0 ttl=62 time=1.545 ms
1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -s 1389 2001:db8:c:106::2
1397 bytes from 2001:db8:c:106::2: seq=1 ttl=62 time=1.566 ms
2 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 50% packet loss
  • Case 2 uses IPv6 in VRF BLUE, through colour 300. The limit is 1436. Linux ping6 adds 48 bytes to the data size.
  • A data size of 1388 makes a 1436-byte packet. The reply returns.
  • A data size of 1389 makes a 1437-byte packet. The first packet is lost, and the second packet gets a reply. The loss is 50 percent.
7.5 · Case 2: the captures

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r B-PE1-CE-A.pcap -Y icmpv6      (CE-A is 2001:db8:c:101:5054:ff:fe0b:8f87)
1450 bytes  CE-A > 2001:db8:c:106::2  echo request, seq 0
1450 bytes  2001:db8:c:106::2 > CE-A  echo reply, seq 0
1451 bytes  CE-A > 2001:db8:c:106::2  echo request, the 1437-byte packet
1294 bytes  2001:db8:100::1 > CE-A    Packet Too Big, MTU 1436
1446 and 75 bytes  CE-A > 2001:db8:c:106::2  the second request, in two fragments
1451 bytes  2001:db8:c:106::2 > CE-A  echo reply, seq 1
  • On the access link, we read the packets with tshark. CE-A is the address that the first line shows.
  • The 1436-byte packet is a 1450-byte frame. The request and the reply both pass.
  • The 1437-byte packet is a 1451-byte frame. This is the first try.
  • PE1 answers with an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big. The source is the loopback of PE1. The MTU is 1436, which is our budget.
  • CE-A sends the second request in two fragments, and the reply returns. IPv6 path MTU discovery worked.
7.6 · Case 2: the long way home

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y icmpv6.type==2      (outer header, trimmed)
# PE1 to P2, 1358 bytes
2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005::   hop limit 255   Packet Too Big, toward PE6
# P4 to PE6, 1358 bytes
2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005::   hop limit 253   the same message
# P4 to PE6, 1334 bytes
2001:db8:100::6 > fcbb:bb00:1:e006::   hop limit 255   the message, back toward PE1
# PE1 to P2, 1334 bytes
2001:db8:100::6 > fcbb:bb00:1:e006::   hop limit 253   the same message
# PE1 to CE-A, 1294 bytes
2001:db8:100::1 > CE-A   Packet Too Big, delivered
  • Now look at the path of that Packet Too Big. PE1 made it for a host on its own access link. You expect it to go directly to the host. It did not.
  • PE1 encapsulated it to the BLUE service SID of PE6, and it left PE1 toward P2.
  • The same message crosses the core and arrives on the link P4 to PE6. The hop limit is 253.
  • PE6 decapsulated it, looked up CE-A's address in BLUE, and sent it back to the service SID of PE1.
  • It crosses the core again, and it arrives on the link PE1 to P2.
  • Then PE1 sent it to CE-A. It worked, but it went through the core two times. We did not verify why the ingress makes the message this way. It probably depends on the platform.
7.7 · Case 3: a smaller link in the middle
! P4, the link toward P2
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
 ipv6 mtu 1300
!
! RED traffic from CE-B to CE-A crosses P4 to P2
! inner 1260 + outer 40 = 1300   fits
! inner 1261 + outer 40 = 1301   does not fit
  • Case 3. The ingress has no problem, but a link in the middle is too small. On P4, we set the IPv6 MTU to P2 to 1300.
  • This time, the traffic goes in the opposite direction, from CE-B to CE-A in RED. That direction uses the upper path through P4 and P2.
  • An inner packet of 1260 bytes becomes 1300 bytes. It fits.
  • At 1261 bytes, it does not fit, and P4 must decide what to do. P4 is a P router. It has no VRF, and it does not know CE-B.
7.8 · Case 3: the pings

Router / tool: CE-B

CE-B:~$ sudo ping -c 1 -I 10.2.6.2 -s 1232 10.2.1.2
1240 bytes from 10.2.1.2: seq=0 ttl=62 time=1.796 ms
1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

CE-B:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.2.6.2 -s 1233 10.2.1.2
1241 bytes from 10.2.1.2: seq=1 ttl=62 time=1.558 ms
2 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 50% packet loss
  • Now CE-B sends IPv4 pings to CE-A in RED. This direction crosses P4 and P2.
  • A data size of 1232 makes a 1260-byte packet. It fits, and the reply returns.
  • A data size of 1233 makes a 1261-byte packet. The first packet is lost. The second packet gets a reply. The loss is 50 percent.
7.9 · Case 3: the captures

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r C-PE6-Gi0_0_0_3-CE-B.pcap -Y icmp      (PE6 to CE-B)
1275 bytes  10.2.6.2 > 10.2.1.2  echo request, the 1261-byte packet
110 bytes   10.0.0.4 > 10.2.6.2  destination unreachable, fragmentation needed, MTU 1236
1250 and 59 bytes  10.2.6.2 > 10.2.1.2  the second request, in two fragments
1275 bytes  10.2.1.2 > 10.2.6.2  echo reply

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y icmp.type==3      (the error in the core, outer header)
P2 to P4   190 bytes  2001:db8:100::6 > fcbb:bb00:1:e005::  hop limit 254
PE1 to P2  190 bytes  2001:db8:100::6 > fcbb:bb00:1:e005::  hop limit 253
P4 to PE6  150 bytes  2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e006::  hop limit 252
  • We captured on five links, and we read the files with tshark. First, the access link of CE-B, on PE6.
  • The 1261-byte request leaves CE-B. This is the first try.
  • An ICMPv4 error comes back to CE-B: fragmentation needed, with an MTU of 1236. Its source is 10.0.0.4, the IPv4 loopback of P4.
  • Now the core. P4 sent the error in the same outer header as the dropped packet. It goes from P4 through P2 toward PE1, to the service SID of PE1.
  • PE1 decapsulated it, found CE-B in RED, and sent it back through the core to the service SID of PE6.
  • CE-B learns the MTU, and it sends the second request in two fragments, 1250 and 59 bytes. The reply returns.

Acceptance: Compare each result with its interpretation. Record missing checks as Not verified. Restore the stated baseline before another experiment.

Questions:

  1. What is the L3VPN limit with a 1500-byte core MTU and two stored SRH entries?
  2. Does a PTB value of 1336 prove that a 1400-byte packet cannot pass?

07

EVPN: a frame instead of an IP packet

Experiment focus: Deliver Ethernet instead of IP

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

The L3VPN egress selects a customer IP routing table. The VPWS egress delivers an Ethernet frame to an attachment circuit. Both services can use IPv6 transport, but their final actions and size overhead differ.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter uses uDX2, Next Header, and CE captures to explain VPWS delivery.

Starting state: Save the initial test-port configuration. The VPWS and boundary ACL experiments use different states of the same port.

The service determines the final action

An L3VPN service selects an IP table after decapsulation. A VPWS service delivers an Ethernet frame to a specified attachment circuit. The core can use the same IPv6 transport for the two services.

In the recorded VPWS, BGP EVPN route type 1 carries the service information. The Prefix-SID attribute includes the SRv6 L2 Service TLV. The egress uses uDX2.

The core packet has outer Next Header 143, which identifies Ethernet. A customer ARP broadcast also travels to the one remote PE. This point-to-point service does not use a remote MAC lookup to select a PE.

How e0070 and e00700 encode the same function

The label field in the BGP EVPN update has 24 bits. XR displays the complete 24-bit field. Wireshark displays its high-order 20 bits as a label. SRv6 uses these bits for transposition.

PE6 update, frame 226:   MPLS Label 1: 917616      (decimal)
                         917616 = 0xE0070          (20 bits)
XR on PE1 displays:      Received Label 0xe00700   (24 bits)
                         0xE0070 followed by 4 zero bits = 0xE00700
SID function:            first 16 bits of the field = e007
Prefix-SID structure:    transposition offset 48, length 16
Rebuilt SID:             fcbb:bb00:6:e007::

The numbers are not numerically equal: 0xE00700 equals 16 × 0xE0070. Both displays preserve the same high-order function bits. Use 0xE00700 >> 8 or 0xE0070 >> 4. Both calculations give 0xE007. The field layout determines the shift. PE1 gives 917680 = 0xE00B0 in the same way, and its SID is fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::.

Build the correct port role

PE1 port Gi0/0/0/4 has two different roles in the lab. It is a VPWS attachment circuit during Episode 14. It is an untrusted routed port during Episode 19.

These roles cannot use the same final port configuration simultaneously. For the L2 experiment, the port must have no routed address or ingress IPv6 ACL. For the subsequent boundary experiment, restore the routed state.

The source VPWS configuration includes this service block:

l2vpn
 xconnect group SRV6-VPWS
  p2p ELINE-300
   interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4
   neighbor evpn evi 300 service 300 segment-routing srv6

The complete service also needs l2transport, EVPN SRv6 allocation, and the BGP EVPN address family. This block alone is not a complete service configuration.

Size and fragmentation

The core IPv6 packet contains the complete customer Ethernet frame. With no SRH, the additional budget over customer IP is 54 bytes. This budget includes 40 IPv6 bytes and 14 inner Ethernet bytes.

The recorded 1500-byte core MTU let a 1446-byte customer IP packet go through. At 1447 bytes, PE1 produced outer IPv6 fragments. The far PE did not deliver the customer frame, and the CE received no error.

Thus, a small correct ping cannot show VPWS MTU acceptance. Customer PMTUD can also fail because the outer error terminates at a PE. The actual encapsulation determines the necessary core MTU.

E-LAN: the unmeasured part

E-LAN provides a multipoint bridge service. For known unicast, a destination MAC association is necessary. BUM traffic includes broadcast, unknown unicast, and multicast.

The experiment record describes uDT2U for known unicast and uDT2M for BUM delivery. EVPN route type 2 supplies MAC information. Route type 3 supplies inclusive multicast information. Ingress replication is one possible BUM transport method.

The two tested virtual platforms rejected the bridge domain configuration. The experiment record thus provides no correct E-LAN output. A listed uDT2U or uDT2M capability did not overcome that restriction.

A feature in the capability list is not a supported feature. On our XRv9000, the list shows uDT2U and uDT2M. The commit of a bridge domain still failed:

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1(config)#l2vpn bridge group SRV6-ELAN bridge-domain BD400 evi 400 segment-routing srv6
!!% Invalid argument: VPLS Bridge domains not supported on this platform

This restriction applies to the tested virtual router platforms. On a real network, the support depends on your hardware. Always commit the configuration, and send a packet.

Worked example: Account for the inner Ethernet header

Without an SRH, L3VPN adds a 40-byte outer IPv6 header. VPWS also carries the 14-byte customer Ethernet header. With a 1500-byte core IPv6 MTU, the customer IP limit is 1500 − 40 − 14 = 1446 bytes.

Read the figures: F25 shows cross-connect state. F26 compares 1446 and 1447 bytes. F27 locates the delivery failure after fragmentation. Service state and size acceptance are different checks.

Think first: ARP passes, but a large IPv4 packet fails. Why is this insufficient evidence of a missing EVPN route?

Reason from the evidence: Why does the L3VPN size test fail on VPWS?

A 1460-byte IP packet fits the simple L3VPN encapsulation. Does the same packet fit VPWS on a 1500-byte IPv6 core?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

No. VPWS also carries the inner Ethernet header. Without VLAN tags or SRH, 1460 + 14 + 40 equals 1514.

Compare the same measurement boundary. The corresponding calculated IP limit is 1446. Test delivery after fragmentation; fragment creation alone does not prove reassembly.

L7 — Accept VPWS separately

Starting state: Start with the working underlay. Save the routed configuration of both test ports before assigning the L2 role.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

Stage · Ep14 — Commands and results
14.1 · The configuration on PE1
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4
 description TO-CE L2 attachment circuit
 l2transport
!
l2vpn
 xconnect group SRV6-VPWS
  p2p ELINE-300
   interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4
   neighbor evpn evi 300 service 300 segment-routing srv6
!
evpn
 segment-routing srv6
  locator MAIN
  • This is all the configuration on PE1. PE6 has the same configuration, in the opposite direction. The BGP sessions already carry the Layer 2 VPN EVPN family.
  • The customer port becomes a Layer 2 transport port. It has no IP address. PE1 does not route on this port.
  • A point-to-point cross-connect connects the port to one remote service.
  • This is EVPN instance 300, service 300, over SRv6. The service number must be the same on the two PEs.
  • EVPN allocates its SIDs from locator MAIN. We did not configure route targets. EVPN made 65000:300 from the AS number and the instance.
14.2 · Route type 1 on the wire, part 1

Router / tool: capture

Border Gateway Protocol - UPDATE Message
    Path Attribute - MP_REACH_NLRI
        Address family identifier (AFI): Layer-2 VPN (25)
        Subsequent address family identifier (SAFI): EVPN (70)
        Next hop: 2001:db8:100::1
        EVPN NLRI: Ethernet AD Route
            Route Type: Ethernet AD Route (1)
            Route Distinguisher: 10.0.0.1:300
            ESI: 00:00:00:00:00:00:00:00:00:00
            Ethernet Tag ID: 300
            MPLS Label 1: 917680
    Path Attribute - EXTENDED_COMMUNITIES
        EVPN Layer 2 Attributes: flags: 0x0002, L2 MTU: 0
        Route Target: 65000:300
  • We captured on the core link of PE1 during the commit. In less than two seconds, PE1 sent this update.
  • The family is Layer 2 VPN EVPN. The next hop is the loopback of PE1.
  • The route is type 1, Ethernet auto-discovery. PE1 made the route distinguisher from its router ID and the instance.
  • The Ethernet segment identifier is zero, because the CE connects to one PE only. The Ethernet tag is 300, the service number. The remote PE uses it to match the two ends.
  • There is a label field again: 917680.
  • There are two extended communities. The first is Layer 2 attributes, with MTU zero. Zero means: do not check. The second is the route target.
14.3 · Route type 1 on the wire, part 2

Router / tool: capture

    Path Attribute - BGP Prefix-SID
        SRv6 L2 Service
            Type: SRv6 L2 Service (6)
            SRv6 Service Sub-TLV - SRv6 SID Information
                SRv6 SID Value: fcbb:bb00:1::
                SRv6 Endpoint Behavior: End.DX2 with NEXT-CSID (0x0041)
                SRv6 SID Structure
                    Locator Block Length: 32
                    Locator Node Length: 16
                    Function Length: 16
                    Argument Length: 0
                    Transposition Length: 16
                    Transposition Offset: 48
  • Part 2 has the same Prefix-SID attribute as in Episode 13, with one difference.
  • The TLV is SRv6 L2 Service, type 6. In Episode 13, it was L3 Service, type 5.
  • The SID value is the locator of PE1. The behavior is End.DX2 with NEXT-CSID, code 65. On IOS XR, this is uDX2: remove the outer header and send the frame out of one port.
  • The transposition is the same: 16 bits at offset 48. Thus the function is in the label field again.
14.4 · The cross-connect is up
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show l2vpn xconnect detail
Group SRV6-VPWS, XC ELINE-300, state is up; Interworking none
  AC: GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4, state is up
    MTU 1500; XC ID 0x2; interworking none
  EVPN: PW ID: evi 300, ac-id 300, state is up ( established )
    Encapsulation SRv6
      SRv6              Local                        Remote
      uDX2              fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::           fcbb:bb00:6:e007::
      AC ID             300                          300
      MTU               1514                         0
      Locator Resolved  Yes                          N/A
      SRv6 Headend      H.Encaps.L2.Red              N/A
  • Now the state on PE1.
  • The cross-connect is up. The customer port is also up.
  • The EVPN side is up. The local SID is e00b and the remote SID is e007. These are the SIDs that we built from the capture.
  • The service is 300 on the two ends. PE6 advertised MTU zero, thus there is no MTU check. Remember this. It is important later.
  • The headend behavior is H.Encaps.L2.Red: encapsulate a Layer 2 frame, reduced form.
14.5 · BGP and CEF on PE1
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp l2vpn evpn rd 10.0.0.6:300 [1][0000.0000.0000.0000.0000][300]/120 detail
    2001:db8:100::6 (metric 30) from 2001:db8:100::6 (10.0.0.6)
      Received Label 0xe00700
      Extended community: EVPN L2 ATTRS:0x02:0 RT:65000:300
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: 31
        T:1(Sid information), Sid:fcbb:bb00:6::(Transposed), Behavior:65

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::/64 detail
fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::/64, version 243, SRv6 Endpoint uDX2
   via ::/128, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4, 2 dependencies, weight 0, class 0
    AC Interface: Gi0/0/0/4
    XConnect ID: 0x2
  • This is the same chain as for Layer 3, but the last step is different.
  • PE1 received the type 1 route of PE6. The label shows in its three-byte form.
  • This is the locator check, metric 31, and behavior 65. If the locator of PE6 is not reachable, this service fails. It is the same as fault A in Episode 3.
  • This is the SID of PE1 in CEF. For uDT4, the action was a lookup in a VRF. For uDX2, there is no lookup. The action is a port, Gi0/0/0/4.
14.6 · From CE-A

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ip neigh flush dev eth2
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 172.16.30.6
64 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=0 ttl=64 time=2.686 ms
64 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=1 ttl=64 time=1.449 ms
64 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=2 ttl=64 time=1.362 ms
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 3 2001:db8:30::6
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ip neigh show dev eth2
172.16.30.6 lladdr 52:54:00:34:24:24 ref 1 used 0/0/0 probes 4 REACHABLE
2001:db8:30::6 lladdr 52:54:00:34:24:24 ref 1 used 0/0/0 probes 4 REACHABLE
  • Now we send traffic. First, we clear the neighbor table on CE-A. Then ARP must also go through the service.
  • The table is empty.
  • The IPv4 ping to CE-B gets three replies, with TTL 64. No router decreased it. For the customer, there is no router between the two CEs.
  • IPv6 also operates. The PEs have no IPv6 configuration for this service.
  • This shows that the service is Layer 2. CE-A learned the MAC address of CE-B, which ends in 24:24. In a Layer 3 VPN, CE-A learns only the MAC address of PE1.
14.7 · The frames, captured at three points

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "arp or icmp or ipv6.nxt == 143" -T fields \
    -e frame.len -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.nxt -e ipv6.hlim
# CE-A to PE1
  42                                      ARP request
  60                                      ARP reply
  98                                      echo request
# PE1 to P2
 114   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   143   255     ARP request
 114   fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::   143   253     ARP reply
 152   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   143   255     echo request
# P4 to PE6
 114   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   143   253     ARP request
 152   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   143   253     echo request
  • We captured at three locations during the ping from CE-A, and we read each file with tshark.
  • On the access link, there are an ARP request of 42 bytes, an ARP reply of 60 bytes, and the 98-byte ping.
  • In the core, the ARP broadcast is unicast, to the SID of PE6, with the outer next header 143. A point-to-point service has only one destination for a broadcast.
  • The reply from CE-B comes back to the SID of PE1, e00b.
  • The 98-byte ping is 152 bytes in the core. The next header 143 identifies Ethernet. RFC 8986 defines this value.
  • On the link P4 to PE6, the frames are the same, and the outer hop limit is two lower, as for Layer 3.
14.8 · Testing the edge

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -s 1418 172.16.30.6
PING 172.16.30.6 (172.16.30.6): 1418 data bytes
1426 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=0 ttl=64 time=1.296 ms
1426 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=1 ttl=64 time=1.639 ms
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -s 1419 172.16.30.6
PING 172.16.30.6 (172.16.30.6): 1419 data bytes
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss
  • A ping with 1418 bytes of data is a 1446-byte IP packet: 1418, plus 8 for ICMP, plus 20 for IPv4.
  • The 1446-byte packet goes through.
  • With one more byte, all pings are lost. CE-A gets no error message. It only waits.
14.9 · Where the 1447-byte packet died

Router / tool: CE-A, tshark and routers

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -s 1419 172.16.30.6
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "ipv6.fraghdr" -T fields -e frame.len -e ipv6.src -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.fraghdr.offset
# PE1 to P2
1510   2001:db8:100::1   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   0
  75   2001:db8:100::1   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   181
# P4 to PE6: the same two fragments

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show ipv6 traffic
         2 fragmented into 4 fragments, 0 failed
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show ipv6 traffic
         0 fragments, 0 total reassembled
  • Where did the packet go? We have four items of evidence. First, the ping with 1419 bytes of data.
  • All pings are lost, and CE-A receives no error.
  • PE1 did not drop the frame. It fragmented the outer IPv6 packet into two fragments: 1510 and 75 bytes on the wire.
  • The counters of PE1 agree: two packets, fragmented into four fragments. These are our two pings.
  • The two fragments went through the core and arrived at PE6.
  • But the IPv6 counters of PE6 show zero fragments. The forwarding plane matched the SID and discarded the fragments before reassembly. CE-B received nothing, and no device sent a message.
  • This is the worst type of failure: it is silent, and it occurs only for large packets.

Acceptance: Compare each result with its interpretation. Record missing checks as Not verified. Restore the stated baseline before another experiment.

Questions:

  1. Why does VPWS permit 14 fewer customer IP bytes than the simple L3VPN example?
  2. Does an advertised E-LAN behavior prove that the platform accepts a bridge domain?

Next: Chapter 8. Keep the accepted state and observations before adding the next mechanism.

Field definition: RFC 9252, Sections 4 and 6.1.

08

TI-LFA, BFD, and microloop avoidance

Experiment focus: Separate the stages after a failure

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

A failure starts a sequence of changes. Detection comes first, followed by local repair. Other nodes can use temporary paths while their routes change. BFD, TI-LFA, and microloop avoidance act at different stages.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter traces a path around a failed resource. Its timeline separates repair, convergence, and restoration.

Starting state: The service must work first. Check the installed backup and start captures before the failure.

Three mechanisms with different tasks

BFD detects a failure. TI-LFA supplies a local repair path before normal convergence finishes. Microloop avoidance controls temporary forwarding during distributed convergence.

These mechanisms do not have the same timer. A configured BFD interval is not a measured outage. A microloop delay is not the customer interruption time.

The lab uses a BFD interval of 100 ms and a multiplier of three. Their product gives a nominal 300 ms detection value. Negotiated timers, scheduling, and the failure event affect actual detection. The logs must show the recorded time.

Derive one repair path

Suppose P2–P4 fails. P2 is the point of local repair, or PLR. P2 must reach PE6 without that link.

P-space identifies nodes reachable from the PLR without the failed resource under the applicable repair computation. Q-space identifies nodes that can reach the destination without that resource. The lab example must have a connection between P3 and P5.

A node instruction for P3 alone is not sufficient. From P3, the initial shortest path to P5 returns through P2 and P4. A P3-to-P5 adjacency instruction prevents that return.

The recorded repair container is fcbb:bb00:3:e005::. Here, e005 is the recorded P3-to-P5 uA. The repaired path is P2–P3–P5–P4–PE6. The locator metric is 71.

Use the topology to find the two spaces for the failure P2–P4.

Item Routers How to find it
PLR P2 The router next to the failed link
P-space of P2 PE1, P3 Routers that P2 reaches on normal shortest paths without the failed link
Q-space of PE6 P4, P5, PE6 Routers whose normal shortest path to PE6 does not use the failed link
P node P3 The last router of the P-space on the repair path
Q node P5 The first router of the Q-space on the repair path

No router is in both spaces. Thus the repair connects them. It goes to P3, then uses the P3-to-P5 link with an adjacency SID. In this topology, the P-space and the Q-space have different colors on the topology.

Compare multiple failures

Failed resource PLR Repair
Link PE1–P2 PE1 Plain LFA through P3
Link P2–P4 P2 P3 plus the P3-to-P5 uA
Link P4–PE6 P4 P5 plus the P5-to-PE6 uA
Node P2 PE1 P3 plus the P3-to-P5 uA
Node P4 P2 P3-to-P5 and P5-to-PE6 adjacency instructions

Protected and unprotected uA values differ. The local SID table identifies the selected form. A link-protection result does not automatically prove node protection.

The recorded node-protection configuration includes this tiebreaker under the IS-IS IPv6 address family:

fast-reroute per-prefix tiebreaker node-protecting index 100

A repair cannot deliver a service on PE6 when PE6 itself has failed. “Path not found” for that destination does not mean each repair computation is defective.

Observe three phases

The first recorded failure showed local repair packets with an SRH. Subsequent packets used a shorter repair list. The record does not show why that middle list changed.

A remote PE subsequently installed a temporary explicit path. After the microloop interval, it used the converged path. These are different phases of one event.

One run lost zero of 4000 pings. One more run lost eight pings and showed an approximately one-second gap. The source thus cannot support a guaranteed 50 ms protection claim.

The recorded microloop configuration used a 5000 ms RIB update delay. One explicit path remained for approximately 5.5 seconds. That time does not measure customer loss.

Worked example: Derive the repair instruction

When P2–P4 fails, P2 must avoid that link. Sending only toward P3 is insufficient. The previous P3-to-P5 shortest path returns through P2. A P3-to-P5 uA specifies the required adjacency before forwarding continues toward PE6.

Read the figures: F29 shows the installed repair. F30 shows packets during failure. F31 and F32 compare the temporary and converged paths. F33 shows the restoration sequence.

Think first: Local repair works, but a remote PE still uses a temporary explicit path. Has the network reached its final converged state?

Reason from the evidence: Which timer explains the interruption?

BFD detects failure, P2 installs repair forwarding, and PE1 uses a temporary path. Can the 5000-ms microloop delay describe customer loss?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

No. These values describe different stages. Local repair can carry traffic while another router delays its final route update.

Build one timeline from failure, first repair packet, temporary path, and convergence. Measure customer loss separately. Compare a second run before drawing conclusions.

L8 — Prove protection and restoration

Starting state: Start with working BLUE and an installed repair path. Start captures before each failure.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

Stage · Ep09 — Commands and results
9.1 · Link P2 to P4, repaired by P2

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (link), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2 P3, Metric: 71
         P node: P3.00 [2001:db8:100::3], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:: uN (PSP/USD)
         Q node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:: uA (PSP/USD)

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
    next hop ..., Repair Node(s): 2001:db8:100::5
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:3:e005::}
  • Now the router. First, without node protection, the example that we drew.
  • P2 has a TI-LFA backup through P3. The metric after the repair is 71.
  • The P node is P3, the Q node is P5, and the adjacency SID e005 goes from P3 to P5. This agrees with our prediction.
  • In CEF, the repair is H.Insert.Red with one container, fcbb:bb00:3:e005::. P3's node SID and its adjacency to P5 are in one address.
  • On this platform, the repair inserts a routing header into the packet. It does not add a second outer header.
9.2 · Link P4 to PE6, and link PE1 to P2

Router / tool: P4 and PE1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (link), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2 P5, Metric: 51
         P node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:5:: uN (PSP/USD)
         Q node: PE6.00 [2001:db8:100::6], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:5:e001:: uA (PSP/USD)
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:5:e001::}

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: LFA, via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1, P3, Metric: 71
  • Two more link examples.
  • P4 protects its link to PE6: go to P5, then use the adjacency from P5 to PE6, in one container. The metric is 51. This agrees with the prediction.
  • PE1 protects its link to P2. The backup is a normal LFA through P3, with no SIDs. Not every failure needs a segment list. This example proves it.
9.3 · Asking for node protection
router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  fast-reroute per-prefix tiebreaker node-protecting index 100
  • Link protection expects that only the link failed. If the full neighbor router fails, a link-protecting backup can send traffic back to that router.
  • On this release, we had to request node protection with a tiebreaker. We added it on all six routers.
9.4 · Node P2, repaired by PE1
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (node), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1 P3, Metric: 101
         P node: P3.00 [2001:db8:100::3], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:: uN (PSP/USD)
         Q node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:: uA (PSP/USD)
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:3:e005::}
  • Now the node examples. First, P2 fails, as PE1 sees it.
  • PE1 now has a node-protecting backup through P3, with metric 101.
  • The list is one container: go to P3, then use the adjacency to P5. It is shorter than our manual calculation, which had three segments.
  • Why? P3 is PE1's direct neighbor, so the first hop needs no adjacency SID; the outgoing interface is sufficient. From P5, the normal path to PE6 goes through P4, not through P2. Thus PE6 needs no segment.
  • The router found the shortest list. Our manual calculation was correct, but not the shortest. Remember this difference when you check your predictions.
9.5 · Node P4, repaired by P2

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (node), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2 P3, Metric: 91
         P node: P3.00 [2001:db8:100::3], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:: uN (PSP/USD)
         Q node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:: uA (PSP/USD)
         Q node: PE6.00 [2001:db8:100::6], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:5:e001:: uA (PSP/USD)
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::}
  • Now P4 fails, as P2 sees it.
  • There is a node-protecting backup through P3, with metric 91.
  • The repair has three parts: go to P3, use the adjacency from P3 to P5, then use the adjacency from P5 to PE6. This agrees with the manual calculation.
  • Look at the encoding: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::. The second adjacency, e001, is P5's adjacency. P5's node SID is not in front of it. After P3 shifts the address, P5 finds e001 as its own local SID.
  • Three instructions are in one container, and there is no routing header.
9.6 · When node protection is impossible

Router / tool: P4

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (link), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2 P5, Metric: 51
       TI-LFA Path Fallback Information:
         TI-LFA link: Path valid
         TI-LFA node: Path not found
  • One more example, which was not in the predictions. P4 protects traffic to PE6, with node protection requested.
  • P4 still uses a link-protecting backup.
  • P4 gives the reason: it did not find a node-protecting path. The destination, PE6, is the neighbor. You cannot protect traffic to a router against the failure of that router.

Router / tool: PE1 and P4

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 4000 timeout 1
Sending 4000, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.30.6.6 timeout is 1 seconds:

  • Now the main test. We make a failure while traffic flows. First, in CML, we start captures on the core links.
  • Then, on PE1, we start a long GREEN ping: 4000 packets, with a timeout of 1 second.
  • While the ping runs, we shut the interface of P4 toward P2. This is the failure. P2 is the point of local repair.

Router / tool: P2 and PE1

%ROUTING-ISIS-5-ADJCHANGE : ISIS (CORE): Adjacency to P4 (GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1) (L2) Down, BFD session DOWN

L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [81/115] Label: None, low priority

 5  2001:db8:100::6
  • What did the routers record? First, the log of P2.
  • BFD on P2 reports that the session to P4 is down. Then IS-IS removes the adjacency to P4.
  • A few seconds later, PE1 has a new IS-IS route. The metric is 81, not 31. The next hop is still P2.
  • The traceroute shows the new path: P2, P3, P5, P4, and then PE6. It has five hops, not three.
9.10 · A repair, caught on the wire

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r fail-P2-P3.pcap -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.routing.segleft -e ipv6.nxt | sort | uniq -c
   44  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::   1   43
   15  fcbb:bb00:3:e005::        1   43
 1481  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::     4

# time of the first packet of each group, in seconds
9.645  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::
9.749  fcbb:bb00:3:e005::
9.787  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::
  • Now the most important part: the packets on the link from P2 to P3. We count the echo requests by destination. The last two columns are Segments Left and the next header.
  • Phase 1: 44 packets. P2 inserted its node-protecting repair. The routing header has Segments Left 1, and the next header is 43.
  • Phase 2: 15 packets with a shorter list: P3 and the adjacency to P5, still with a routing header. We did not verify which router state caused this short phase.
  • Phase 3: 1481 packets with no routing header. The next header is 4. PE1 uses its new path, and P2 stopped the repair. Episode 10 explains this phase.
  • The times show how short the repair was. Phase 1 starts at 9.645 seconds, and phase 3 starts at 9.787. The repair carried traffic for about 0.14 seconds.
9.11 · Following phase 1 to PE6

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.routing.segleft -e ipv6.nxt | sort | uniq -c
# P2 to P3
   44  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::   1   43
# P3 to P5
   44  fcbb:bb00:e001::          1   43
 1496  fcbb:bb00:6:e008::            4
# P5 to PE6
   44  fcbb:bb00:6:e008::            4
  • Follow the 44 repaired packets to PE6. We read the capture of each link with the same command.
  • On the link P2 to P3, P2 inserted the repair in front of the service SID.
  • P3 did its adjacency instruction and shifted the address. The remaining instruction is e001, P5's adjacency to PE6.
  • P5 did e001 and sent the packet on the direct link to PE6. P5 is the penultimate endpoint, thus it removed the routing header. PE6 received only the service SID.
  • The other 1496 packets on the link P3 to P5 are the later traffic of phases 2 and 3. They have the same destination, and they have no routing header.
  • The functions from Episodes 4, 5 and 6 worked together in less than a quarter of a second.
9.12 · Run it twice
# run 1
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 4000 timeout 1
Success rate is 100 percent (4000/4000), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/13 ms

# run 2, the same failure
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 6000 timeout 1
Success rate is 99 percent (5992/6000), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/17 ms
  • We did the same failure again, and we got a different result. You must see this too.
  • In the first test, the repair carried traffic for about 0.14 seconds, and no ping was lost.
  • In the second test, no repaired packet appeared, and 8 pings were lost. There were no packets on the wire for approximately one second. Then PE1's new path started.
  • We did not verify why the two tests were different. This is a software forwarder in a virtual lab. It proves that the repair is there and shows its format. It cannot tell you the speed of protection. Measure the speed on hardware.

10.6 · The explicit path on the wire

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r fail2-P2-P3.pcap -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e ipv6.dst | sort | uniq -c
  979  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::

# first and last packet of the explicit path, in seconds
9.897   first   fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::
14.087  last    fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::
  • Now we can explain phase 3 from Episode 9. This capture is from the second test of that failure. We count the echo requests on the link P2 to P3 by destination.
  • Immediately after the failure, GREEN traffic is in one container: P3, the adjacency to P5, then PE6's service SID. This is the explicit path, with the service, in one address. There are 979 packets.
  • Later, the packets use only the service SID again. They follow the new shortest path through P2, P3, P5 and P4. There are 2621 packets.

10.7 · Did anything loop?

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e eth.src -e ipv6.hlim | sort | uniq -c
# link P2 to P3, run 1
 1540  56:54:00:1c:70:f9  254
# link P2 to P3, run 2
 3600  56:54:00:1c:70:f9  254
  • A microloop leaves evidence on the wire. Thus we looked for it on the link between P2 and P3, the two routers from our manual example. We count the packets by source MAC address and hop limit.
  • In the first test, one source sent all 1540 packets, with hop limit 254. The source is P2.
  • The second test gave the same result: 3600 packets, one source, hop limit 254.
  • No packet came from P3. A looping packet would appear in the two directions, with a decreasing hop limit. With microloop avoidance on, we saw none.
  • We did not verify if a loop occurs with avoidance off. This is a good test for your lab.
10.8 · BFD
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show running-config router isis CORE interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  bfd minimum-interval 100
  bfd multiplier 3
  bfd fast-detect ipv6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bfd ipv6 session
Gi0/0/0/0            fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1
No                   n/a             0s(0s*0)         300ms(100ms*3)   UP
  • Detection is the first step. This is how we made it fast.
  • BFD runs on each IS-IS interface, every 100 milliseconds. After 3 missed packets, BFD declares the session down.
  • Thus the detection time is 300 milliseconds, and the session is up. Without BFD, IS-IS waits for its hello holdtime, which is many seconds.
  • In our test, P4 shut its own interface, so P2 learned about the failure from BFD. Thus the BFD event and the adjacency event occurred in the same millisecond.
10.9 · Restoration is an event too

Router / tool: P4, P2 and PE1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4(config)#no interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 shutdown
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4(config)#commit

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show logging last 12
03:52:07.575  %L2-BFD-6-SESSION_STATE_UP : BFD session to neighbor ... on interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1 is up
03:52:14.102  %ROUTING-ISIS-5-ADJCHANGE : ISIS (CORE): Adjacency to P4 (GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1) (L2) Up, New adjacency

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [31/115] Label: None, low priority
   Installed Oct 03 03:52:20.122 for 00:00:04

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 6000 timeout 1
Success rate is 100 percent (6000/6000), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/12 ms
  • Then we restored the link while the pings continued. The restoration is also an event.
  • On P4, we remove the shutdown, and we commit.
  • BFD came up first, at 07.575 seconds after 03:52.
  • IS-IS brought the adjacency up at 14.102, six and a half seconds later.
  • PE1 changed its route back to metric 31 at 20.122, six seconds after that. This agrees with the same 5000-millisecond delay for an up event.
  • No ping was lost: 6000 of 6000. For the whole test, the traffic stayed on the detour. A repaired network changes back step by step, more than ten seconds later.

Acceptance: Compare each result with its interpretation. Record missing checks as Not verified. Restore the stated baseline before another experiment.

Questions:

  1. Why is an adjacency instruction necessary for the P2–P4 repair?
  2. Does a 5000 ms microloop delay mean five seconds of customer interruption?

Next: Chapter 9. Keep the accepted state and observations before adding the next mechanism.

09

SR Policy and on-demand next hop

Experiment focus: Verify the required path

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

IGP forwarding provides reachability. An SR Policy adds path requirements, but a node list does not necessarily select every link. First calculate the actual route through the list. Then observe fallback and compare ODN with PCE computation.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter examines why P3–P5–PE6 can take an indirect path. A successful ping alone does not prove policy compliance.

Starting state: Keep the working Chapter 5 service. Add color, candidate paths, and PCE functions one at a time.

The path and the service

A service SID identifies the egress service. An SR Policy selects how traffic reaches that service. A policy can change the transport path without changing the egress VRF.

The lab policy on PE1 has color 100 and endpoint 2001:db8:100::6. PE6 attaches color 100 to its BLUE IPv4 routes. PE1 matches the route color and next hop to the policy.

The policy contains candidate paths. The valid candidate with the highest preference becomes active. A Binding SID identifies the associated policy on the headend.

The recorded Binding SID uses uB6 with reduced insertion. CEF first gives information about the service encapsulation, then the path insertion. This description does not mean that the wire necessarily contains two outer IPv6 headers.

Why the node list takes an unexpected path

The node list is P3, P5, PE6. Each node segment uses its IGP shortest path.

Segment Selected path Cost comparison
PE1 to P3 PE1–P2–P3 20 instead of direct 40
P3 to P5 P3–P2–P4–P5 30 instead of direct 40
P5 to PE6 P5–P4–PE6 20 instead of direct 40

The complete path is PE1–P2–P3–P2–P4–P5–P4–PE6. The policy is operational, but no lower horizontal link carries the packet.

The recorded container is fcbb:bb00:3:5:6:e004::. It identifies the waypoints and the service. It does not identify each link between the waypoints.

Make selected links explicit

The strict-path test adds P3-to-P5 and P5-to-PE6 uA instructions. A recorded container becomes fcbb:bb00:3:e005:5:e003:6:e004.

The path becomes PE1–P2–P3–P5–PE6. PE1 reaches P3 through P2. The experiment made two links explicit, not the complete path from PE1.

Only PE6's export has color 100. Return traffic thus uses the normal PE6–P4–P2–PE1 path. For symmetric steering, the opposite direction must have a related service configuration.

Why adjacency SIDs, and their risk

A node SID only says where the packet goes. The IGP decides how it gets there. Only an adjacency SID selects one link. Thus a strict path needs adjacency SIDs.

There is a risk. On this platform, the dynamic uA values can change after a reload, or after an outage of more than three minutes. If a value changes, the SID in your segment list can select another link. Or it can select nothing. The policy can then go down, or use a wrong path.

  1. After a reload or a long outage, read the SIDs again. Run show segment-routing srv6 sid on the two routers.
  2. Compare the values with the segment list.
  3. Do not hard-code adjacency SIDs in production. Let a PCE compute the list, as in the ODN section below. Or use node SIDs and Flex-Algo, which do not depend on one link.
segment-lists
 segment-list VIA-P3-P5-UA
  srv6
   index 10 sid fcbb:bb00:3:e005::
   index 20 sid fcbb:bb00:5:e003::
policy BLUE-C100
 candidate-paths
  preference 200
   explicit segment-list VIA-P3-P5-UA

e005 is the P3-to-P5 adjacency SID. e003 is the P5-to-PE6 adjacency SID. We read both on P3 and P5 immediately before this test.

Failure and fallback

When the recorded policy was administratively down, BGP kept the color. CEF used plain service encapsulation through the locator. Customer pings passed on the shortest path.

Reachability thus did not prove the requested path. For a service with mandatory path constraints, select fallback or discard behavior explicitly. The source configuration used fallback. For a discard option, do a different acceptance test on the selected release.

ODN creates the policy, not the computation capability

ODN uses a template when a matching colored route arrives. The template specifies requirements. A path computation mechanism must supply a valid path.

Source test Result Customer path
Fresh template without a PCE Headend computation unsupported Normal shortest path
P4 as PCE, metric type latency Policy operational PE1–P3–P5–PE6
PCE with SID algorithm 128 constraint Empty path and SID verification error Normal shortest path

These results apply to the tested releases. They are not universal limits of ODN. The XRv9000 comparison also failed these two tests. Cisco’s IOS XR 25.x guide lists two restrictions. It excludes PCE delegation with a Flex-Algo constraint and headend dynamic path computation. The lab and the document agree. If results differ, check the platform, release, configuration, and packet evidence.

P4 can calculate the path without carrying the customer packets. PCEP is a control-plane connection. The selected adjacency list determines the data-plane path.

The working PCE result uses algorithm 0 adjacency SIDs selected by delay. It is not automatically a Flex-Algo 128 path. In the capture, local adjacency instructions can appear without a previous node identifier. Their meaning depends on the node that receives them.

Worked example: Expand each part of the node list

For P3–P5–PE6, calculate each shortest path separately. PE1 reaches P3 through P2. P3 reaches P5 through P2 and P4. P5 reaches PE6 through P4. The complete path is PE1–P2–P3–P2–P4–P5–P4–PE6. Repeated nodes do not prove policy failure in this example.

Read the figures: F34 shows the observed links. F35 adds adjacency instructions. F36 shows fallback after policy shutdown. A successful ping in F36 does not prove that the policy remains active.

Think first: If ordinary IGP forwarding is prohibited for this service, which policy-failure behavior needs a separate acceptance test?

Dynamic SID values after recovery

The recorded SID holdtime is three minutes. A short interruption kept the recorded values. After a 240-second interruption, the recovery sequence changed dynamic assignments.

An explicit list that contains a dynamic uA can thus become incorrect. An external reference to a dynamic Binding SID has the same risk. Current SID tables must show the values after recovery.

The controlled test proves reassignment. Events without captures have no verified cause.

Reason from the evidence: When does successful fallback mean failure?

A policy goes down. Pings still pass through the shortest path. The customer requires a specified transit path. Has the service passed?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

Reachability passed, but the path requirement may have failed. A node list, adjacency list, and fallback route impose different constraints.

Write the required links before testing. Compare captures with those links. Decide whether fallback is acceptable before accepting the service.

L9 — Prove intent and fallback

Starting state: Start with working BLUE and RED. Verify current adjacency SIDs before applying an explicit list.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

Router / tool: PE6

end-set
!

end-policy
!
vrf BLUE

  • Now the egress side. PE6 selects which of its routes use color 100.
  • A color is an opaque extended community. Here, its value is 100.
  • A route policy sets it.
  • The BLUE IPv4 export uses this policy. Only BLUE IPv4 gets the color. BLUE IPv6, RED and GREEN do not change.

15.6 · On the wire: every core link

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 -I 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.hlim | sort -u
# PE1 to P2       fcbb:bb00:3:5:6:e004::   255
# P2 to P3        fcbb:bb00:3:5:6:e004::   254
# P3 back to P2   fcbb:bb00:5:6:e004::     253
# P2 to P4        fcbb:bb00:5:6:e004::     252
# P4 to P5        fcbb:bb00:5:6:e004::     251
# P5 back to P4   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::       250
# P4 to PE6       fcbb:bb00:6:e004::       249
  • We captured on all eight core links while CE-A sent a ping to CE-B in BLUE. All three pings got a reply. We read each file with tshark. These are all the links that carried a request.
  • PE1 sends the packet to P2. It does not send it to P3.
  • P2 sends it to P3, with no change.
  • P3 removes its micro-SID, and the packet goes back to P2.
  • Then the packet goes to P4 and P5. P5 removes its micro-SID.
  • Then it goes back to P4, and then to PE6. This is seven hops, not three, with two U-turns. The packet did not use the lower links.
  • The hop limit shows this: it decreases from 255 to 249, one for each router.

  segment-lists
   segment-list VIA-P3-P5-UA
    srv6
     index 10 sid fcbb:bb00:3:e005::

  • To use the lower links, we need adjacency SIDs, from Episode 4. Read them on P3 and P5 immediately before the test. Dynamic uA values can change after a reboot, or after an outage of more than three minutes.
  • The adjacency SID of P3 to P5 is e005.
  • The adjacency SID of P5 to PE6 is e003.
  • We add them as a second candidate path, with preference 200. It becomes active, and we do not delete the first path.
  • CEF now inserts fcbb:bb00:3:e005:5:e003::. The Binding SID did not change. Thus BGP and the VRF route also did not change.
15.8 · Strict path on the wire

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 -I 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8 or icmp.type == 0" \
    -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.hlim -e icmp.type | sort -u
# PE1 to P2    fcbb:bb00:3:e005:5:e003:6:e004   255   request
# P2 to P3     fcbb:bb00:3:e005:5:e003:6:e004   254   request
# P3 to P5     fcbb:bb00:5:e003:6:e004::        253   request
# P5 to PE6    fcbb:bb00:6:e004::               252   request
# P4 to PE6    fcbb:bb00:1:e004::               255   reply
# P2 to P4     fcbb:bb00:1:e004::               254   reply
# PE1 to P2    fcbb:bb00:1:e004::               253   reply
  • These are the addresses on the wire, for the same ping.
  • One address has six micro-SIDs: P3, its adjacency, P5, its adjacency, PE6 and the service. The address is full, but there is no routing header. The size is still 138 bytes.
  • P2 forwards it with no change.
  • P3 removes two micro-SIDs: its node SID and its adjacency SID. Then it sends the packet on the link from P3 to P5.
  • P5 does the same, to PE6.
  • What about the replies? They went PE6, P4, P2, PE1, on the IGP path, to the BLUE SID of PE1. Only the export of PE6 adds a color. A policy steers one direction only. To steer both directions, add a color on the other side too.
15.9 · When the policy goes down
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing traffic-eng policy color 100
    Admin: down  Operational: down for 00:00:08 (since Oct  3 08:23:46.018)
    Preference: 200 (configuration) (inactive) (shutdown)
    Preference: 100 (configuration) (inactive) (shutdown)

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
    2001:db8:100::6 (metric 30) from 2001:db8:100::6 (10.0.0.6)
      Extended community: Color:100 RT:65000:100

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
   via fcbb:bb00:6::/128, 11 dependencies, recursive
    next hop fcbb:bb00:6::/128 via fcbb:bb00:6::/48
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e004::}
  • This is the last test: what occurs when the policy fails? We shut it down.
  • The policy is admin down. The two candidate paths are down. PE1 releases the Binding SID.
  • The route still has color 100. But BGP does not point it to a policy now.
  • CEF goes back to the locator of PE6 and a plain encapsulation, as in Episode 13. The capture showed PE1, P2, P4, PE6, and all pings got a reply.
  • On this platform, this fallback is the default, because invalidation drop is off. If a service must always stay on its path, for example for separation, set invalidation drop on. Then test that it drops the traffic.
  • After no shutdown, the policy came back with the same Binding SID value. But the value is dynamic. Do not make a design that needs this number.

      SR policy color 200, up, registered, bsid fcbb:bb01:1:e004::

   via local-srv6-sid fcbb:bb01:1:e004::, 3 dependencies, recursive
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e006::}

  • The steering is the same as in Episode 15.
  • The RED route now points to the Binding SID of the ODN policy.
  • This is the RED service SID, e006, and the inserted list: fcbb:bb00:e004:e002::. There are only two micro-SIDs for three adjacencies, and there are no node numbers. We decode this now.
  • The first hop is GigabitEthernet 0/0/0/1, directly to P3.

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark
