A node SID with Flex-Algo follows that algorithm’s shortest path. It does not guarantee a particular adjacency. A PCE must enforce any required link constraint. Verify its computed list and the observed path.

Documentation: Cisco NCS 5500, IOS XR 25.x — SRv6 TE restrictions. This is an NCS guide, not an XRv9000 feature matrix. The XRv9000 test results are separate evidence.

10

Flex-Algo and service path selection

Experiment focus: Apply different calculations to one network

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

Flex-Algo changes the conditions used to calculate routes. Separate the FAD definition, node participation, and locator association. Then select the calculated topology through the service SID.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter compares mechanisms that use the same physical path. It checks for missing backups before traffic fails.

Starting state: Check algorithm 0 and algorithm 128 before changes. Do not change the metric and participating nodes together.

One physical network, two computations

Algorithm 0 uses the ordinary IGP metric in this lab. Algorithm 128 uses the advertised delay metric. The number 128 does not inherently mean low delay.

A Flexible Algorithm Definition, or FAD, specifies the computation. Routers select a definition according to the election rules. Each router must also participate in that algorithm.

The lab has three necessary elements:

Element Source design
Definition PE1 advertises priority 200. PE6 advertises priority 100.
Participation All six routers participate in algorithm 128.
Locator Each router has a different FA128 locator.

PE1's definition wins in this example. With equal priorities, the highest system ID wins the election. Receiving a FAD does not itself enable participation.

The lab separates MAIN and FA128 into two blocks. This is a design selection. The use of different blocks also makes the SRH example easier to observe.

What does 128 mean?

RFC 9350 reserves the numbers 128 to 255 for the operator. You choose the meaning. The numbers 0 to 127 are not for this use.

The numbers do not have to be continuous. You can use 128, 140 and 200. You do not need the numbers between them.

Several routers can advertise a definition for the same number. The network selects one. It selects the highest priority. If the priorities are equal, it selects the highest System-ID. The number itself means nothing. The selected definition gives the meaning, for example the delay metric.

In our lab, we use only 128. XRd shows Max Locators: 16, so the router can hold many algorithms. Your platform can have a different limit. Check the winning definition on a router that advertises none:

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P3#show isis flex-algo 128
Flex-Algo 128:
  Level-2:
    Definition Priority: 200
    Definition Source: PE1.00
    Definition Metric Type: Delay
  Local Priority: 128

The definition comes from PE1 at priority 200. P3 has the default local priority 128, because it does not advertise a definition.

Calculate the two paths

The three lower links each advertise 1000 microseconds. The other links each advertise 5000 microseconds. These are configured values, not measured customer delay.

Destination locator Computation Path Recorded metric
fcbb:bb00:6::/48 IGP cost PE1–P2–P4–PE6 31
fcbb:bb01:6::/48 Advertised delay PE1–P3–P5–PE6 3001

The additional one is the locator contribution in this implementation. A metric of 3001 does not mean a measured customer delay of 3001 microseconds.

The FA128 locator has an algorithm 128 association. IS-IS must also have the locator attachment. Each participating router must have the correct definition and topology information.

Put the service on the selected topology

PE6 allocates RED IPv6 from FA128. Its recorded service SID is fcbb:bb01:6:e004::. PE1 resolves that SID through the algorithm-128 locator route.

No color or SR Policy is necessary for this method. The service destination already selects the applicable locator. The return service SID stays in MAIN, so the return path differs.

A PCE latency policy is a different method. It can select the same physical links with algorithm 0 adjacency SIDs. Equal recorded paths do not make the mechanisms the same.

A failure that ordinary pings miss

If P2 and P4 stop participating in algorithm 128, the lower path can stay usable. Ordinary RED IPv6 pings can pass. But, algorithm 128 loses the alternate upper path.

When P3–P5 subsequently fails, RED IPv6 has no route in that algorithm. The earlier correct ping did not prove resilience. The missing backup was visible before the failure.

Worked example: Separate three dependencies

The FAD defines the calculation. Participation determines which routers join it. The locator association connects the result to forwarding. Algorithm 128 uses advertised delay in this lab. The number 128 does not itself mean low latency.

Read the figures: F40 compares locator routes. F41 assigns RED IPv6 to FA128. F42 changes one delay to test the path-selection result.

Think first: P2 and P4 leave algorithm 128, but the primary path works. Which output reveals the risk before another link fails?

Reason from the evidence: Why can algorithm 128 work without resilience?

RED IPv6 still passes after P2 and P4 leave algorithm 128. The remaining path is PE1–P3–P5–PE6. What changed before any packet loss?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

The topology lost its alternate path. Successful traffic proves current reachability, not a backup inside the same algorithm.

Compare the route and backup before the change. Predict the P3–P5 failure before introducing it. Algorithm 0 reachability cannot replace a missing algorithm 128 path.

L10 — Change one metric, then remove one dependency

Starting state: Start with working services. Add algorithm 128 on all participating routers before selecting its locator.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

Stage · Ep11 — Commands and results
11.1 · The configuration
! PE1: defines and advertises algorithm 128
router isis CORE
 flex-algo 128
  priority 200
  metric-type delay
  advertise-definition
!
! P3: takes part, does not advertise a definition
router isis CORE
 flex-algo 128
  metric-type delay
!
! every router: a locator in algorithm 128
segment-routing srv6 locators locator FA128
 prefix fcbb:bb01:1::/48
 algorithm 128
  • This is our configuration, in three parts.
  • PE1 defines algorithm 128 with the delay metric, at priority 200, and advertises the definition. PE6 does the same, at priority 100.
  • P3 participates, with the same metric type, but it does not advertise a definition. P2, P4 and P5 have the same configuration.
  • Each router has a second locator in the fcbb:bb01 block, for algorithm 128. In this lab, we use a separate block for Flex-Algo. This is our choice, not a rule of the RFC.
11.2 · Who defines algorithm 128?

Router / tool: P3

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P3#show isis flex-algo 128
Flex-Algo 128:
  Level-2:
    Definition Priority: 200
    Definition Source: PE1.00
    Definition Equal to Local: Yes
    Definition Calculation Type: SPF
    Definition Metric Type: Delay
  Topologies supported:
    IPv6 Unicast
  Local Priority: 128
  • Two routers advertise a definition. Which definition does the network use? We ask P3, which advertises none.
  • The selected definition comes from PE1, at priority 200.
  • It is the same as P3's local configuration. If it were different, P3 would still use the selected definition, and this line would tell you to compare them.
  • The metric type is delay.
  • P3's local priority is 128, the default value, because P3 does not compete. RFC 9350 selects the highest priority. If two are equal, it selects the highest system ID.
11.3 · The delays we advertise
! PE1
performance-measurement
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  delay-measurement
   advertise-delay 5000
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
  delay-measurement
   advertise-delay 1000
  • The delay values must come from a source. In a real network, the router measures them. In this lab, we advertise fixed values. Then you can build the same lab.
  • PE1 advertises 5000 microseconds for its upper link to P2.
  • It advertises 1000 for its lower link to P3. Each lower link has 1000. Each upper link and cross link has 5000. This is the opposite of the costs, on purpose.
11.4 · Two routes, two paths
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb01:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 3001, SRv6-locator (algo 128), type level-2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1
 1  2001:db8:200:12::1
 2  2001:db8:200:24::1
 3  2001:db8:100::6
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute fcbb:bb01:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1
 1  2001:db8:200:13::1
 2  2001:db8:200:35::1
 3  2001:db8:100::6
  • The router gives the same result.
  • There are two routes to PE6, one for each locator. Algorithm 0 has metric 31. Algorithm 128 has metric 3001: 3000 microseconds plus 1 for the locator.
  • A traceroute to PE6's algorithm 0 SID goes through P2 and P4.
  • A traceroute to its algorithm 128 SID goes through P3 and P5. The routers and the links are the same, but there are two topologies. The destination address selects the topology.
11.5 · Every algorithm has its own SIDs
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 sid
*** Locator: 'FA128' ***
fcbb:bb01:1::               uN (PSP/USD)      'default':1                       sidmgr
fcbb:bb01:1:e000::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/0, Link-Local]:128:P     isis-CORE
fcbb:bb01:1:e001::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/0, Link-Local]:128       isis-CORE
fcbb:bb01:1:e002::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/1, Link-Local]:128:P     isis-CORE
fcbb:bb01:1:e003::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/1, Link-Local]:128       isis-CORE
  • Each algorithm has its own SIDs. Episode 8 showed this in the LSP.
  • PE1 has a second node SID, fcbb:bb01:1::, in algorithm 128.
  • It also has a second pair of adjacency SIDs for each link, with the mark 128. A packet with these SIDs follows the algorithm 128 paths on each hop, not only on the first hop.
11.6 · Protection stays inside the algorithm
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute flex-algo 128 fcbb:bb01:6::/48 detail
     via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1, P3
       Backup path: TI-LFA (node), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 P2, Metric: 15001
         P node: P4.00 [2001:db8:100::4], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb01:4:: uN (PSP/USD)

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb01:6::/48 detail
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb01:4::}
  • TI-LFA also works in each algorithm.
  • The primary path to PE6's algorithm 128 locator goes through P3. Its node-protecting backup goes through P2, with a delay metric of 15001.
  • The repair SID is P4's algorithm 128 node SID, fcbb:bb01:4::. The repair stays in the same topology as the traffic that it protects.
11.7 · Putting a customer on algorithm 128

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show running-config router bgp 65000 vrf RED
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator FA128

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 sid | include RED
fcbb:bb01:6:e004::          uDT6              'RED'                             bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:6:e006::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000
  • Now the result. How do you put a customer on the low-delay topology? In SRv6, the simplest method is one line on the egress PE.
  • For RED IPv4, PE6 allocates its service SID from MAIN, algorithm 0.
  • For RED IPv6, PE6 allocates it from FA128, algorithm 128.
  • Thus RED IPv6's service SID is in the fcbb:bb01 block. Each packet that PE1 sends to it follows algorithm 128 automatically. No policy and no colour are necessary.
11.8 · RED IPv6, both directions

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 3 2001:db8:c:206::2
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmpv6.type == 128 or icmpv6.type == 129" -T fields -e ipv6.dst
# PE1 to P3, CE-A to CE-B
fcbb:bb01:6:e004::     (outer destination, algorithm 128)
# PE1 to P2, CE-B to CE-A
fcbb:bb00:1:e007::     (outer destination, algorithm 0)
  • Now the result on the wire. We pinged from CE-A to CE-B in RED IPv6. We captured the two core links of PE1, and we read each file with tshark.
  • All three pings succeed.
  • To CE-B, the packets go out on the lower link, to the algorithm 128 service SID.
  • The replies come back on the upper link. PE1's own RED IPv6 SID is still in MAIN, so the return path uses algorithm 0. The two directions are different, because we configured only one end.
  • If you want low delay in the two directions, allocate from the algorithm 128 locator on the two PEs.

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb01:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 15001, SRv6-locator (algo 128), type level-2
    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, from 2001:db8:100::6, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, Protected

 1  2001:db8:200:12::1

3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

# captures after the change, from the same ping
PE1 to P2: fcbb:bb01:6:e004::  and  fcbb:bb00:1:e007::
PE1 to P3: no echo request
  • These are the results, after the delay of the P3 to P5 link became 20000. We start with the routes on PE1.
  • Algorithm 0 did not change. It has the same metric 31 and the same path. It does not use delay.
  • Algorithm 128 now has metric 15001, and the next hop is P2, the upper link. The lower path has a total of 22000 microseconds, and the upper path, at 15000, is better.
  • The traceroute to the algorithm 128 SID confirms this: P2, P4, then PE6.
  • The customer ping still works. The service did not change.

11

Troubleshooting, boundaries, and capacity

Experiment focus: Find a cause from observed differences

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

A missing reply does not identify where a packet stopped. Compare local SID state, IGP information, CEF, service attributes, and delivery in both directions. Use one controlled change to test the suspected cause.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter separates forward-path faults from return-path faults. Packet evidence verifies boundary filtering.

Starting state: Reproduce one fault at a time. Do not change the MTU, RT, and locator together.

Start at the first difference

A useful fault report contains a symptom, a hypothesis, and test records that can reject the hypothesis. It also contains the healthy reference state. The first difference determines the next investigation step.

Layer Necessary test records
1. Local Locator state, local SID, and behavior owner
2. IGP Advertisement, algorithm participation, and installed route
3. Forwarding CEF exit, encapsulation, and backup
4. Service RT, service SID, color, and policy
5. Delivery Captures and customer results in the two directions

A high-layer success does not remove lower-layer faults. BGP can keep a best path when its SID locator is inaccessible. A policy can stay operational while its service traffic fails.

Four source faults

Symptom Decisive observation Source repair
Small L2 packets pass, large packets fail Large packets stop at the reduced-MTU core link Restore the link MTU
CE-A receives no reply Request reaches CE-B, but reply stops at PE6 Restore PE1 export RT to 65000:100
Only GREEN fails Service SID uses an inactive TEST locator Allocate from MAIN again
RED IPv6 fails only after a link failure Algorithm 128 had no alternate path Restore P2 and P4 participation

The inactive TEST locator was fcbb:bb00:66::/48. Its failure affected the service that selected it. Other services could continue normally.

A direct ping to a SID is a limited OAM test. In the recorded test, multiple SID pings received replies from the PE loopback. Those replies did not prove the associated customer behavior. The multi-node checksum case in Chapter 3 must use packet captures.

Fault 1 in detail: the change, and the arithmetic

The planted change is one command on P2, on the link toward P4:

interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
 ipv6 mtu 1400

The interface MTU stays at 1514, and IPv6 can use only 1400. The largest customer IP packet over the Layer 2 service is 1400 − 40 (outer IPv6 header) − 14 (inner Ethernet header) = 1346 bytes. This agrees with the pings: 1300 bytes passed and 1400 bytes failed. The repair is no ipv6 mtu on the same interface.

Fault 3 in detail: the changes and the repair

The fault has two steps on PE6. In step 1, a new locator TEST is created, and RED IPv4 allocates its service SID from it. The locator is not added under IS-IS. This is the missing step.

segment-routing srv6 locators locator TEST
 micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
 prefix fcbb:bb00:66::/48
router bgp 65000 vrf RED address-family ipv4 unicast
 segment-routing srv6 locator TEST

RED recovered after the transition because the policy uses P5’s adjacency SID to reach PE6. P5 owns that adjacency SID. PE6 owns the final service SID in TEST. This explicit path bypasses the missing locator route on PE1. In step 2, RED goes back to MAIN and GREEN moves to TEST. Now only GREEN depends on the broken locator.

router bgp 65000 vrf RED address-family ipv4 unicast
 segment-routing srv6 locator MAIN
router bgp 65000 vrf GREEN address-family ipv4 unicast
 segment-routing srv6 locator TEST

On PE6, show isis segment-routing srv6 locators shows TEST as Inactive. The repair has two steps: move GREEN back to MAIN, then remove the unused locator.

router bgp 65000 vrf GREEN address-family ipv4 unicast
 segment-routing srv6 locator MAIN
segment-routing srv6 locators
 no locator TEST

Remove a locator only after no VRF allocates from it.

Traceroute and SRv6

  1. A plain traceroute works. To the node SID of PE6, it shows P2, P4, then PE6, on the IGP path.
  2. Cisco documents two SRv6 forms of traceroute. Neither is in the ipv6 help tree of XRd 26.2.2. Our statement is only about the ipv6 syntax. The router rejects an srv6 keyword after the address.
  3. This release has traceroute segment-routing srv6 policy name <name>. It traces a policy. We did not run it.
  4. A document does not always match your release. Use the question mark on your router, and test the syntax.
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6:: srv6
% Invalid input detected at '^' marker.
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute segment-routing srv6 policy ?
  name  srv6 TE policy name

Protect the SR domain

A service SID is an IPv6 address. An untrusted source can attempt to send packets to it if routing and filtering permit that traffic. Customer isolation and domain-boundary filtering solve different problems.

The laboratory ACL blocks the two lab SID blocks and packets with a routing header. The /31 covers fcbb:bb00::/32 and fcbb:bb01::/32.

ipv6 access-list SRV6-BOUNDARY-IN
 10 deny ipv6 any fcbb:bb00::/31 log
 20 deny ipv6 any any routing log
 30 permit ipv6 any any
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4
 ipv6 access-group SRV6-BOUNDARY-IN ingress

This is a laboratory boundary policy, not a complete production security policy. Line 20 matches routing headers more broadly than SRH type 4. The release accepted routing but rejected the attempted routing-type 4 syntax.

The manager also prints a broader base block. A production boundary must include each approved SID block without unintended exclusions. A VRF must not import SID reachability accidentally through route leaking.

The recorded deny counters stayed at zero while captures showed that the ACL blocked traffic. Counter values alone did not show success or failure.

Capacity has multiple different dimensions

The recorded dynamic local range is e000 through fdff. This range contains 7680 values. Service, adjacency, and Binding SIDs can consume local allocation resources.

Five hundred dual-stack VRFs can use 1000 service SIDs with different per-VRF IPv4 and IPv6 allocation. That arithmetic excludes adjacency SIDs, L2 SIDs, policies, and other consumers. It does not show a supported hardware scale.

Locator count, local SID count, and packet depth are different limits. The recorded XRd manager reports 16 locators and 64000 SIDs. Hardware limits must come from the exact platform and release documentation.

The number of SIDs depends on the allocation mode. Take an example with 500 VRFs, each with IPv4 and IPv6. The numbers are an example, not a measurement.

Mode SIDs per SIDs for 500 VRFs Tested
per-vrf VRF and address family 500 × 2 = 1000 Mode tested; 500-VRF scale not tested
per-vrf-46 VRF, one SID for IPv4 and IPv6 (uDT46) 500 × 1 = 500 no
per-ce CE and address family 500 × 4 CEs × 2 = 4000 no
Local range one block 7680

Per-CE allocation can use more than half of the local range. Adjacency and Binding SIDs can also consume allocation resources. These totals are estimates, not capacity measurements. The Cisco 8000 guide describes per-vrf-46. We did not test it.

Worked example: Follow the reply

A missing CE-A ping reply does not prove failed forward encapsulation. If CE-B receives the request and sends a reply, inspect the return route on PE6. An RT mismatch can prevent its import into BLUE. It does not erase the request already delivered to CE-B.

Read the figures: Compare F44 with the complete case in Appendix B. Then compare the MTU fault in F43 and the locator fault in F45. Similar symptoms have different first failures.

Think first: After the RT repair, why must the test include RED and captures in both directions?

Reason from the evidence: Where did the reply stop?

CE-B receives the request and sends a reply. CE-A receives nothing. Would an ingress encapsulation change explain all three observations?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

The delivered request already proves part of the forward path. Start with the reply path and the VRF route at PE6.

Check route import and RT before changing encapsulation. After repair, repeat the failed test and an isolation test. A successful reply must use the correct tenant context.

L11 — Diagnose and protect

Starting state: Start with the accepted services. Use one fault at a time. Restore routed ports before the ACL test.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

 7   *  *  *

  • Now a traceroute to an address that we made manually: fcbb:bb00:3:5:6::. This is the loose path of Episode 15.
  • Hop 1 is P2.
  • Hop 2 is P3. It replies from its loopback, because the address was its node SID. Then hop 3 is P2 again. This is the first U-turn of Episode 15, and we see it without a capture.
  • Then P4, then P5 from its loopback, then P4 again. This is the second U-turn.
  • PE6 does not reply. This agrees with Episodes 4 and 5. The checksum of the probe uses the first destination, thus the last node discards it. We see the path, but not the last hop.
Stage · Ep18 — Commands and results
18.1 · Fault 1: capture the path

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -s 1300 172.16.30.6
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -s 1400 172.16.30.6          (no reply)

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "ipv6.nxt == 143 or icmpv6.type == 2" -T fields -e frame.len -e ipv6.src -e ipv6.dst
# PE1 to P2
1396   2001:db8:100::1   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::    1300-byte ping, request
1396   2001:db8:100::6   fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::    1300-byte ping, reply
1496   2001:db8:100::1   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::    1400-byte ping, request
1294   2001:db8:100::1   (to PE1's loopback)   Packet Too Big, MTU 1336
# P2 to P4, and P4 to PE6
1396   the 1300-byte request and reply only
  • Layer 5 tells us where to look: the wire. We captured on three core links while CE-A sent pings of three sizes. We read each file with tshark.
  • The 1300-byte pings are answered. The 1400-byte pings get no reply.
  • The 1300-byte pings are 1396-byte frames, and they cross the core in both directions.
  • The 1400-byte request leaves PE1 as a 1496-byte frame, and it arrives at P2.
  • P2 sent an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big to the encapsulation source, the loopback of PE1. For a Layer 2 frame, PE1 cannot use this message. Thus the customer gets no message.
  • On the links from P2 to P4 and from P4 to PE6, there are only the small frames. The large frames stop at P2. Thus the fault is on P2, on its link to P4.
18.2 · Fault 1: the cause

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show ipv6 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
  MTU is 1514 (1400 is available to IPv6)

Packet Too Big, captured on PE1 to P2:
    Type: Packet Too Big (2)
    MTU: 1336
        Source Address: 2001:db8:100::1
        Destination Address: fcbb:bb00:6:e007::

Fix on P2:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
 no ipv6 mtu
  • Layer 3 on P2 shows the cause.
  • The interface MTU is still 1514, but IPv6 can use only 1400. Somebody set an IPv6 MTU on this one link. This is the fault. In a real network, it is often a change on one link that nobody relates to a customer.
  • The Packet Too Big contains the outer packet from PE1, to the Layer 2 SID of PE6. Its MTU field shows 1336, not 1400.
  • We tested this later on XRd and on XRv9000. Both platforms show the MTU minus 64 when the destination route has a TI-LFA repair path. With no repair path, the value is correct.
  • Forwarding always uses the real MTU. We think that the 64 bytes are space for a repair header, but Cisco does not document this. Trust the capture, not only the reported value.
  • We removed one line, and the 1418-byte ping went through again. The finding: test with different sizes. When a size fails, capture on each link until the packet disappears.
18.3 · Fault 1: the configuration change

Router / tool: P2

! On P2, toward P4
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
 ipv6 mtu 1400

# Largest customer IP packet over E-Line with this limit:
# 1400 - 40 (outer IPv6 header) - 14 (inner Ethernet header) = 1346 bytes
  • This is the change on P2.
  • One command sets the IPv6 MTU to 1400 on the link toward P4. The interface MTU stays at 1514.
  • The arithmetic: 1400, minus 40 for the outer IPv6 header, minus 14 for the inner Ethernet header, is 1346. A customer packet larger than 1346 bytes cannot cross this link. This agrees with the pings: 1300 passed and 1400 failed.
18.4 · Fault 2: one direction

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 -W 2 -I 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2
3 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8 or icmp.type == 0" -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e icmp.type | sort | uniq -c
# CE-A to PE1       3 requests
# PE1 to P2         3 requests   fcbb:bb00:3:5:6:e004::
# P4 to PE6         3 requests   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::
# PE6 to CE-B       3 requests, and 3 replies from CE-B
  • Fault 2. BLUE does not operate: CE-A cannot ping CE-B. On PE1, all the layers look correct for the prefix of CE-B. Thus we go directly to the wire.
  • Three requests leave CE-A, and no replies come back.
  • The requests go through the core to the BLUE service SID on PE6.
  • CE-B receives them and replies three times. The replies arrive at PE6 and stop there. The forward direction is correct. The return direction is broken. A ping cannot show which direction is broken. A capture can.
18.5 · Fault 2: layer 4, on the other PE
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show route vrf BLUE 10.1.1.0/24
% Network not in table
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show bgp vpnv4 unicast rd 65000:101 10.1.1.0/24
Paths: (0 available, no best path)

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.1.1.0/24 detail
  Advertised to peers (in unique update groups):
    2001:db8:100::6
      Extended community: RT:65000:110
  • PE6 sends the return traffic. Thus we examine the layers on PE6, for the prefix of CE-A.
  • PE6 has no route to the subnet of CE-A in BLUE.
  • BGP has no path for it.
  • But PE1 shows that it advertised the route to PE6, with route target 65000:110. PE6 imports 65000:100. One digit is different.
  • PE6 received the route, found no VRF that matches, and discarded it. We set the export on PE1 back to 65000:100, and the fault was repaired.
  • The finding: when a ping fails, examine the two directions. Examine the PE where the reply stops, also when the customer who reports the problem is on the other side.

    unresolved

18.7 · Fault 3: down to layers 1 and 2

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 locator
FA128                 1        128   fcbb:bb01:6::/48          Up       U
MAIN                  2        0     fcbb:bb00:6::/48          Up       U
TEST                  3        0     fcbb:bb00:66::/48         Up       U

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show isis segment-routing srv6 locators
FA128                 1        128   fcbb:bb01:6::/48          Active
MAIN                  2        0     fcbb:bb00:6::/48          Active
TEST                  3        0     fcbb:bb00:66::/48         Inactive

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
    SRv6-VPN SID: fcbb:bb00:66:e008::/64
    Alloc Mode/Locator ID: per-vrf/3
  • Inaccessible points to layer 2. Thus we go to the owner, PE6.
  • Layer 1 shows a third locator, TEST. It is up locally.
  • Layer 2: IS-IS knows the locator, but shows it as inactive. Nobody added it under IS-IS. Thus the other routers cannot reach it.
  • The BGP configuration of GREEN allocates from it, locator ID 3. This is an incomplete change. Somebody made a new locator and moved a VRF to it, but did not do the IGP step.
  • We moved GREEN back to MAIN, and the fault was repaired. During the change, for approximately forty seconds, PE1 used the old SID, and PE6 had already removed it.
  • A change of SID is also an outage. Plan it.
18.8 · Fault 3: the configuration changes

Router / tool: PE6

! Step 1, on PE6: a new locator, and RED allocates from it
segment-routing srv6 locators locator TEST
 micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
 prefix fcbb:bb00:66::/48
router bgp 65000 vrf RED address-family ipv4 unicast
 segment-routing srv6 locator TEST
! (the locator is NOT added under router isis: the missing step)

! Step 2, on PE6: RED goes back to MAIN, and GREEN moves to TEST
router bgp 65000 vrf RED address-family ipv4 unicast
 segment-routing srv6 locator MAIN
router bgp 65000 vrf GREEN address-family ipv4 unicast
 segment-routing srv6 locator TEST
  • These are the configuration changes of fault 3, all on PE6. We made them in two steps.
  • Step 1 creates a locator TEST, and RED IPv4 allocates its service SID from it.
  • Look at the last line. The locator is not added under IS-IS. This is the missing step. Thus no other router has a route to it.
  • Step 2 puts RED back on MAIN, and moves GREEN to TEST. Now only GREEN depends on the broken locator. The twist after this page explains why RED survived in step 1.
18.9 · Fault 3: the repair

Router / tool: PE6

! Repair 1, on PE6: GREEN back to MAIN
router bgp 65000 vrf GREEN address-family ipv4 unicast
 segment-routing srv6 locator MAIN

! Repair 2, on PE6: remove the unused locator
segment-routing srv6 locators
 no locator TEST
  • Now the repair, also on PE6, in two steps.
  • Repair 1 moves GREEN back to the MAIN locator. The traffic recovers after the new SID is advertised.
  • Repair 2 removes the locator TEST, which nobody uses. Do this last. Remove a locator only after no VRF allocates from it.
18.10 · Fault 4: hidden until a link fails
Before the change:
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb01:6::/48
    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, from 2001:db8:100::6, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, Backup (TI-LFA)
    fe80::5454:ff:fec1:58eb, from 2001:db8:100::6, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1, Protected

After the change on P2 and P4, everything still passes:
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb01:6::/48
    fe80::5454:ff:fec1:58eb, from 2001:db8:100::6, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
  • Fault 4 is the most difficult type. When we make the change, nothing fails. We removed Flex-Algo 128 from P2 and P4. An engineer can make this change to make those routers simpler. RED IPv6 uses the algorithm 128 locator, and it continued to operate.
  • Before the change, the route on PE1 to the algorithm 128 locator of PE6 was protected, with a TI-LFA backup through P2.
  • After the change, there is one path and no protection. The algorithm 128 topology became one line: PE1, P3, P5, PE6. All pings still went through.
  • Only layer 2 showed the problem, and only when we compared it with the reference.
18.11 · Fault 4: the link fails
P3: interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1 shutdown   (the link to P5)

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 3 -W 2 -I 2001:db8:c:201::2 2001:db8:c:206::2
3 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb01:6::/48
% Network not in table
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf RED ipv6 2001:db8:c:206::/64
    unresolved
    0     Y   recursive                 drop

BLUE: 2 of 2.  RED IPv4: 2 of 2 (the PCE recomputed: latency 15000, via PE6's node SID).
  • Now the topology event: the link from P3 to P5 fails.
  • We shut it on P3.
  • RED IPv6 does not operate.
  • Layer 2: the algorithm 128 locator is not there. P2 and P4 are not in the algorithm, thus the algorithm has no other path. Layer 3 shows unresolved and drop.
  • All the other services continue. BLUE uses algorithm 0. RED IPv4 uses the policy from the PCE, and the PCE calculated a new path on the remaining links.
  • The customer that paid for the special path is the customer that lost service. We set the link and the algorithm back, and the route was protected again.
18.12 · The four configuration changes
! fault 1, on P2: a smaller IPv6 MTU toward P4
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
 ipv6 mtu 1400
! fault 2, on PE1: a different export route target
vrf BLUE
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  export route-target
   no 65000:100
   65000:110
! fault 3, on PE6: a locator that IS-IS does not advertise
! (full configuration on the Fault 3 pages)
locator TEST  prefix fcbb:bb00:66::/48
router bgp 65000 vrf RED address-family ipv4 unicast
 segment-routing srv6 locator TEST
! fault 4, on P2 and P4
router isis CORE
 no flex-algo 128
  • Here are the four changes, as the answer key. You can repeat each one in your lab, and then find it with the five layers, before you look at this page.
  • Fault 1: on P2, the IPv6 MTU of the link toward P4 is 1400.
  • Fault 2: on PE1, the export route target of BLUE IPv4 changes from 65000:100 to 65000:110.
  • Fault 3: on PE6, RED allocates its service SID from a new locator. IS-IS does not advertise this locator.
  • Fault 4: on P2 and P4, we remove Flex-Algo 128. The service is fine until a link fails.
Stage · Ep19 — Commands and results
19.1 · The untrusted port
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4
 description UNTRUSTED outside
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:ffff:1::1/64

Outside host, on CE-A's third port:
CE-A:~$ sudo ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:ffff:1::2/64 dev eth2
CE-A:~$ sudo ip -6 route add fcbb:bb00::/31 via 2001:db8:ffff:1::1
CE-A:~$ sudo ip -6 route add 2001:db8:100::/64 via 2001:db8:ffff:1::1
  • Now the test. The port for the Layer 2 service in Episode 14 becomes a port that is not trusted, in the global table of PE1. In a real network, it can be an internet peering, a management network or a customer that makes mistakes.
  • It has a plain IPv6 address, with no VRF.
  • The outside host gets an address on that link.
  • The host also gets routes to the two SID blocks and to the loopbacks, through PE1. A real attacker does not need these routes. A default route does the same.
19.2 · Before: the outside reaches the core

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -W 2 fcbb:bb00:6::
64 bytes from 2001:db8:100::6: seq=0 ttl=61 time=3.693 ms
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -W 2 fcbb:bb00:4::
64 bytes from 2001:db8:100::4: seq=0 ttl=62 time=1.757 ms
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -W 2 fcbb:bb00:6:e000::
64 bytes from 2001:db8:100::6: seq=0 ttl=61 time=1.801 ms
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -W 2 fcbb:bb00:6:e004::
64 bytes from 2001:db8:100::6: seq=0 ttl=61 time=1.656 ms
  • There is no filter yet. The outside host tries the SIDs of the core.
  • The node SID of PE6 gets a reply, from the loopback of PE6.
  • The node SID of P4, a transit router, gets a reply.
  • One of the adjacency SIDs of PE6 gets a reply.
  • The BLUE service SID also gets a reply. From outside the network, an unknown person touched the door to the VRF of a customer.
  • As Episode 17 showed, a ping does not cause a VRF lookup. But it shows that packets from outside arrive at the SID. A host that also makes the inner packet needs nothing more. We did not do that attack. It was not necessary.
19.3 · Before, on the wire

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmpv6.type == 128 or icmpv6.type == 129" \
    -T fields -e ipv6.src -e ipv6.dst -e icmpv6.type | sort | uniq -c
# PE1 to P2: requests and replies
  2  2001:db8:ffff:1::2   fcbb:bb00:6::         128
  2  2001:db8:ffff:1::2   fcbb:bb00:4::         128
  2  2001:db8:100::6      2001:db8:ffff:1::2    129
  2  2001:db8:100::4      2001:db8:ffff:1::2    129
# P4 to PE6
  2  2001:db8:ffff:1::2   fcbb:bb00:6::         128
  2  2001:db8:100::6      2001:db8:ffff:1::2    129
  • This is the capture from that test. We read each file with tshark. Type 128 is a request, and type 129 is a reply.
  • On the link PE1 to P2, the requests of the outside host went into the core with no change, to the SIDs. The loopbacks of the routers replied.
  • The same request arrived at PE6. Nothing at the edge stopped a packet from outside the domain to an instruction in the domain.
19.4 · What the platform lists

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 manager
  Security rules:
    SEC-1
    SEC-2
    SEC-3
  • Does the router protect itself? The SRv6 manager shows security rules.
  • These are SEC-1 to SEC-3. The names come from RFC 8754, section 5.1. It describes filters at the domain edge and on SR nodes.
  • The list shows what the software supports. Our test shows the result without our filter: each SID replied to the outside host. A rule in the list is not a configured rule. Episode 14 gave the same finding about capabilities.
19.5 · The boundary ACL
ipv6 access-list SRV6-BOUNDARY-IN
 10 deny ipv6 any fcbb:bb00::/31 log
 20 deny ipv6 any any routing log
 30 permit ipv6 any any
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4
 ipv6 access-group SRV6-BOUNDARY-IN ingress
  • The repair is an access list on each interface that faces outside the SR domain.
  • Line 10: no packet from outside can go to the SID space. One slash 31 prefix includes the two blocks: fcbb:bb00 for algorithm 0 and fcbb:bb01 for algorithm 128. This is an advantage of blocks that are next to each other.
  • Line 20: no packet with a routing header can go in. On this release, the ACL did not accept routing-type 4. It accepted the general routing keyword.
  • All other packets are permitted.
  • We apply the ACL inbound on the port that is not trusted.
19.6 · After: the door is shut

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -W 2 -I 2001:db8:ffff:1::2 fcbb:bb00:6::
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -W 2 -I 2001:db8:ffff:1::2 fcbb:bb00:4::
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -W 2 -I 2001:db8:ffff:1::2 fcbb:bb00:6:e000::
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -W 2 -I 2001:db8:ffff:1::2 fcbb:bb00:6:e004::
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -W 2 -I 2001:db8:ffff:1::2 2001:db8:100::6
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
  • We do the same tests with the ACL.
  • The four SIDs get no reply.
  • The loopback of PE6 still replies. The boundary stops only the SID space. Usual reachability does not change.
  • Look at the -I option. Without it, the outside host used a different address as the source. PE6 had no route back to that address, thus the loopback ping also failed. When a test fails, examine the source address before you blame the filter.
19.7 · After, on the wire

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmpv6.type == 128" -T fields -e ipv6.src -e ipv6.dst | sort | uniq -c
# outside host to PE1, on the port that is not trusted
  2  2001:db8:ffff:1::2   fcbb:bb00:4::
  2  2001:db8:ffff:1::2   fcbb:bb00:6::
  1  2001:db8:ffff:1::2   fcbb:bb00:6:e000::
# PE1 to P2
(no echo request)
  • Did the ACL drop the packets? We use captures to see this, with the same command.
  • The requests arrived at the port of PE1 that is not trusted.
  • None of them appeared on the core link of PE1. Thus PE1 dropped them at the edge.
  • On this platform, the deny counters of the ACL showed no matches. Verify the filter with a packet from outside and a capture inside. Do not use a counter as your only evidence.
19.8 · Planning the SID space for the boundary

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 manager
  SRv6 Operational Mode:
    Micro-segment:
      SID Base Block: fcbb:bb00::/24

Blocks in use:     fcbb:bb00::/32 (algorithm 0)   fcbb:bb01::/32 (algorithm 128)
Our ACL line:      deny ipv6 any fcbb:bb00::/31
Whole base block:  deny ipv6 any fcbb:bb00::/24
  • One more design point: how large must the deny prefix be?
  • The manager shows the micro-SID base block: fcbb:bb00::/24. All the blocks that this router can use are in it.
  • This lab uses two SID blocks, and our ACL line includes only those two.
  • If you deny all the base block, you also include each block that you add later. This can be another algorithm, or a migration block in Module 6.
  • The small prefix is precise. With the large prefix, you do not forget a block when the network grows. Select one, and record the reason.
19.9 · Scale: the numbers on PE6

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 manager
      uSID LIB Range:
        LIB Start   : 0xe000
        ELIB Start  : 0xfe00
Summary:
  Number of Locators: 2 (2 operational)
  Number of SIDs: 14 (0 stale)
  Max SID resources: 64000
  Number of free SID resources: 63986
    Block fcbb:bb00::/32:
        Number of SIDs free: 7671
        Max SIDs: 7680
  Max Locators: 16
  • Now scale. The layer 1 command from Episode 17 shows the numbers.
  • The local SID range starts at e000 and stops before fe00. All the functions in this lab came from this range: e004, e007, e00b. They are local, and each router uses the same values again, as Episode 16 showed.
  • PE6 uses 14 SIDs from 64000 resources.
  • Each block has 7680 SIDs. This is the size of the range from e000 to fdff. Thus the real limit for each locator is the local range, not the total.
  • The maximum is 16 locators.

Acceptance: Compare each result with its interpretation. Record missing checks as Not verified. Restore the stated baseline before another experiment.

Questions:

  1. Why can a forward-path capture miss an RT fault?
  2. Which two checks reveal a protection fault before customer pings fail?

12

Migration, hardware checks, and integrated experiments

Experiment focus: Accept each migration state

Core topology: link cost and service endpoints

Migration has intermediate states that need separate checks. The two directions can use different transports. Control sessions can still depend on the previous transport after customer migration. Remove an old dependency only after its remaining users are identified.

Observations and interpretation: This chapter records which direction changes after one egress PE changes. It defines rollback conditions and identifies untested hardware requirements.

Starting state: Complete one migration and its rollback before you try another migration method.

Migrate one dependency at a time

The source migrations follow one sequence: coexistence, new-path acceptance, service transfer, bidirectional checks, and previous-system removal. A rollback restores a known state and includes the same acceptance checks.

The change plan must have a measurable rollback condition. Examples include missing customer routes, failed size tests, or an incorrect policy path. A correct configuration commit is not a migration acceptance condition.

Reason from the evidence: When can the old transport be removed?

GREEN uses SRv6 in both directions. Label 16006 still counts traffic. Does the customer capture justify immediate SR-MPLS removal?

Predict the result, then compare the explanation

No. The IPv4 BGP session can still use that transport. Customer packets and control sessions have separate dependencies.

Identify the remaining label user. Move or remove that dependency, then observe counters and captures again. The measured 1251→1251 interval proves only that observation window.

LDP to SRv6

LDP: GREEN {24009 24000} · VPNv4 10.0.0.1 ↔ 10.0.0.6

The egress PE advertises the service information that the ingress uses. Thus, changing PE6's GREEN allocation changes PE1-to-PE6 traffic first. The opposite direction can stay MPLS.

Stage PE1 to PE6 PE6 to PE1
Initial MPLS VPN MPLS MPLS
PE6 allocates an SRv6 service SID SRv6 MPLS
PE1 also allocates an SRv6 service SID SRv6 SRv6
PE6 allocation returns to the MPLS state MPLS SRv6

The route can arrive over an IPv4 BGP session and carry SRv6 service information. Session transport does not determine customer encapsulation. The selected route attributes and forwarding resolution determine it.

The source kept LDP until the two directions passed. The service packet increased by 32 bytes relative to its two-label form. MTU acceptance thus preceded removal of the previous transport.

Start with the topology. Customer GREEN is attached through CE-A and CE-B. The core runs IS-IS for IPv4, with LDP on every core link. PE1 and PE6 have a VPNv4 session over IPv4, between the loopbacks 10.0.0.1 and 10.0.0.6. BLUE and RED stay on SRv6, with their IPv6 session. A GREEN packet goes through P2 and P4.

On PE1, check the three facts of this starting point:

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show mpls ldp neighbor brief
10.0.0.2:0   N   N   00:01:26 ...
10.0.0.3:0   N   N   00:01:24 ...

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
      Received Label 24000

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
     next hop 10.12.0.1/32 GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 labels imposed {24009 24000}

The first output shows LDP sessions to P2 and P3. The second shows a real MPLS label, 24000, from PE6. The third shows two labels: 24009 is the LDP label to PE6, and 24000 is the VPN label. Compare this with one IPv6 header and one SID.

SR-MPLS to SRv6

SR-MPLS: prefix SID labels 16001–16006 · No LDP

The source SR-MPLS transport label for PE6 is 16006. It comes from SRGB start 16000 and prefix index 6. For this index, the same SRGB start value is necessary for equal labels on each hop. Different SRGBs can produce different labels.

After the customer migration, the label counter increased by 99 bytes in 60 seconds. The capture showed a 59-byte BGP keepalive and a 40-byte TCP acknowledgment. The IPv4 BGP session itself used SR-MPLS transport.

After removal of that session, the counter stopped increasing during the observation period. GREEN passed. Thus, customer migration alone did not prove that the previous transport was no longer in use.

Start with the topology. The core runs IS-IS for IPv4 with segment routing for MPLS, and no LDP. Each router has a prefix SID index. The label is 16000 plus that index: PE1 16001, P2 16002, P3 16003, P4 16004, P5 16005, PE6 16006. A GREEN packet leaves PE1 with two labels: 16006 reaches PE6, and 24000 is the VPN label.

Follow four steps. In each step, run the commands and compare the output.

Step 1: configure SR-MPLS. On every router (here P2, with index 2) and on the PEs:

router isis CORE
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  segment-routing mpls
 interface Loopback0
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   prefix-sid index 2

On PE1, the result is:

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
     next hop 10.12.0.1/32 GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 labels imposed {16006 24000}

Step 2: move GREEN to SRv6. On PE6 and PE1, allocate the GREEN service SID from the locator:

router bgp 65000
 vrf GREEN
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
    alloc mode per-vrf

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e008::}

Step 3: find the remaining users of label 16006. After the move, the counter of label 16006 still grew. A BGP keepalive of 59 bytes and a TCP acknowledgment of 40 bytes use the label. Remove the IPv4 VPN session, and read the counter twice, about one minute apart:

router bgp 65000
 no neighbor 10.0.0.6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show mpls forwarding prefix 10.0.0.6/32     (00:28:51)
16006  16006   SR Pfx (idx 6)   Gi0/0/0/0   10.12.0.1   1251
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show mpls forwarding prefix 10.0.0.6/32     (00:29:53)
16006  16006   SR Pfx (idx 6)   Gi0/0/0/0   10.12.0.1   1251

The counter is 1251 both times. It stopped. GREEN still works over SRv6. PE6 removes the neighbor 10.0.0.1 in the same way.

Step 4: remove SR-MPLS. Do this last, and only after the counter stopped. On every router (here PE1):

no router isis CORE address-family ipv4 unicast
no router isis CORE interface Loopback0 address-family ipv4 unicast
no router isis CORE interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 address-family ipv4 unicast
no router isis CORE interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1 address-family ipv4 unicast
commit

The running configuration of IS-IS then has only the SRv6 lines. Then run a ping to confirm that GREEN still works.

OSPF to IS-IS

OSPF 110 → IS-IS 100 → OSPF removed · Link cost 10/40

The source ran the two IGPs with matching costs and no redistribution. OSPF distance 110 selected the loopback route. IS-IS distance 115 selected the locator route because OSPF did not advertise that locator in this setup.

Changing the IS-IS IPv6 distance to 100 made IS-IS select the loopback route too. The source then checked routes, protection, services, and policy paths. OSPF removal followed those checks.

A missing OSPF next-hop route can cause an IS-IS route to become active. Next-hop resolution fails only when there is no usable resolution path. OSPF's presence does not inherently prevent SRv6 operation. OSPFv3 SRv6 extensions exist, but this lab did not build that alternative.

Ordinary route redistribution does not keep all SRv6 advertisements and algorithm information. Two-way redistribution also introduces loop-prevention requirements. The source avoided those dependencies by changing route preference.

Start with the topology. IS-IS runs on all six routers and advertises the loopbacks and the SRv6 locators. Add OSPF for IPv4 and OSPFv3 for IPv6 on all six routers, in area 0. The link costs are the same in both IGPs: 40 on the lower links (PE1–P3, P3–P5, P5–PE6), and 10 on the others. Thus both IGPs select the same paths.

Follow the owner of two routes through three states.

State PE6 loopback 2001:db8:100::6 PE6 locator fcbb:bb00:6::/48
1. Both IGPs, default distance OSPF, distance 110 IS-IS, distance 115
2. After step 1: IS-IS distance 100 IS-IS, distance 100 IS-IS, distance 100
3. After step 2: OSPF removed IS-IS, distance 100 IS-IS, distance 100

Check state 1 on PE1:

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 2001:db8:100::6/128
  Known via "ospf LEGACY", distance 110, metric 30, type intra area
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2

Step 1: prefer IS-IS. On every router:

router isis CORE
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  distance 100
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  distance 100

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 2001:db8:100::6/128
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 100, metric 30, type level-2

Step 2: remove OSPF. On every router:

no router ospf LEGACY
no router ospfv3 LEGACY

No OSPF neighbors remain. The selected routing table does not change, because IS-IS already supplies these routes. BLUE and GREEN pings receive replies. The real change is step 1. Step 2 only removes a protocol that nobody uses.

Hardware acceptance

The virtual experiments show specified control-plane and packet-format results. They do not show NPU capacity, line-card support, or guaranteed recovery time.

Test the hardware families that you run. Examples are the Cisco NCS 540, the ASR 9000 and the Cisco 8800. Each family has its own guide, its own limits and its own restrictions. Read the guide for your release. Then compare it with the output of show segment-routing srv6 manager on XRd. Some hardware needs a micro-SID hardware profile and a reload. Our virtual routers did not need this step.

A target hardware acceptance plan must include the following items:

  1. Record the exact chassis, line cards, software, and feature licenses.
  2. Read the matching Cisco feature restrictions.
  3. Apply any necessary hardware profile in the documented maintenance procedure.
  4. After a necessary reload, make sure that the profile is active.
  5. Do the longest policy and repair packet tests again.
  6. Do the MTU tests with each installed backup type again.
  7. Measure loss and restoration under the necessary traffic load.
  8. Do a capacity check with the planned service allocation.
  9. Do the E-LAN tests on a supported forwarding implementation.
  10. Do the EVPN IRB anycast gateway tests (below).

Hardware-only test: EVPN IRB anycast gateway

We could not test this. Our virtual platforms rejected the bridge domain (see the E-LAN section of the EVPN chapter). Test it on hardware, in two cases.

Case 1: an OLT with a bundle to two PEs. The two links form one Ethernet segment (ESI). EVPN multihoming uses route types 1 and 4. Both PEs have an IRB interface with the same IP address and the same MAC address. This is the anycast gateway. The OLT can use either PE.

OLT bundle · shared ESI · PE-A / PE-B: IRB 10.50.0.1, same MAC

Case 2: two firewalls in a square. PE-A and PE-B connect to FW1 and FW2 in a square. Option 1: both PEs have the same anycast gateway, and each firewall uses it. Option 2: the firewalls run HSRP or VRRP between them, and the PEs only carry the VLAN. We did not test either option. Compare them on your hardware.

PE-A ↔ SRv6 core ↔ PE-B · Firewall square

Verify these points in both cases:

  1. Control plane: capture route types 1, 2 and 4, with the ESI and the MAC and IP of the gateway.
  2. Gateway: both PEs answer ARP or ND for the gateway with the same MAC address.
  3. Failure: shut one PE link, and measure how long the traffic stops. Check that it recovers.
  4. Loops and MAC moves: capture on both PEs. Look for loops and for repeated MAC moves.
  5. Path: capture on the core. Check which PE sends the packet, and with which SID.

Worked example: Change one egress first

First let PE6 allocate an SRv6 service SID. PE1 uses that advertised service information, so PE1-to-PE6 traffic changes first. The return direction can still use the MPLS information advertised by PE1. The directions do not have to change together.

Read the figures: F51–F54 show the initial, one-sided, two-sided, and rollback states. F55 identifies a remaining old-transport user: the IPv4 BGP session.

Think first: Which evidence separates completed customer migration from permission to remove the previous transport?

L12 — Migration and integrated experiments

Starting state: Treat LDP, SR-MPLS, and OSPF migration as separate starting states. Rebuild the stated baseline for each.

Run commands at the named router or tool. Prompts and results are evidence; do not paste them as commands.

Enter configuration blocks in configuration mode. Commit each complete change before its verification step. Read output before the next change.

Start packet capture on the named links before sending test traffic. Match packet direction, addresses, and header fields.

Excerpts omit unrelated lines. Dynamic SIDs and counters can differ. A configuration block alone does not prove success.

20.1 · The legacy configuration on PE1
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
 ipv4 address 10.12.0.0 255.255.255.254
router isis CORE

  metric-style wide

  address-family ipv4 unicast

  remote-as 65000

mpls ldp

  • IPv4 is in the same IS-IS instance, with the same metrics as IPv6.
  • There is a VPNv4 session to the IPv4 loopback of PE6.
  • LDP is on the core interfaces. GREEN has no SRv6 allocation on any router.
20.2 · GREEN on MPLS
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show mpls ldp neighbor brief
10.0.0.2:0         N   N    00:01:26    1     0     4     0     14     0
10.0.0.3:0         N   N    00:01:24    1     0     4     0     14     0

    10.0.0.6 (metric 30) from 10.0.0.6 (10.0.0.6), if-handle 0x00000000
      Received Label 24000

    next hop 10.0.0.6/32 via 24011/0/21

  • This is GREEN on MPLS, as an older network shows it.
  • There are LDP sessions to P2 and P3.
  • The GREEN route from PE6 has next hop 10.0.0.6 and a real MPLS label, 24000.
  • CEF pushes two labels. 24009 is the LDP label to PE6, and 24000 is the VPN label. Compare this with Episode 13: one IPv6 header with one SID.
20.3 · Both worlds on one wire
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 3
Success rate is 100 percent (3/3), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf BLUE 10.100.6.6 source 10.100.1.1 count 2
Success rate is 100 percent (2/2), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "mpls or ipv6.nxt == 4" -T fields -e frame.len -e mpls.label -e ipv6.dst -e icmp.type
# PE1 to P2        122   24009,24000          GREEN request, MPLS
#                  154   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::   BLUE request, SRv6
# P2 to P4         122   24009,24000          GREEN request
#                  154   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::   BLUE request
# P4 to PE6        118   24000                GREEN request, top label popped
#                  154   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::   BLUE request
  • We captured on three core links while PE1 sent 100-byte pings to GREEN and to BLUE. We read each file with tshark.
  • Both pings work. When they leave PE1, GREEN has two labels, 122 bytes. BLUE has an IPv6 header, 154 bytes.
  • It is the same on the link from P2 to P4.
  • On the last link, GREEN has no top label. P4 removed it: this is penultimate-hop popping. BLUE does not change from end to end. The two technologies use each router and each link, and they do not affect each other.
  • Look at the sizes. The SRv6 packet is 32 bytes larger than the MPLS packet with two labels. When GREEN moves, it loses 32 bytes of MTU. Examine this before you migrate, with the method of Episode 7.
20.4 · Reading the labels hop by hop

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "mpls" -T fields -e frame.len -e mpls.label -e icmp.type
# GREEN request, from PE1 to PE6
PE1 to P2     122   24009,24000
P2 to P4      122   24009,24000
P4 to PE6     118   24000          (the top label was popped by P4)
# GREEN reply, from PE6 to PE1
P4 to PE6     122   24001,24000
P2 to P4      122   24000,24000
PE1 to P2     118   24000          (the top label was already popped)
  • We look at MPLS again, because it shows what SRv6 removes.
  • PE1 sends 24009 on top. This is the label of P2 for PE6. Below it is 24000, the VPN label of PE6.
  • P2 replaces the top label with the label of P4 for PE6. This label is also 24009. Each router has its own labels. The equal numbers are a coincidence.
  • P4 removes the top label before PE6.
  • The replies show the same pattern in the opposite direction, and PE6 starts with 24001. Each router keeps a label table for each PE. With SRv6, the transit routers forwarded one IPv6 destination that did not change. They used their usual routing table.
20.5 · Step 1: PE6 moves first
router bgp 65000
 vrf GREEN
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
    alloc mode per-vrf

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
    10.0.0.6 (metric 30) from 10.0.0.6 (10.0.0.6), if-handle 0x00000000
      Received Label 0xe0080
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: 31

Success rate is 100 percent (3/3), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/3/6 ms
  • Step 1. Only PE6 changes.
  • PE6 allocates an SRv6 SID for GREEN. These are the same five lines as for BLUE in Episode 12.
  • On PE1, the GREEN route now arrives with a SID. Look at the next hop: it is still 10.0.0.6, the IPv4 session. PE6 advertised the SID on the two sessions, and PE1 selected the path from the IPv4 session.
  • This is not important. The SID selects the encapsulation. The session does not.
  • CEF now encapsulates with the GREEN SID of PE6.
  • GREEN operates.
20.6 · Step 1: one route, two paths
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast rd 65000:306 10.30.6.6/32
Paths: (2 available, best #1)
  Path #1: Received by speaker 0
    10.0.0.6 (metric 30) from 10.0.0.6 (10.0.0.6)
      Received Label 0xe0080
      Origin incomplete, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal, best, group-best
  Path #2: Received by speaker 0
    2001:db8:100::6 (metric 30) from 2001:db8:100::6 (10.0.0.6)
      Received Label 0xe0080
      Origin incomplete, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal
  • Why did PE1 use the path from the IPv4 session? This is the route from PE6 on PE1, before the import into GREEN.
  • The same route has two paths, one from each session.
  • Path 1 is over IPv4, with the SID. It is the best path.
  • Path 2 is over IPv6, with the same SID. All the attributes in the output are equal. Thus the last BGP tie-break rules selected the path.
  • The two paths go to the same SID and make the same packet. During a migration, two sessions are usual. Know which path is best, and why.

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 3
Success rate is 100 percent (3/3), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/3/6 ms

  • The wire shows the result of step 1, on the link PE1 to P2. The ping works.
  • The requests from PE1 to PE6 are SRv6, because their egress, PE6, moved.
  • The replies from PE6 to PE1 are still MPLS, because their egress, PE1, did not move. One customer and one ping use two technologies, and the ping operates. One end can move first.

router bgp 65000

  address-family ipv4 unicast

      Received Label 24000

Success rate is 100 percent (3/3), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/4/6 ms
  • Now the test that each change plan needs: can we go back? PE1 had already moved, and we rolled back step 1 on PE6.
  • One line on PE6 removes the SRv6 allocation of GREEN.
  • PE1 receives label 24000 again.
  • CEF uses the two labels again. LDP was still in operation, thus the transport label was ready.
  • GREEN goes through. On the wire, the requests were MPLS again. The replies stayed SRv6, because we did not roll back PE1. The two directions use different technologies again, but in the opposite way.
  • We applied step 1 again, and the two directions were SRv6 again.
20.10 · Rollback on the wire
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 3

  3   154                       fcbb:bb00:1:e00a::   10.30.6.6    GREEN reply: still SRv6
  • This is the capture during the rollback. The ping works.
  • The requests to PE6 are MPLS again, with two labels, because PE6 withdrew its SID.
  • The replies to PE1 stay SRv6, to the GREEN SID of PE1. The rule is also true in the opposite direction: each direction follows its egress, when the egress moves forward or back.

router bgp 65000
 no neighbor 10.0.0.6
no mpls ldp                                 (on all six routers)

  • Step 3: remove the MPLS configuration, in sequence.
  • First, remove the IPv4 BGP session on the two PEs.
  • Then remove LDP on all six routers.
  • The GREEN route now comes from the IPv6 loopback of PE6, with its SID.
  • The MPLS forwarding table is empty, and there are no LDP neighbors.
  • GREEN and BLUE go through. On the wire, GREEN is SRv6 in the two directions. The migration is complete.

21.1 · Step 1: SR-MPLS configuration
On every router, here P2:

21.6 · Step 3: who still uses label 16006?
Before the move:
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show mpls forwarding prefix 10.0.0.6/32
Local  Outgoing    Prefix             Outgoing     Next Hop        Bytes
16006  16006       SR Pfx (idx 6)     Gi0/0/0/0    10.12.0.1       872

After the move, GREEN on SRv6:
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show mpls forwarding prefix 10.0.0.6/32
Local  Outgoing    Prefix             Outgoing     Next Hop        Bytes
16006  16006       SR Pfx (idx 6)     Gi0/0/0/0    10.12.0.1       1415
  • GREEN uses SRv6 now. Does SR-MPLS still carry traffic?
  • Before migration, the label entry for PE6 showed 872 switched bytes.
  • After migration, the counter showed 1415 bytes. Some traffic still used label 16006. We tested the cause later. During sixty seconds with no customer traffic, the counter increased by 99 bytes.
  • The capture showed two labeled packets for the IPv4 BGP session to 10.0.0.6. A BGP keepalive was 59 bytes. A TCP acknowledgement was 40 bytes. Together, they account for the 99-byte increase.
  • After we removed that session, the counter stopped increasing. The old transport still carried control traffic. Identify all traffic that uses the old transport before you remove it.

10.0.0.2        1     FULL/  -        00:00:37    10.12.0.1       GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0

On every router:

  • Step 1 makes IS-IS preferred. Both protocols remain configured.
  • We set IS-IS distance 100 in both address families on all six routers. It is lower than the OSPF distance of 110. OSPF adjacencies remain Full, so its routes remain available.

  • The IPv4 metric is 30. Under OSPFv2, it was 31 because OSPFv2 added the loopback interface cost of 1. Equal link costs did not produce equal totals. Compare total costs and selected paths before you rely on a mixed network.

Questions:

  1. Which traffic direction changes when only PE6 allocates the new SRv6 service SID?
  2. Why can an MPLS label counter increase after the customer service moves to SRv6?

Build and complete the integrated experiments in five stages

Accept each stage before the next. The following cases combine earlier tests. An integrated A–E run is Not verified.

Case A

Do： Flap a test loopback, then capture its BGP update.

Measure： Reconstruct the function from the label and SID structure.

Proof： Use L5, stages 13.2–13.7. The example 0xE0040 >> 4 gives e004.

Case B

Do： Start continuous traffic and captures, then fail P2–P4.

Measure： Count loss and identify repair, convergence, and restoration.

Proof： Use L8, stages 9.8–9.12. Repeat the event; do not infer a fixed recovery time.

Case C

Do： Increase the customer IP size in L3VPN and VPWS separately.

Measure： Find the largest passing size, then add one byte.

Proof： Use L6 and L7. Without SRH, 1500−40=1460 and 1500−40−14=1446.

Case D

Do： Introduce one RT fault and trace both directions.

Measure： Find where the reply stops.

Proof： Use L11, stages 18.4–18.5. Restore the RT, then repeat delivery and isolation checks.

Case E

Do： Restore the routed port, then compare probes before and after the ACL.

Measure： Compare captures and a permitted control probe.

Proof： Use L11, stages 19.1–19.7. Zero deny counters do not prove that traffic passed.

A

Appendix A — Controlled terminology

These definitions control the technical meanings in this experiment record. Product names, protocol names, commands, and field names keep their initial spelling.

Term Meaning
SID Segment identifier. An IPv6 value associated with an SRv6 behavior.
locator A routable prefix that directs traffic to an SRv6 node.
behavior The packet operation associated with a local SID.
function The local operation identified by the function bits.
argument The part of a SID that carries more information for its behavior.
uSID A compressed segment identifier in the lab encoding.
NEXT-CSID The compressed-SID mechanism that advances identifiers in a container.
container A 128-bit address that can contain multiple compressed instructions.
DA Destination Address. The IPv6 address that selects the current forwarding destination.
SRH Segment Routing Header. IPv6 routing header type 4.
Segments Left The SRH field for remaining segment-list processing. It does not count each compressed instruction.
PSP / USP / USD Endpoint flavors for specified header-removal operations.
headend The router that applies the SR Policy to traffic.
ingress / egress The entry and exit points of the service transport.
PE / P / CE Provider edge router, provider core router, and customer edge device.
underlay The network that supplies transport reachability.
RIB / FIB / CEF Routing information base, forwarding information base, and Cisco Express Forwarding.
LSP In IS-IS, a link-state PDU. In a PCE context, a label-switched path object.
VRF A different routing and forwarding context for a service.
RD / RT Route distinguisher and route target. RD distinguishes VPN routes. RT controls their import.
NLRI Network Layer Reachability Information in a BGP update.
transposition The encoding that places selected SID bits in an NLRI label field.
Binding SID A SID associated with an SR Policy.
color The route attribute used for policy selection in this lab.
ODN On-demand next hop. A template-based mechanism for policy creation.
PCE / PCC / PCEP Path computation element, path computation client, and their communication protocol.
FAD Flexible Algorithm Definition. The parameters for a flexible algorithm.
TI-LFA / PLR Topology-different loop-free alternate and point of local repair.
microloop A temporary forwarding loop during inconsistent route updates.
BFD Bidirectional Forwarding Detection. A failure-detection protocol.
MTU / PMTUD / PTB Maximum transmission unit, path MTU discovery, and Packet Too Big.
packet / frame An IP packet contains an IP header. An Ethernet frame also contains the Ethernet header.
FCS Frame check sequence. The size tables exclude it.
DSCP / Traffic Class The differentiated-services code point and the IPv6 field that includes it.
VPWS / E-LAN / BUM Point-to-point service, multipoint Ethernet service, and broadcast/unknown-unicast/multicast traffic.
attachment circuit The local customer connection of an L2 service.
SRGB Segment Routing Global Block. The label range used with SR-MPLS prefix indices.
fallback Use of an alternative forwarding method when the requested policy is unavailable.
capture A stored observation of packets at a specified interface.
baseline The recorded working state used for comparison and restoration.

Reading conventions

Packet and frame sizes have different measurement boundaries. Read each size with its encapsulation conditions. State values, commands, and error messages retain their original spelling.

B

Appendix B — Answers and a worked diagnosis

Each row answers the two questions in the specified chapter.

Chapter Answer
01 Core routers keep IGP, locator forwarding, local SID, and protection state. The role depends on the packet destination.
02 Different prefixes permit different reachability checks. The final test-port configuration has a routed address and boundary ACL, not VPWS configuration.
03 Six positions stay. A SID ping reply does not prove customer decapsulation or a BLUE lookup.
04 Yes. Compare the originating LSP and SPF route with the local RIB. A local filter can affect only the latter.
05 The function is e005. Correct forward delivery does not prove a usable return route or matching reverse-direction RT.
06 The limit is 1420 bytes: 1500 minus 40 minus 8 minus 32. A PTB report can differ from the actual forwarding limit.
07 VPWS carries the more inner Ethernet header. A listed behavior does not prove bridge-domain support.
08 The adjacency avoids the previous shortest path through the failed resource. The microloop delay gives information about temporary path use, not customer loss.
09 Each uN uses the IGP shortest path to its node. The PCE location does not determine the customer path.
10 FAD receipt and local participation are different conditions. A service SID from FA128 can select its topology without a color or policy.
11 An RT error can affect only the return route. Algorithm participation and installed backup checks reveal the latent protection fault.
12 PE1-to-PE6 changes first. A remaining IPv4 BGP session can use MPLS transport for its own packets.

Worked case: one direction fails

Symptom: CE-A sends a BLUE ping to CE-B. CE-A receives no reply.

Initial hypothesis: The forward SRv6 path is broken.

Observation 1: The CE-B access capture contains the request. This observation rejects the initial hypothesis for that packet.

Observation 2: CE-B sends a reply to PE6. The PE6 core capture contains no related return packet.

Observation 3: PE6's BLUE table has no route to the source network of CE-A. PE1 exports that route with RT 65000:110. PE6 imports 65000:100.

Cause: The route-target mismatch prevents return-route import. The missing reply does not prove failed forward encapsulation.

Repair procedure:

  1. Restore the intended PE1 export RT.
  2. Make sure that PE6 BLUE has the correct return route.
  3. Make sure that the return CEF entry is usable.
  4. Do the initial ping again.
  5. Capture the two directions.
  6. Do a RED test to detect an unintended change again.

Evidence of completion: The two access captures contain the request and reply. The two core directions use their correct service SIDs. RED keeps its specified behavior.

Common service commands

These are read commands. Some detailed forms change by release. The source logs contain the exact commands accepted in each source test.

Linux size example

For these examples, use a Linux ping implementation with the shown options. The stock BusyBox command can have different options. These commands are examples for BLUE at CE-A, not host configuration commands.

# IPv4: 1432 data + 8 ICMP + 20 IP = 1460 bytes
ping -4 -I 10.1.1.2 -M do -s 1432 -c 3 10.1.6.2
# IPv4: one byte above the simple L3VPN limit
ping -4 -I 10.1.1.2 -M do -s 1433 -c 3 10.1.6.2
# IPv6: 1388 data + 8 ICMPv6 + 40 IPv6 = 1436 bytes
ping -6 -I 2001:db8:c:101::2 -M do -s 1388 -c 3 2001:db8:c:106::2

The IPv6 example assumes the one-entry SRH policy. A plain one-container service has a different limit. An explicit source does not create a missing route on the CE. The host must also have the correct gateway and source-routing state.

Useful Wireshark display filters

ipv6.dst == fcbb:bb00:6:e004::
ipv6.nxt == 43
icmpv6.type == 2
icmp.type == 3 && icmp.code == 4
bgp
mpls

The first filter uses a recorded SID. The current value can differ. A missing match is meaningful only when the capture covers the correct interface, time, and traffic direction.

Ep01 · Where the State Lives

1.1 What P2 actually holds

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show bgp summary
% BGP instance 'default' not active

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show route vrf all summary
VRF: **iid
connected                        0          0          0           0
Total                            0          0          0           0

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show segment-routing srv6 locator
Name                  ID       Algo  Prefix                    Status   Flags
FA128                 1        128   fcbb:bb01:2::/48          Up       U
MAIN                  2        0     fcbb:bb00:2::/48          Up       U

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show segment-routing srv6 manager | include Number of SIDs
  Number of SIDs: 12 (0 stale)
  • Now we examine P2 in the finished lab. All the services in this lab go through it.
  • BGP does not run on P2.
  • There is no customer VRF. The only entry is an internal entry with no routes.
  • P2 has two locators. MAIN is the locator that we use most. The second locator is for Flex-Algo. Episode 11 explains it.
  • P2 has 12 local SIDs: its node and adjacency SIDs. With three customers or three thousand customers, P2 keeps the same state.

1.2 And what PE1 holds

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 sid
fcbb:bb00:1:e004::          uDT4              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e005::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e006::          uDT6              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e007::          uDT6              'RED'                             bgp-65000           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e00a::          uDT4              'GREEN'                           bgp-65000           InUse  Y

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route vrf all summary
VRF: RED     ...  bgp 65000      2
VRF: BLUE    ...  bgp 65000      2
VRF: GREEN   ...  bgp 65000      1
  • Now the edge. This is PE1 in the same finished lab.
  • PE1 has a service SID for each customer and address family: two for BLUE, two for RED and one for GREEN.
  • PE1 also keeps the remote routes of each customer, from BGP. The per-customer state is on the edge, and only on the edge.

1.3 What the customer sees

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo traceroute -n -s 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2 -w 1 -q 1 -m 8
traceroute to 10.1.6.2 (10.1.6.2) from 10.1.1.2, 8 hops max, 46 byte packets
 1  10.1.1.1  1.259 ms
 2  10.1.6.1  2.902 ms
 3  10.1.6.2  1.610 ms
  • We examine the same fact from the customer side, with a traceroute from CE-A to CE-B.
  • The first hop is PE1, the gateway of the customer.
  • The next hop is PE6, then CE-B. The four core routers do not appear. They do not touch the customer packet. They touch only the outer header.

Ep02 · Build the lab

2.1 Know what you are running

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show version
Cisco IOS XR Software, Version 26.2.2 LNT
Copyright (c) 2013-2026 by Cisco Systems, Inc.

Build Information:
 Built By     : cisco
 Built On     : Thu Sep 10 00:39:05 UTC 2026
 Workspace    : /auto/srcarchive13/prod/26.2.2/xrd-vrouter/ws/
 Version      : 26.2.2
 Label        : 26.2.2

cisco XRd vRouter
cisco XRd-vRouter-C-01 processor with 9GB of memory
XRd vRouter Container
  • Before you configure anything, record the software that you use. This is the first line of every lab report.
  • The version is IOS XR 26.2.2.
  • The platform is XRd vRouter, a container. Most output uses this platform and release. XRv9000 comparisons identify their platform separately.

2.2 Step 1: addresses

interface Loopback0
 description router-id and SRv6 encapsulation source
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:100::1/128
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
 description TO-P2 cost 10
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:200:12::/127
 no shutdown
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
 description TO-P3 cost 40
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:200:13::/127
 no shutdown
  • The configuration has three steps. This is PE1. The other five nodes use the same pattern.
  • Step 1 is the addresses. Loopback0 gets the /128 from our plan. It is the router ID and the source of every encapsulated packet.
  • The two core interfaces get their /127 addresses. There is no IPv4 address, no MPLS and no LDP.

2.3 Step 2: SRv6 and the locator
