segment-routing
 srv6
  encapsulation
   source-address 2001:db8:100::1
  !
  locators
   locator MAIN
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fcbb:bb00:1::/48
   !
  !
 !
  • Step 2 enables SRv6. Only four lines are important.
  • The encapsulation source address is the loopback. When this router encapsulates a customer packet, this address is the outer source.
  • The locator has the name MAIN. Its prefix is the /48 of this node.
  • This line makes it a micro-SID locator. The node SID is a uN with the PSP and USD flavors. Episode 4 explains these flavors.
  • On hardware platforms, you can also need a hardware profile and a reload. This virtual router needs neither.

2.4 Step 3: IS-IS carries the locator

router isis CORE
 is-type level-2-only
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  metric-style wide
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
 !
 interface Loopback0
  passive
  address-family ipv6 unicast
 !
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  point-to-point
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   metric 10
  • Step 3 is IS-IS. Most of this configuration is normal IS-IS.
  • We enable the IPv6 address family with wide metrics.
  • These two lines are the SRv6 part. They attach the locator to IS-IS. Then IS-IS advertises the locator and creates the adjacency SIDs.
  • If you do not include them, the commit is still successful. The locator is on this router, but no other router can reach it.
  • Each core interface is point-to-point, with the metric from our plan.

2.5 Check 1: IS-IS neighbors

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show isis neighbors

IS-IS CORE neighbors:
System Id      Interface        SNPA           State Holdtime Type IETF-NSF
PE1            Gi0/0/0/0        *PtoP*         Up    28       L2   Capable
P3             Gi0/0/0/2        *PtoP*         Up    23       L2   Capable
P4             Gi0/0/0/1        *PtoP*         Up    28       L2   Capable

Total neighbor count: 3
  • Check 1, on P2. First, count the neighbors and compare them with the diagram.
  • P2 has three neighbors: PE1, P3 and P4. All are up, level 2 and point-to-point.
  • The diagram also shows three. Each PE has two neighbors, and each P router has three.

2.6 Check 2: what the router says it can do

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 manager
Parameters:
  SRv6 Enabled: Yes
  SRv6 Operational Mode:
    Micro-segment:
      SID Base Block: fcbb:bb00::/24
  Encapsulation:
    Source Address:
      Default: 2001:db8:100::1
      Configured: 2001:db8:100::1
  SID Formats:
    f3216 <32B/16NFA> (2)
      uSID LIB Range:
        LIB Start   : 0xe000
        ELIB Start  : 0xfe00
      uSID WLIB Range:
        EWLIB Start : 0xfff7
  • Check 2 is one command: show segment-routing srv6 manager. The output is long, so we read it in three parts.
  • SRv6 is enabled, and the operational mode is micro-segment.
  • The encapsulation source is the loopback that we configured.
  • The SID format is f3216. This is a 32-bit block, then 16-bit node and function IDs.
  • Local functions start at hexadecimal e000. Remember this number. You will see it in every SID table in this series.

2.7 Check 2, continued: behaviors

Platform Capabilities:
  SRv6: Yes
  TILFA: Yes
  Microloop-Avoidance: Yes
  Endpoint behaviors:
    uN (PSP/USD)
    uA (PSP/USD)
    uDT6
    uDT4
    uDT46
    uDX2
    uDT2U
    uDT2M
    uB6 (Insert.Red)
  Headend behaviors:
    T
    H.Insert.Red
    H.Encaps.Red
    H.Encaps.L2.Red
  • The second part lists the behaviors that this router supports.
  • uN and uA are the node and adjacency behaviors. Every path uses them.
  • The uDT and uDX entries are service behaviors. They are for Layer 3 VPN and for point-to-point Ethernet.
  • uB6 is the Binding SID. A behavior in this list does not prove that every related feature works. For example, this platform rejects bridge domains.
  • The headend list has H.Insert.Red and H.Encaps.Red, the reduced forms. It does not have plain H.Encaps.
  • This missing line changes the packets in all later episodes. Read this output before you design anything.

2.8 Check 2, continued: depth

  Signaled parameters:
    Max-SL          : 3
    Max-End-Pop-SRH : 3
    Max-H-Insert    : 3 sids
    Max-H-Encap     : 3 sids
    Max-End-D       : 4
  Default parameters (under srv6):
    Encapsulation:
      Hop-Limit     : value=0, propagate=No
      Traffic-class : value=0, propagate=No
  Max Locators: 16
  Max SIDs: 64000
  • The third part is about limits.
  • The router signals these depths to its neighbors. It can insert or encapsulate 3 SIDs.
  • Here, a SID is a full 128-bit container. One container holds several micro-SIDs. Thus the limit of 3 is larger than it looks.
  • By default, the router does not copy the hop limit and the traffic class from the customer packet to the outer header. Episode 13 checks this on the wire.
  • The limits are 16 locators and 64000 SIDs. These are the limits of a virtual router. Do not use them for hardware.

2.9 Check 3: the locator and the local SIDs

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 locator
Name                  ID       Algo  Prefix                    Status   Flags
--------------------  -------  ----  ------------------------  -------  --------
MAIN                  1        0     fcbb:bb00:1::/48          Up       U

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 sid

*** Locator: 'MAIN' ***

SID                         Behavior          Identification                    Owner               State  RW
--------------------------  ----------------  --------------------------------  ------------------  -----  --
fcbb:bb00:1::               uN (PSP/USD)      'default':1                       sidmgr              InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e000::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/0, Link-Local]:0         isis-CORE           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:1:e001::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/1, Link-Local]:0         isis-CORE           InUse  Y
  • Check 3 uses two commands. You will use them more than any other commands in this series.
  • The locator MAIN is up, in algorithm 0, with the prefix that we configured.
  • The first SID is the node SID, a uN. The SID manager owns it. It is available when the locator is up.
  • The next two SIDs are adjacency SIDs, one for each core interface. IS-IS owns them. That is why step 3 is important.
  • Their functions are e000 and e001. These are the first two values of the local range.

2.10 The remote locator, as PE1 sees it

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 isis

i L2 2001:db8:100::6/128
      [115/30] via fe80::5454:ff:fe9b:6d1f, 01:12:13, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
i L2 fcbb:bb00:2::/48
      [115/11] via fe80::5454:ff:fe9b:6d1f, 01:12:32, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
i L2 fcbb:bb00:4::/48
      [115/21] via fe80::5454:ff:fe9b:6d1f, 01:12:13, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
i L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
      [115/31] via fe80::5454:ff:fe9b:6d1f, 01:12:13, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  • A local SID is useful only when other routers can reach it. Thus, on PE1, we examine the routes from IS-IS.
  • PE6's loopback has metric 30, through GigabitEthernet 0. This is the upper path, as we predicted.
  • PE6's locator is a different route, with metric 31. On this release, the router adds 1 to the path cost for the locator.
  • The locators of P2 and P4 are also here, with metric 11 and 21. The locator of each node is a normal IPv6 route.
  • This is an important property of SRv6. A router in the middle needs no new function to forward a packet to a SID. It needs only a route.

2.11 Check 4: ping the node SID

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 2
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 2, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!
Success rate is 100 percent (2/2), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms
  • This is the ping command on PE1. The destination is the node SID of PE6, fcbb:bb00:6::.
  • The source option sets the source address. We use the loopback of PE1, because every router can reach it. The reply needs this address to come back. The count option sends two packets.
  • The router sends two echo requests, each with 100 bytes.
  • Each exclamation mark is one reply that came back.
  • The success rate is 100 percent: 2 of 2. The ping works. But the ping alone does not show the path. For this, we need the captures.

2.12 Check 4: the packet on three links

Router / tool: tcpdump

# PE1 to P2
IP6 (hlim 60) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6::: ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P2 to P4
IP6 (hlim 59) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6::: ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P4 to PE6
IP6 (hlim 58) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6::: ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
IP6 (hlim 64) 2001:db8:100::6 > 2001:db8:100::1: ICMP6, echo reply, seq 0
  • This is the output of tcpdump. Each line is one packet. The first part of each line shows the hop limit. Then we see the source address, the destination address, and the packet type. We show the first echo request of each capture.
  • On the first link, the destination is the SID, and the hop limit is 60.
  • On the second link, the destination is the same, and the hop limit is 59.
  • On the third link, the hop limit is 58. P2 and P4 did not do anything special. They routed the packet. Each router lowered the hop limit by 1.
  • This last line is the reply, on the third link. It comes from the loopback of PE6, 2001:db8:100::6, not from the SID.

Ep03 · SIDs, Locators and the Two Lookups

3.1 The egress tables behind it

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 sid fcbb:bb00:6:e006:: detail
fcbb:bb00:6:e006::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000           InUse  Y
  SID Function: 0xe006
  SID Identification (Context): { table-id=0xe0000001 ('RED':IPv4/Unicast) }

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6:e006::/64
fcbb:bb00:6:e006::/64, version 179, SRv6 Endpoint uDT4
    next hop VRF - 'RED', table - 0xe0000001
    0     Y   recursive                 Lookup in table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show route vrf RED 10.2.6.2
Routing entry for 10.2.6.0/24
  Known via "connected", distance 0, metric 0 (connected)
    directly connected, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/3
  • These are the egress tables that did the work.
  • The SID is a uDT4. Its context is the IPv4 table of VRF RED.
  • In CEF, the SID is a normal /64 entry. Its action is a lookup of the inner packet in the RED table.
  • In RED, the customer address is directly connected on the port to CE-B. This is the evidence for condition 4.

3.2 Healthy 1: the loopback ping and the locator route

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping 2001:db8:100::6 source 2001:db8:100::1 count 2
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 2, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 2001:db8:100::6, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!
Success rate is 100 percent (2/2), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
Routing entry for fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 100, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2
  Routing Descriptor Blocks
    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, from 2001:db8:100::6, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, Protected
      Route metric is 31
    fe80::5454:ff:fec1:58eb, from 2001:db8:100::6, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1, Backup (TI-LFA)
      Repair Node(s): 2001:db8:100::5
      Route metric is 101
  • We start with the healthy lab. First, the check that most engineers do first: a ping to the loopback of PE6.
  • The destination is 2001:db8:100::6, the loopback of PE6. The source is the loopback of PE1.
  • Both replies return, and the success rate is 100 percent. This ping tests only the loopback. It does not use the locator.
  • Now the locator. PE1 has a route to fcbb:bb00:6::/48. IS-IS installed it, and the route type is SRv6-locator.
  • The primary path leaves PE1 on Gi0/0/0/0. The route metric is 31.
  • A backup path leaves on Gi0/0/0/1, with metric 101. Remember this: in the healthy state, PE1 has a primary path and a backup path to the locator.

3.3 Healthy 2: the customer route in BGP

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
Paths: (1 available, best #1)
    2001:db8:100::6 (metric 30) from 2001:db8:100::6 (10.0.0.6)
      Received Label 0xe0080
      Origin incomplete, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal, best, group-best
      Extended community: RT:65000:300
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: 31
        T:1(Sid information), Sid:fcbb:bb00:6::(Transposed), Behavior:63
         Length [Loc-blk,Loc-node,Func,Arg]:[32,16,16,0], Tpose-len:16, Tpose-offset:48

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32
Routing entry for 10.30.6.6/32
  Known via "bgp 65000", distance 200, metric 0, type internal
    2001:db8:100::6, from 2001:db8:100::6
      Nexthop in Vrf: "default", Table: "default", IPv6 Unicast, Table Id: 0xe0800000
  • Next, the customer route. On PE1, we read the BGP detail of the prefix 10.30.6.6 in VRF GREEN.
  • BGP has one path. It comes from PE6. The next hop is the loopback of PE6, and the IGP metric to it is 30.
  • The received label is 0xe0080. It holds the SID function e008. Fault B changes this line.
  • The path is valid and best. The route target 65000:300 puts the route into VRF GREEN.
  • BGP also checks the locator of the SID. The locator route is in the RIB, with metric 31. Fault A changes this line.
  • In the VRF, the route is a BGP route. Its next hop is in the default VRF, in the IPv6 table. PE1 must resolve the next hop in that table.

3.4 Healthy 3: the forwarding entry and the customer ping

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32
10.30.6.6/32, version 9, SRv6 Headend
   via fcbb:bb00:6::/128, 3 dependencies, recursive
    next hop VRF - 'default', table - 0xe0800000
    next hop fcbb:bb00:6::/128 via fcbb:bb00:6::/48
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e008::}
    Hash  OK  Interface                 Address
    0     Y   GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 3
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 3, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.30.6.6 timeout is 2 seconds:
!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (3/3), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/1/3 ms
  • Now forwarding. The CEF entry shows what PE1 does with a packet for this customer.
  • The entry is an SRv6 Headend. It has 3 dependencies. This means that the router resolved the entry.
  • The next hop is the locator of PE6. PE1 resolves it with the /48 route. This is condition 1.
  • The action is H.Encaps.Red. The SID list has one SID: fcbb:bb00:6:e008::. This is the service SID of GREEN on PE6.
  • The last line shows the result. The packet leaves PE1 on Gi0/0/0/0.
  • Now the customer ping. The source is an address of PE1 in VRF GREEN. All three packets succeed.

3.5 Healthy 4: the customer ping on the wire

Router / tool: tshark

# PE1 to P2: the first request and its reply
frame 113, 154 bytes, request
  IPv6  2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e008::    hlim 255
  IPv4  10.30.1.1 > 10.30.6.6                   ICMP echo request
frame 114, 154 bytes, reply
  IPv6  2001:db8:100::6 > fcbb:bb00:1:e00a::    hlim 253
  IPv4  10.30.6.6 > 10.30.1.1                   ICMP echo reply
  • Now the packets. We captured the customer ping on the link from PE1 to P2. Each frame has 154 bytes: 14 for Ethernet, 40 for the outer IPv6 header, and 100 for the customer packet.
  • The request has an outer IPv6 header. Its destination is the service SID of PE6, fcbb:bb00:6:e008::. The source is the loopback of PE1.
  • Inside is the customer packet: an IPv4 echo request from 10.30.1.1 to 10.30.6.6. There is no SRH, because the SID list has only one SID.
  • The reply goes the other way. Its outer destination is fcbb:bb00:1:e00a::. This is the uDT4 SID of GREEN on PE1.
  • The hop limit of the reply is 253. PE6 sent it with 255. P4 and P2 each lowered it by 1.
  • This is the healthy reference. In the two faults, we capture the same link, and we compare.

3.6 Fault A: PE6 stops advertising its locator

! PE6
router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  segment-routing srv6
   no locator MAIN
!
commit
  • Fault A. On PE6, we remove one line: the locator under IS-IS. Episode 2 told you about this line.
  • IS-IS still advertises the loopback. The locator is still on PE6. Only the advertisement of the locator is gone.

3.7 Fault A: what PE1 sees

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping 2001:db8:100::6 source 2001:db8:100::1 count 2
Success rate is 100 percent (2/2), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
% Network not in table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
Paths: (1 available, best #1)
      Received Label 0xe0080
      Origin incomplete, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal, best, group-best
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: inaccessible
  • Now we do the same checks from PE1.
  • The loopback ping is successful. This is the check that gave the wrong answer in the phone call.
  • The locator route is gone: Network not in table. Condition 1 is false.
  • But BGP still shows the path as valid and best.
  • Only this line shows the problem: the SID locator is inaccessible. You see it only when you read the detail.

3.8 Fault A: forwarding

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32
10.30.6.6/32, version 9, SRv6 Headend
   via fcbb:bb00:6::/128, 0 dependencies, recursive
    unresolved
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e008::}
    0     Y   recursive                 drop

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 3
Success rate is 0 percent (0/3)
  • What does forwarding do with a best path whose locator is not reachable?
  • The entry is still there, but nothing resolves it: zero dependencies, unresolved.
  • The SID list is still in the entry. A fast look can make you think that the encapsulation is ready.
  • The last column shows drop.
  • The customer ping fails.

3.9 Fault A: PE6 still looks healthy

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 locator
Name                  ID       Algo  Prefix                    Status   Flags
--------------------  -------  ----  ------------------------  -------  --------
MAIN                  2        0     fcbb:bb00:6::/48          Up       U

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 sid
SID                         Behavior          Identification                    Owner               State  RW
--------------------------  ----------------  --------------------------------  ------------------  -----  --
fcbb:bb00:6::               uN (PSP/USD)      'default':6                       sidmgr              InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:6:e008::          uDT4              'GREEN'                           bgp-65000           InUse  Y
  • Now we examine the egress during fault A. This check tells you where the fault is not.
  • The locator MAIN is up. PE6 still owns the prefix fcbb:bb00:6::/48.
  • The service SID e008 for GREEN is a uDT4. BGP owns it, and it is in use. Condition 2 is true.
  • PE6 owns everything that it needs. But the rest of the network does not know the locator. The fault is in the advertisement.

3.10 Fault B: PE6 stops allocating the service SID

! PE6
router bgp 65000
 vrf GREEN
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   no segment-routing srv6
!
commit
  • Fault B is different. On PE6, under BGP, we remove the SRv6 allocation for VRF GREEN.
  • The locator, IS-IS and the loopback do not change. Only the service SID for this one customer is gone.

3.11 Fault B: the egress

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 sid
*** Locator: 'MAIN' ***
fcbb:bb00:6::               uN (PSP/USD)      'default':6                       sidmgr
fcbb:bb00:6:e004::          uDT4              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:6:e005::          uDT6              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:6:e006::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:6:e007::          uDX2              300:300                           l2vpn_srv6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
    Local Label: 24004 (with rewrite);
  Advertised to peers (in unique update groups):
    2001:db8:100::1
  • Start at the location of the fault: the egress.
  • PE6's SID table has service SIDs for BLUE, for RED and for a Layer 2 service. It has nothing for GREEN. Condition 2 is false.
  • This result is not expected. Without an SRv6 SID, BGP used an MPLS label, 24004.
  • BGP advertised this label to PE1. No warning appeared.

3.12 Fault B: the ingress

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 100, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
      Received Label 24004
      Origin incomplete, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal, best, group-best

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32
   via 2001:db8:100::6/128, 0 dependencies, recursive
    unresolved
     labels imposed {24004}
    0     Y   recursive                 drop
  • Now PE1.
  • This time, the locator route is correct. Condition 1 is true.
  • BGP received label 24004. The path is still valid and best.
  • Forwarding tries to push an MPLS label to PE6's loopback. This core has no MPLS path. Thus the entry is unresolved, and it drops the packet.
  • One missing line on the egress changed an SRv6 service into an MPLS service that cannot work.

3.13 Fault B: the ping and the wire

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 3
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 3, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.30.6.6 timeout is 2 seconds:
...
Success rate is 0 percent (0/3)

# Captures on PE1 to P2 and on P4 to PE6, during this ping
no echo request on either link
  • We run the customer ping during fault B.
  • Each dot is one timeout. There are three dots, and no reply.
  • The success rate is 0 percent.
  • We also captured on the link PE1 to P2, and on the link P4 to PE6. Neither link has an echo request. PE1 drops the packet before the wire.
  • In both faults, the customer sees the same symptoms: no ping, and no packet on the wire. Only the router outputs show the difference.

3.14 Read the label field

Healthy:
      Received Label 0xe0080
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: 31
        T:1(Sid information), Sid:fcbb:bb00:6::(Transposed), Behavior:63
           Length [Loc-blk,Loc-node,Func,Arg]:[32,16,16,0], Tpose-len:16, Tpose-offset:48

Fault B:
      Received Label 24004
  • This is a fast method to identify the two cases. Read the received label.
  • In the healthy state, the label is a hexadecimal value, e0080. This is the SID function, e008, in the label field.
  • The next lines show the method. BGP sends the locator one time, and puts the 16-bit function in the label field. The receiver builds the full SID again.
  • RFC 9252 calls this method transposition. Episode 13 reads it field by field from a captured update.
  • In fault B, the label is a normal decimal MPLS label. In a core with only SRv6, this tells you that there is a problem.

3.15 The moment in between: on the wire

Router / tool: tshark

# P4 to PE6, in an earlier version of the lab (VRF RED)
frame 116, 154 bytes
  IPv6  2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e004::    hlim 253
  IPv6  2001:db8:a:201::1 > 2001:db8:a:206::6   ICMPv6 echo request
frame 117, 206 bytes
  IPv6  2001:db8:200:46::1 > 2001:db8:100::1    hlim 63
  ICMPv6 type 1, code 0: destination unreachable
  • This capture is from an earlier version of the lab. The customer was in VRF RED, with IPv6 addresses. The idea is the same.
  • The request arrives at PE6. The outer destination is the old SID, fcbb:bb00:6:e004::.
  • Inside is the customer packet: an ICMPv6 echo request.
  • PE6 does not own this SID. It replies from its own address with ICMPv6 type 1, code 0: destination unreachable.
  • The packet reached the correct router, but the router has no instruction for the SID. This is why you read the SID table on PE6.

Ep04 · Endpoint Behaviors and Flavors

4.1 UN in the forwarding table

Router / tool: P3

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P3#show segment-routing srv6 sid
fcbb:bb00:3::               uN (PSP/USD)      'default':3                       sidmgr              InUse  Y

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P3#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:3::/48 detail
fcbb:bb00:3::/48, version 5, SRv6 Endpoint uN (shift)
   via ::/128, 0 dependencies, weight 0, class 0 [flags 0x0]
    next hop ::/128
  • We now look at these behaviors in the forwarding table of a real router, P3.
  • P3 has the uN fcbb:bb00:3::, with the PSP and USD flavors. We explain the flavors later in this episode.
  • In CEF, it is a /48 entry. Its action is SRv6 Endpoint uN, shift. This is step 1 of the procedure, as the router shows it.
  • There is no outgoing interface here. After the shift, the router looks up the new address.

4.2 UA in the forwarding table

Router / tool: P3

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P3#show segment-routing srv6 sid
fcbb:bb00:3:e004::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/1, Link-Local]:0:P       isis-CORE           InUse  Y
fcbb:bb00:3:e005::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/1, Link-Local]:0         isis-CORE           InUse  Y

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P3#show isis neighbors
P5             Gi0/0/0/1        *PtoP*         Up    29       L2   Capable

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P3#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:3:e005::/64 detail
fcbb:bb00:3:e005::/64, version 114, SRv6 Endpoint uA (shift)
   via fe80::5454:ff:feb1:be7a/128, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1, 8 dependencies
  • Now we look at an adjacency SID on the same router.
  • P3 has two uA SIDs for interface GigabitEthernet 0/0/0/1. One has the mark P, for protected. The other has no mark.
  • The router can repair a protected adjacency around a failure. Use the unprotected one when you want only that link. Episode 9 uses this difference.
  • That interface goes to P5.
  • In CEF, the uA is a /64. The block, the node and the function make 64 bits.
  • The uA has a fixed next hop, out of GigabitEthernet 0/0/0/1 to P5. The uN has no fixed next hop.

4.3 Ping the uA address

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 2
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 2, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
..
Success rate is 0 percent (0/2)

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 2
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 2, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!
Success rate is 100 percent (2/2), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms
  • Now we use that uA. You can do the same in your lab. First, in CML, start a packet capture on every link of the path. Then ping from PE1.
  • The destination is fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6::. After the block, it has three parts. 3 is the node P3, e005 is the uA of P3 toward P5, and 6 is the node PE6.
  • The ping fails: two dots, and 0 percent. This does not mean that the packet is lost. We show the reason later in this episode.
  • For comparison, we ping the node SID of PE6 in the same way.
  • This ping works: two replies, and 100 percent. A normal address gets replies. The first address gets none. The captures show the difference.

4.4 The capture, link by link

Router / tool: tcpdump

$ tcpdump -nn -t -v -r <capture file> icmp6
# PE1 to P2
IP6 (hlim 60) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6::: [icmp6 sum ok] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P2 to P3
IP6 (hlim 59) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6::: [icmp6 sum ok] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P3 to P5
IP6 (hlim 58) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6::: [bad icmp6 cksum 0x0316 -> 0xe31e!] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P5 to P4
IP6 (hlim 57) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6::: [bad icmp6 cksum 0x0316 -> 0xe31e!] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
# P4 to PE6
IP6 (hlim 56) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6::: [bad icmp6 cksum 0x0316 -> 0xe31e!] ICMP6, echo request, seq 0
  • Now we read the captures. We save each capture from CML, and we read it with tcpdump on our own computer. We show the first echo request of each file.
  • On the link PE1 to P2, the destination holds all three instructions. The hop limit is 60. tcpdump says that the checksum is correct.
  • On the link P2 to P3, the destination is the same. P2 has no matching SID. It routes the packet, and it lowers the hop limit by one.
  • After P3, the destination is fcbb:bb00:6::. P3 removed its node instruction and the uA, and it shifted PE6 to the front. Now tcpdump reports a bad checksum. Remember this.
  • P5 and P4 route the packet like a normal address. The packet arrives at PE6 with hop limit 56, after four routers. Each change agrees with the prediction.

4.5 The shifted ping from PE1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 3
Sending 3, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (3/3), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/3/3 ms

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:2:4:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 3
Sending 3, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
...
Success rate is 0 percent (0/3)
  • The capture showed a strange result. The shifted packet arrived at PE6, but PE6 did not reply. We compare two pings from PE1.
  • First, a ping directly to the node SID of PE6. All three packets get a reply.
  • Second, a ping to fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::. This address holds three instructions: P2, then P4, then PE6. It gets no reply. The cause is on PE6.

4.6 PE6 counters after each ping

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show ipv6 traffic      (ICMP statistics, three times)
before the pings
  Rcvd: 23 input, 6 checksum errors, 0 too short
        13 echo request, 0 echo reply
after 3 direct pings
  Rcvd: 26 input, 6 checksum errors, 0 too short
        16 echo request, 0 echo reply
after 3 shifted pings
  Rcvd: 29 input, 9 checksum errors, 0 too short
        16 echo request, 0 echo reply
  • On PE6, we read the ICMP statistics before the pings, and after each ping. The command is show ipv6 traffic.
  • This is the starting point: 6 checksum errors, and 13 echo requests.
  • After three direct pings, the echo request counter increased by three, to 16. The checksum error counter did not change.
  • After three shifted pings, the checksum error counter increased by three, to 9. The echo request counter did not change. PE6 discarded the packets as damaged.

4.7 Why PE6 discards the packet

Router / tool: analysis

# ICMPv6 checksum, calculated again from the capture on P4 to PE6
direct: arriving DA fcbb:bb00:6::, checksum in packet 0xfd85
   computed with the arriving DA                     0xfd85  match
   computed with the sender's DA fcbb:bb00:6::       0xfd85  match
shifted: arriving DA fcbb:bb00:6::, checksum in packet 0xfd34
   computed with the arriving DA                     0xfd3a  MISMATCH
   computed with the sender's DA fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::   0xfd34  match
  • We calculated the ICMPv6 checksum again from the capture of the link P4 to PE6.
  • For the direct ping, the packet arrives with the same address that PE1 sent to. The checksum matches.
  • For the shifted ping, the arriving destination gives 0xfd3a. The packet carries 0xfd34. They do not match.
  • The destination that PE1 sent to, fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::, gives 0xfd34. This matches. PE1 calculated the checksum with its own destination.
  • RFC 9800, section 6.5, says that the source must calculate the checksum with the final destination: the address of the packet when it arrives. Our ping used the container as a normal address.
  • This does not affect customer traffic, because its checksum is in the inner packet. The finding is for tests: use captures, not ping replies, to examine a shifted path.

4.8 PSP: the policy that PE1 uses

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf BLUE ipv6 2001:db8:c:106::/64 detail
2001:db8:c:106::/64, version 22, SRv6 Headend
   via fcbb:bb00:1:e009::/128, 3 dependencies, recursive
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e005::}
      SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb01:3:5::}
    Hash  OK  Interface                 Address
    0     Y   GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1    fe80::5454:ff:fec1:58eb
  • Now PSP, in the lab. The route to the BLUE customer in IPv6 uses an SR policy. Episode 6 explains the policy. Here we only read the forwarding entry.
  • The first SID list is the service SID of PE6, fcbb:bb00:6:e005::. PE1 puts it in the routing header.
  • The second SID list is the policy. It is one container, fcbb:bb01:3:5::, with two instructions: P3, then P5. PE1 puts it in the destination address.
  • The packet needs both lists, so it needs a routing header. Now we ping from CE-A, and we capture on the links.

4.9 PSP on the wire

Router / tool: tcpdump

# CE-A: sudo ping6 -c 2 2001:db8:c:106::2   (2 received, 0% packet loss)
# PE1 to P3, 182 bytes
IP6 (hlim 255, next-header Routing (43)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb01:3:5::: RT6 (segleft=1, [0]fcbb:bb00:6:e005::)
# P3 to P5, 182 bytes
IP6 (hlim 254, next-header Routing (43)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb01:5::: RT6 (segleft=1, [0]fcbb:bb00:6:e005::)
# P5 to P4, 158 bytes
IP6 (hlim 253, next-header IPv6 (41)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005:::
# P4 to PE6, 158 bytes
IP6 (hlim 252, next-header IPv6 (41)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005:::
  • In the lab, we start captures on the links of the path. Then, on CE-A, we ping the customer address on the far side. Both replies return.
  • On the link PE1 to P3, the destination is the container fcbb:bb01:3:5::. The routing header has one entry: the service SID of PE6. Segments Left is 1. The frame has 182 bytes.
  • After P3, the destination is fcbb:bb01:5::. P3 shifted out its own instruction. The routing header is still there, with one segment left.
  • P5 is the penultimate endpoint. It copies the last SID into the destination, and it removes the routing header. This is PSP. The frame is 24 bytes smaller: 158 bytes.
  • On the link P4 to PE6, there is no routing header. PE6 receives a normal encapsulated packet, and the service SID e005 does the rest.

4.10 uDT4: a service decapsulates by itself

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6:e006::/64
fcbb:bb00:6:e006::/64, version 179, SRv6 Endpoint uDT4
    next hop VRF - 'RED', table - 0xe0000001
    0     Y   recursive                 Lookup in table
  • Do not mix up USD and service decapsulation.
  • A uDT4 is a different behavior. It does not need a flavor to remove the outer header. To remove the outer header is its function.
  • Then it looks up the inner packet in a specified VRF, here RED. Thus it is a service, not a waypoint.

Ep05 · How a uSID Container Shifts

5.1 Test 1: ping and capture

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:2:4:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 1
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 1, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
.
Success rate is 0 percent (0/1)

$ tcpdump -nn -t -v -r shift-PE1-P2.pcap icmp6
IP6 (hlim 60) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:2:4:6:::  [icmp6 sum ok] ICMP6, echo request
$ tcpdump -nn -t -v -r shift-P2-P4.pcap icmp6
IP6 (hlim 59) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:4:6:::  [bad icmp6 cksum 0xde68 -> 0xde6a!] ICMP6, echo request
$ tcpdump -nn -t -v -r shift-P4-PE6.pcap icmp6
IP6 (hlim 58) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:::  [bad icmp6 cksum 0xde68 -> 0xde6e!] ICMP6, echo request
  • Now we run the first test. In CML, start a packet capture on each core link. Then ping the test address from PE1.
  • The destination is fcbb:bb00:2:4:6::. It holds three instructions: P2, then P4, then PE6.
  • The ping gets no reply. Episode 4 showed the reason: the checksum. Thus we read the path from the captures.
  • On the link PE1 to P2, the destination is the full address. The hop limit is 60.
  • On the link P2 to P4, P2 shifted the address. The destination is fcbb:bb00:4:6::, and the hop limit is 59. tcpdump now reports a bad checksum.
  • On the link P4 to PE6, the destination is fcbb:bb00:6::, with hop limit 58. All eight links agree with the table, and no other link carried the packet.

5.2 Why normal VPN traffic looks simpler

Healthy GREEN customer ping, captured on PE1 to P2:
  154 bytes   outer destination fcbb:bb00:6:e008::   inner 10.30.1.1 to 10.30.6.6

Shortest path PE1 to PE6:  PE1, P2, P4, PE6   (cost 30)
  • Why did the VPN traffic in Episode 3 show no shift?
  • The customer packets had only one instruction: PE6's service SID. P2 and P4 had nothing to do.
  • The shortest path already goes through P2 and P4, so it is not necessary to name them. A headend adds waypoints only for a different path. Thus, in this episode, we make test addresses manually.

5.3 Test 2: ping the waypoints

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:3:5:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 1
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 1, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:3:5:6::, timeout is 2 seconds:
.
Success rate is 0 percent (0/1)
  • Test 2 is the ping to fcbb:bb00:3:5:6::. Start the captures on all eight core links first.
  • The destination has three instructions: P3, then P5, then PE6.
  • Again, there is no reply. We read the path from the captures, not from the ping.

5.4 The capture for fcbb:bb00:3:5:6::

$ tcpdump -nn -t -v -r shift-<link>.pcap icmp6     (eight files, merged in time order)
link        destination            hop limit
PE1 - P2    fcbb:bb00:3:5:6::      60
P2 - P3     fcbb:bb00:3:5:6::      59     toward P3
P3 - P2     fcbb:bb00:5:6::        58     P3 shifted, sends it back
P2 - P4     fcbb:bb00:5:6::        57
P4 - P5     fcbb:bb00:5:6::        56     toward P5
P5 - P4     fcbb:bb00:6::          55     P5 shifted, sends it back
P4 - PE6    fcbb:bb00:6::          54

PE1 - P3, P3 - P5, P5 - PE6:  nothing
  • This is one ping. We read the capture of each core link with tcpdump, and we put the results in time sequence.
  • PE1 to P2, then P2 to P3, with no change. P2 had no instruction here, so it only routed the packet.
  • P3 shifts and sends the packet back to P2, then to P4.
  • P4 forwards the packet to P5. P5 shifts and sends it back to P4.
  • P4 sends it to PE6 with hop limit 54. The packet used seven links. The shortest path has three links.
  • The three lower links carried nothing. The prediction is correct on each link.

5.5 A full container

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:2:3:5:4:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 1
Sending 1, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:2:3:5:4:6:0, timeout is 2 seconds:
.
Success rate is 0 percent (0/1)

fcbb:bb00:0002:0003:0005:0004:0006:0000    five instructions, one zero group

link        destination              hop limit
PE1 - P2    fcbb:bb00:2:3:5:4:6:0    60
P2 - P3     fcbb:bb00:3:5:4:6::      59     P2 executed its own instruction
P3 - P2     fcbb:bb00:5:4:6::        58
P2 - P4     fcbb:bb00:5:4:6::        57
P4 - P5     fcbb:bb00:5:4:6::        56
P5 - P4     fcbb:bb00:4:6::          55
P4 - PE6    fcbb:bb00:6::            54
  • How many instructions can one address contain? We fill one address.
  • Test 3 is the ping to fcbb:bb00:2:3:5:4:6::. The router shows the address with the last zero group, :0. The ping gets no reply, as before.
  • After the 32-bit block, there are six 16-bit positions. We put five node SIDs in them: P2, P3, P5, P4 and PE6. One zero group shows the end.
  • This time, P2 is first. Thus P2 does its instruction and shifts the address before it sends the packet to P3.
  • Then the packet uses the same path as before, through P3, P2, P4, P5 and P4 again.
  • PE6 receives fcbb:bb00:6:: with hop limit 54. Five instructions are in one address, and there is no routing header.

5.6 Test 4: ping with a service SID

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping fcbb:bb00:2:4:6:e008:: source 2001:db8:100::1 count 1
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 1, 100-byte ICMP Echos to fcbb:bb00:2:4:6:e008::, timeout is 2 seconds:
.
Success rate is 0 percent (0/1)
  • Test 4 puts a service function at the end of the list. The ping is to fcbb:bb00:2:4:6:e008::.
  • The address has four instructions: P2, P4, PE6, and the service function e008 of PE6.
  • There is no reply, as in the other tests. The captures show the shifts.

Ep06 · SRH and Encapsulation Size

6.1 Run the pings

Router / tool: PE1 and CE-A

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 2
!!
Success rate is 100 percent (2/2), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 2001:db8:c:106::2
64 bytes from 2001:db8:c:106::2: seq=0 ttl=62 time=7.698 ms
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -s 1000 2001:db8:c:106::2
1008 bytes from 2001:db8:c:106::2: seq=0 ttl=62 time=2.140 ms
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
  • Three pings produce the frames in this episode. In CML, first start a capture on every core link, and on the link between CE-A and PE1.
  • First, a GREEN ping from PE1. The source is the GREEN interface of PE1. Both packets succeed.
  • Second, a BLUE IPv6 ping from the host CE-A to the far side of the BLUE customer. The default ping packet has 56 data bytes.
  • Third, the same ping with 1000 data bytes. We use the two sizes to measure how the frame size changes. Both pings succeed.

6.2 Configure the policy on PE1

! PE1 (trimmed)
segment-routing
 traffic-eng
  segment-lists
   srv6
    sid-format usid-f3216
   segment-list TWO-BLOCKS
    srv6
     index 10 sid fcbb:bb01:3::
     index 20 sid fcbb:bb01:5::
     index 30 sid fcbb:bb00:6::
  policy BLUE6-C300
   srv6
    binding-sid dynamic behavior ub6-insert-reduced locator MAIN
   color 300 end-point ipv6 2001:db8:100::6
   candidate-paths
    preference 100
     explicit segment-list TWO-BLOCKS
  • To make condition 2 on purpose, we configure one explicit policy on PE1. Episode 15 explains each command.
  • First, a segment list that uses the micro-SID format f3216. Its name is TWO-BLOCKS.
  • The first two SIDs, P3 and P5, are from the block fcbb:bb01. They are Flex-Algo SIDs.
  • The last SID, PE6, is from the block fcbb:bb00. It is a normal SID.
  • The policy BLUE6-C300 has color 300 and the end point PE6. Its Binding SID is dynamic, from the locator MAIN.
  • The only candidate path uses the segment list TWO-BLOCKS.

6.3 Color the BLUE IPv6 routes on PE6

! PE6 (trimmed)
extcommunity-set opaque COLOR-300
 300
end-set
route-policy BLUE6-EXPORT-C300
 set extcommunity color COLOR-300
end-policy
vrf BLUE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  export route-policy BLUE6-EXPORT-C300
  • The policy needs traffic. PE6 adds the color 300 to the BLUE IPv6 routes that it advertises. PE1 then matches the color and the end point with the policy.
  • First, an extended community with the value 300.
  • Second, a route policy that sets this color.
  • Third, PE6 applies the route policy when it exports the BLUE IPv6 routes.

6.4 A policy that mixes two blocks

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing traffic-eng policy color 300 detail
Color: 300, End-point: 2001:db8:100::6
    Admin: up  Operational: up
      Explicit: segment-list TWO-BLOCKS (valid)
          SID[0]: fcbb:bb01:3::/48
          SID[1]: fcbb:bb01:5::/48
          SID[2]: fcbb:bb00:6::/48
      Binding SID: fcbb:bb00:1:e009::
  • Now we check the policy on PE1. BLUE IPv6 traffic to PE6 goes into this policy.
  • The first two waypoints, P3 and P5, are Flex-Algo SIDs from the fcbb:bb01 block.
  • The last waypoint, PE6, is a normal SID from fcbb:bb00.
  • The policy is up, and it has a Binding SID. There are two blocks, so there must be at least two containers.

6.5 What PE1 programs

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf BLUE ipv6 2001:db8:c:106::/64 detail
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e005::}
      SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb01:3:5::}
  • Now the forwarding entry for the BLUE destination. It has two important lines.
  • Line 1: H.Encaps.Red to PE6's service SID, e005. This is the VPN part. PE1 encapsulates the customer packet and sends it to the BLUE service on PE6.
  • Line 2: H.Insert.Red with the path container fcbb:bb01:3:5::. This is the policy. PE1 inserts the path in front of the service SID.
  • The third SID of the policy, PE6's node SID, is not there. The service SID already ends at PE6, so the router does not use it.

6.6 The SRH, field by field

Router / tool: capture

$ tshark -r c300-PE1-P3.pcap -Y "ipv6.nxt == 43" -V     (first packet, trimmed)
Internet Protocol Version 6, Src: 2001:db8:100::1, Dst: fcbb:bb01:3:5::
    Payload Length: 128
    Next Header: Routing Header for IPv6 (43)
    Hop Limit: 255
    Routing Header for IPv6 (Segment Routing)
        Next Header: IPv6 (41)
        Length: 2
        [Length: 24 bytes]
        Type: Segment Routing (4)
        Segments Left: 1
        Last Entry: 0
        Address[0]: fcbb:bb00:6:e005::
Internet Protocol Version 6, Src: 2001:db8:c:101:5054:ff:fe0b:8f87, Dst: 2001:db8:c:106::2
  • Now we decode one of the 182-byte packets from the capture of the PE1 to P3 link. We use tshark with the verbose option.
  • The outer destination is the path container: P3, then P5, in the Flex-Algo block. Next header 43 means that a routing header follows.
  • This is the SRH. Type 4 means segment routing. Its next header is 41, an IPv6 packet: the customer packet. Its length is 24 bytes.
  • It has one entry: the service SID. Segments Left is 1. One more SID is in the list after the current destination.
  • Then there is the customer IPv6 header, with no change.

6.7 Segments Left along the path

Router / tool: tcpdump

$ tcpdump -nn -t -v -r <capture file> 'ip6[6] == 43 or ip6[6] == 41'   (first packet, trimmed)
# PE1 to P3, 182 bytes
IP6 (hlim 255, next-header Routing (43)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb01:3:5::: RT6 (segleft=1, [0]fcbb:bb00:6:e005::)
# P3 to P5, 182 bytes
IP6 (hlim 254, next-header Routing (43)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb01:5::: RT6 (segleft=1, [0]fcbb:bb00:6:e005::)
# P5 to P4, 158 bytes
IP6 (hlim 253, next-header IPv6 (41)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005:::
# P4 to PE6, 158 bytes
IP6 (hlim 252, next-header IPv6 (41)) 2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005:::
  • Follow the Segments Left field on the path. We read the capture of each link with tcpdump. The RT6 part is the routing header.
  • When the packet leaves PE1, the destination is the container fcbb:bb01:3:5::. Segments Left is 1, and the entry is the service SID of PE6.
  • After P3, the destination has shifted to fcbb:bb01:5::, and Segments Left is still 1. A shift in a container does not change the SRH.
  • At P5, the container has no more micro-SIDs. P5 decreases Segments Left to zero, and it copies the next SID into the destination. P5 is the penultimate endpoint, thus it also removes the SRH.
  • The next header is now 41, and the frame is 24 bytes smaller. This is step 2 of the procedure from Episode 4, on the wire.

6.8 The BLUE packet, measured

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmpv6.type == 128 and icmpv6.echo.sequence_number == 0" -T fields -e frame.len
link                   small  large  what is added
CE-A to PE1            118    1062   nothing: the customer packet
PE1 to P3, P3 to P5    182    1126   + 40 outer IPv6 + 24 SRH = 64
P5 to P4, P4 to PE6    158    1102   + 40 outer IPv6 only
  • Now we count each byte. For each capture file, tshark prints the frame length of the echo requests. The small ping and the large ping give two values.
  • On the access link, the frames are 118 and 1062 bytes. This is the customer packet.
  • From PE1 to P5, each frame is 64 bytes larger: 40 for the outer IPv6 header and 24 for the SRH.
  • After P5, each frame is only 40 bytes larger. P5 was the penultimate endpoint, and PSP removed the SRH, as Episode 4 showed.
  • Thus the overhead of the same flow changes on the path: 64 bytes in the first part, 40 bytes in the second part.

6.9 Why our lab never shows 1596

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 manager
  Headend behaviors:
    T
    H.Insert.Red
    H.Encaps.Red
    H.Encaps.L2.Red
  Signaled parameters:
    Max-H-Insert    : 3 sids
    Max-H-Encap     : 3 sids
  • Our captures do not show a 1596-byte packet. This is the reason.
  • This headend has only the reduced forms. There is no plain H.Encaps, so the first SID is never in the SRH also. In this lab, the 1596 case is only a calculation.
  • It can insert or encapsulate a maximum of 3 SIDs. Each SID can be a full container of micro-SIDs. Thus 3 is a limit on containers, not on instructions.

Ep07 · MTU, Fragmentation and ICMP

7.1 Case 1: what PE1 programs

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf RED 10.2.6.0/24 detail | include SID-list
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e006::}
      SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:e004::}
  • Case 1 uses IPv4 in VRF RED. First, we check what PE1 programs for the RED prefix 10.2.6.0/24.
  • The service SID is fcbb:bb00:6:e006::. It is the uDT4 of RED on PE6.
  • The path is one container, fcbb:bb00:e004::. PE1 inserts it in front of the service SID.
  • Each list has one SID, so the packet has no routing header. The overhead is 40 bytes, and the limit is 1460.

7.2 Case 1: the pings

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 1 -I 10.2.1.2 -s 1432 10.2.6.2
1440 bytes from 10.2.6.2: seq=0 ttl=62 time=1.495 ms
1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 -I 10.2.1.2 -s 1433 10.2.6.2
3 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss

CE-A:~$ sudo cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_no_pmtu_disc
0
  • Now CE-A sends IPv4 pings to the RED far side. The option -s is the data size, and -I sets the source address.
  • A data size of 1432 makes a 1460-byte IPv4 packet. This is the limit, and the reply returns.
  • A data size of 1433 makes a 1461-byte packet. All three pings are lost. The packet loss is 100 percent.
  • The Linux host sets the don't-fragment bit, because this kernel setting is 0.

7.3 Case 1: the captures

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y icmp
# PE1 to CE-A, the 1460-byte ping
1474 bytes  10.2.1.2 > 10.2.6.2  echo request
1474 bytes  10.2.6.2 > 10.2.1.2  echo reply
# PE1 to CE-A, the 1461-byte ping
1475 bytes  10.2.1.2 > 10.2.6.2  echo request   (no reply follows)
# PE1 to P3, the 1460-byte ping
1514 bytes  10.2.1.2 > 10.2.6.2  echo request, inside the outer IPv6 header
# PE1 to P2, PE1 to P3, P4 to PE6, P5 to PE6, the 1461-byte ping
no echo request on any core link
  • We captured on the access link and on the core links, and we read each file with tshark. The frame length includes 14 bytes of Ethernet header.
  • On the access link, the 1460-byte packet is a 1474-byte frame. The reply returns.
  • The 1461-byte packet is a 1475-byte frame. It arrives at PE1, and no reply follows.
  • The 1460-byte packet crosses the core in a 1514-byte frame. This is the largest frame that the link carries.
  • For the 1461-byte packet, no core link carries an echo request. PE1 dropped it before the encapsulation.

7.4 Case 2: the pings

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 1 -s 1388 2001:db8:c:106::2
1396 bytes from 2001:db8:c:106::2: seq=0 ttl=62 time=1.545 ms
1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 -s 1389 2001:db8:c:106::2
1397 bytes from 2001:db8:c:106::2: seq=1 ttl=62 time=1.566 ms
2 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 50% packet loss
  • Case 2 uses IPv6 in VRF BLUE, through colour 300. The limit is 1436. Linux ping6 adds 48 bytes to the data size.
  • A data size of 1388 makes a 1436-byte packet. The reply returns.
  • A data size of 1389 makes a 1437-byte packet. The first packet is lost, and the second packet gets a reply. The loss is 50 percent.

7.5 Case 2: the captures

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r B-PE1-CE-A.pcap -Y icmpv6      (CE-A is 2001:db8:c:101:5054:ff:fe0b:8f87)
1450 bytes  CE-A > 2001:db8:c:106::2  echo request, seq 0
1450 bytes  2001:db8:c:106::2 > CE-A  echo reply, seq 0
1451 bytes  CE-A > 2001:db8:c:106::2  echo request, the 1437-byte packet
1294 bytes  2001:db8:100::1 > CE-A    Packet Too Big, MTU 1436
1446 and 75 bytes  CE-A > 2001:db8:c:106::2  the second request, in two fragments
1451 bytes  2001:db8:c:106::2 > CE-A  echo reply, seq 1
  • On the access link, we read the packets with tshark. CE-A is the address that the first line shows.
  • The 1436-byte packet is a 1450-byte frame. The request and the reply both pass.
  • The 1437-byte packet is a 1451-byte frame. This is the first try.
  • PE1 answers with an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big. The source is the loopback of PE1. The MTU is 1436, which is our budget.
  • CE-A sends the second request in two fragments, and the reply returns. IPv6 path MTU discovery worked.

7.6 Case 2: the long way home

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y icmpv6.type==2      (outer header, trimmed)
# PE1 to P2, 1358 bytes
2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005::   hop limit 255   Packet Too Big, toward PE6
# P4 to PE6, 1358 bytes
2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e005::   hop limit 253   the same message
# P4 to PE6, 1334 bytes
2001:db8:100::6 > fcbb:bb00:1:e006::   hop limit 255   the message, back toward PE1
# PE1 to P2, 1334 bytes
2001:db8:100::6 > fcbb:bb00:1:e006::   hop limit 253   the same message
# PE1 to CE-A, 1294 bytes
2001:db8:100::1 > CE-A   Packet Too Big, delivered
  • Now look at the path of that Packet Too Big. PE1 made it for a host on its own access link. You expect it to go directly to the host. It did not.
  • PE1 encapsulated it to the BLUE service SID of PE6, and it left PE1 toward P2.
  • The same message crosses the core and arrives on the link P4 to PE6. The hop limit is 253.
  • PE6 decapsulated it, looked up CE-A's address in BLUE, and sent it back to the service SID of PE1.
  • It crosses the core again, and it arrives on the link PE1 to P2.
  • Then PE1 sent it to CE-A. It worked, but it went through the core two times. We did not verify why the ingress makes the message this way. It probably depends on the platform.

7.7 Case 3: a smaller link in the middle

! P4, the link toward P2
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
 ipv6 mtu 1300
!
! RED traffic from CE-B to CE-A crosses P4 to P2
! inner 1260 + outer 40 = 1300   fits
! inner 1261 + outer 40 = 1301   does not fit
  • Case 3. The ingress has no problem, but a link in the middle is too small. On P4, we set the IPv6 MTU to P2 to 1300.
  • This time, the traffic goes in the opposite direction, from CE-B to CE-A in RED. That direction uses the upper path through P4 and P2.
  • An inner packet of 1260 bytes becomes 1300 bytes. It fits.
  • At 1261 bytes, it does not fit, and P4 must decide what to do. P4 is a P router. It has no VRF, and it does not know CE-B.

7.8 Case 3: the pings

Router / tool: CE-B

CE-B:~$ sudo ping -c 1 -I 10.2.6.2 -s 1232 10.2.1.2
1240 bytes from 10.2.1.2: seq=0 ttl=62 time=1.796 ms
1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

CE-B:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.2.6.2 -s 1233 10.2.1.2
1241 bytes from 10.2.1.2: seq=1 ttl=62 time=1.558 ms
2 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 50% packet loss
  • Now CE-B sends IPv4 pings to CE-A in RED. This direction crosses P4 and P2.
  • A data size of 1232 makes a 1260-byte packet. It fits, and the reply returns.
  • A data size of 1233 makes a 1261-byte packet. The first packet is lost. The second packet gets a reply. The loss is 50 percent.

7.9 Case 3: the captures

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r C-PE6-Gi0_0_0_3-CE-B.pcap -Y icmp      (PE6 to CE-B)
1275 bytes  10.2.6.2 > 10.2.1.2  echo request, the 1261-byte packet
110 bytes   10.0.0.4 > 10.2.6.2  destination unreachable, fragmentation needed, MTU 1236
1250 and 59 bytes  10.2.6.2 > 10.2.1.2  the second request, in two fragments
1275 bytes  10.2.1.2 > 10.2.6.2  echo reply

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y icmp.type==3      (the error in the core, outer header)
P2 to P4   190 bytes  2001:db8:100::6 > fcbb:bb00:1:e005::  hop limit 254
PE1 to P2  190 bytes  2001:db8:100::6 > fcbb:bb00:1:e005::  hop limit 253
P4 to PE6  150 bytes  2001:db8:100::1 > fcbb:bb00:6:e006::  hop limit 252
  • We captured on five links, and we read the files with tshark. First, the access link of CE-B, on PE6.
  • The 1261-byte request leaves CE-B. This is the first try.
  • An ICMPv4 error comes back to CE-B: fragmentation needed, with an MTU of 1236. Its source is 10.0.0.4, the IPv4 loopback of P4.
  • Now the core. P4 sent the error in the same outer header as the dropped packet. It goes from P4 through P2 toward PE1, to the service SID of PE1.
  • PE1 decapsulated it, found CE-B in RED, and sent it back through the core to the service SID of PE6.
  • CE-B learns the MTU, and it sends the second request in two fragments, 1250 and 59 bytes. The reply returns.

Ep08 · IS-IS from LSP to CEF

8.1 Where the LSP content comes from

! PE6 (trimmed)
router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  metric-style wide
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
   locator FA128
 flex-algo 128
  metric-type delay
  advertise-definition
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  point-to-point
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   fast-reroute per-prefix ti-lfa
   metric 10
performance-measurement
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  delay-measurement
   advertise-delay 5000
  • Before we read the LSP, we look at the configuration that creates it. This is PE6, trimmed to the lines that matter. You can copy the same structure on each router.
  • Wide metrics are necessary for segment routing. The IPv6 address family carries everything.
  • Two locators are attached to IS-IS: MAIN for algorithm 0, and FA128 for Flex-Algo 128. Each one becomes a locator in the LSP.
  • The flex-algo 128 block gives the metric type, delay, and it advertises the definition. We use it in Episode 11.
  • Each core interface is point-to-point, with a metric. The metric is the link metric that we read in the LSP.
  • The link delay of 5000 microseconds comes from the performance-measurement block. It is a static value that we configured, not a measurement.

8.2 Layer 1: the adjacency

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis adjacency detail
P2             Gi0/0/0/0                *PtoP*         Up    25   06:50:33 Yes None Up
  Neighbor IPv6 Address:  fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1*
  END.X SID:              fcbb:bb00:1:e000::/64 uA (PSP/USD), Algorithm 0
  Non-FRR END.X SID:      fcbb:bb00:1:e001::/64 uA (PSP/USD), Algorithm 0
  END.X SID:              fcbb:bb01:1:e000::/64 uA (PSP/USD), Algorithm 128
  Non-FRR END.X SID:      fcbb:bb01:1:e001::/64 uA (PSP/USD), Algorithm 128
  Topology:               IPv6 Unicast
    Usable by Flex-algo:  128
  BFD Status:             Neighbor Useable (BFD Required)
  • Layer 1, on PE1, for the neighbor P2.
  • The adjacency is up. It uses IPv6 link-local addresses. There is no IPv4 here.
  • IS-IS allocated two adjacency SIDs for this link in algorithm 0. Fast reroute can protect one of them. The SID with the Non-FRR mark is never protected.
  • There are two more for algorithm 128, the Flex-Algo of Episode 11. One link has four adjacency SIDs.
  • The topology is IPv6 unicast, and Flex-Algo 128 can use it. BFD is necessary, and it is up. Each of these lines can be the cause of a missing path.

8.3 Layer 2: the LSP, capabilities

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis database verbose PE6.00-00
PE6.00-00             0x00000034   0x359c        1145 /1200         0/0/0
  IPv6 Router ID: 2001:db8:100::6
  Router Cap:     0.0.0.0 D:0 S:0
    SR Algorithm:
      Algorithm: 0
      Algorithm: 1
      Algorithm: 128
    SRv6: O:0
    Node Maximum SID Depth:
      SRH Max SL:       3
      SRH Max End Pop:  3
      SRH Max T.insert: 3
      SRH Max T.encaps: 3
      SRH Max End D:    4
  • Layer 2 is PE6's link-state packet on PE1. We read it in three parts. Use verbose. The detail option does not show most of the information.
  • This is PE6's LSP, with a sequence number, a remaining lifetime and an IPv6 router ID.
  • PE6 gives the algorithms that it uses: 0 and 1, which are the defaults, and 128, which we configured.
  • RFC 9352 defines this SRv6 capability flag. It tells that PE6 can process SRv6.
  • These are the maximum SID depths. They are the same values that the manager showed in Episode 2. Each router learns the limits of the other routers from here.

8.4 Layer 2: the LSP, locators

  SRv6 Locator:   MT (IPv6 Unicast) fcbb:bb00:6::/48 D:0 Metric: 1 Algorithm: 0
    END SID: fcbb:bb00:6:: uN (PSP/USD)
      SID Structure:
        Block Length: 32, Node-ID Length: 16, Func-Length: 0, Args-Length: 80
  SRv6 Locator:   MT (IPv6 Unicast) fcbb:bb01:6::/48 D:0 Metric: 1 Algorithm: 128
    END SID: fcbb:bb01:6:: uN (PSP/USD)

  Metric: 1          MT (IPv6 Unicast) IPv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  • Part 2: the locators.
  • The SRv6 locator TLV contains fcbb:bb00:6::/48, in algorithm 0, with a metric of 1. This is the additional 1 in the metric 31 from Episode 2.
  • Below it is the End SID, PE6's uN, with its structure: block 32, node 16, function 0, argument 80. The 80 bits of argument are the space for the next micro-SIDs.
  • This is a second locator, in algorithm 128, for Flex-Algo.
  • The same locator is here again, as a normal IPv6 prefix. RFC 9352 permits this. Then routers without SRv6 can also route to the locator.

8.5 Loopback and locator, side by side

  Metric: 0          MT (IPv6 Unicast) IPv6 2001:db8:100::6/128
    Prefix Attribute Flags: X:0 R:0 N:1 E:0 A:0
    Source Router ID: 2001:db8:100::6
  Metric: 1          MT (IPv6 Unicast) IPv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
    Prefix Attribute Flags: X:0 R:0 N:0 E:0 A:0
  • In the LSP, compare PE6's two most important prefixes. The first fault in Episode 3 is here.
  • The loopback has metric 0 and the N flag. The N flag means that this prefix identifies the node.
  • The locator has metric 1, and it is a different prefix. These are two lines in the same LSP, from different parts of the configuration. One can disappear while the other stays.

8.6 Layer 2: the LSP, links

  Metric: 10         MT (IPv6 Unicast) IS-Extended P4.00
    Interface IPv6 Address: 2001:db8:200:46::1
    Neighbor IPv6 Address: 2001:db8:200:46::
    Link Average Delay: 5000 us
    END.X SID: fcbb:bb01:6:e000:: B:1 S:0 P:0 uA (PSP/USD) Alg:128
    END.X SID: fcbb:bb01:6:e001:: B:0 S:0 P:0 uA (PSP/USD) Alg:128
    END.X SID: fcbb:bb00:6:e000:: B:1 S:0 P:0 uA (PSP/USD) Alg:0
    END.X SID: fcbb:bb00:6:e001:: B:0 S:0 P:0 uA (PSP/USD) Alg:0
      SID Structure:
        Block Length: 32, Node-ID Length: 16, Func-Length: 16, Args-Length: 64
  • Part 3: each link. This is PE6's link to P4.
  • The metric is 10, with the IPv6 addresses of the two ends.
  • The link delay is 5000 microseconds. This is the static value that we configured for Flex-Algo. It is not a measurement. Episode 11 uses it.
  • There are four End.X SIDs, two for each algorithm. The B flag shows the SIDs that can have protection.
  • Their structure is block 32, node 16, function 16, argument 64. Our first plan expected an argument of zero. The router shows 64, and the router is correct.

8.7 Layers 3, 4 and 5

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [31/115]
     via fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2
    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, from 2001:db8:100::6, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, Protected

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
   via fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1/128, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  • Now the last three layers, for the same locator, on PE1.
  • Layer 3: IS-IS calculated the route, with metric 31, through P2.
  • Layer 4: the RIB installed it. It shows the route as an SRv6 locator, protected. Episode 9 explains the word protected.
  • Layer 5: CEF forwards it out of GigabitEthernet 0/0/0/0. All layers show the same next hop. When the layers do not agree, you have found the fault.

8.8 Fault 1: the interface leaves the IPv6 topology

! PE1
router isis CORE
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  no address-family ipv6 unicast
  • Now we break the network, one layer at a time. Fault 1: on PE1, we remove the IPv6 address family from the IS-IS interface to P2.
  • The interface stays up, with its addresses. Only IS-IS stops the use of IPv6 on it. Predict the result before the next page.

8.9 Fault 1: what changed

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis neighbors
P3             Gi0/0/0/1        *PtoP*         Up    22       L2   Capable

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 71, SRv6-locator, type level-2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1
 1  2001:db8:200:13::1
 2  2001:db8:200:23::
 3  2001:db8:200:24::1
 4  2001:db8:100::6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 2
Success rate is 100 percent (2/2), round-trip min/avg/max = 2/2/3 ms
  • This is PE1, twenty seconds later.
  • The adjacency to P2 is gone. When IS-IS runs only IPv6, the IPv6 topology is the only reason to keep a neighbor.
  • PE6's locator now has metric 71, not 31.
  • The traceroute shows the new path: down the expensive link to P3, back to P2, then P4 and PE6. Each packet now goes through two more hops.
  • The customer ping still works. Nobody complains. This fault is quiet, thus it is dangerous. When we restored the address family, P2 came back and the metric became 31 again.

8.10 Fault 2: what PE1 shows

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
% Network not in table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: inaccessible

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32
    unresolved
    0     Y   recursive                 drop

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 3
Success rate is 0 percent (0/3)
  • You saw fault 2 in Episode 3: on PE6, we removed the locator from IS-IS. Here are the outputs on PE1, in the layer model.
  • Layer 4: the RIB has no route to the locator.
  • BGP still has the customer path, but the locator is inaccessible.
  • Layer 5: CEF is unresolved, and the last column shows drop.
  • The customer ping fails.

8.11 Fault 2: layers 1 to 5 on PE1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis adjacency
P2             Gi0/0/0/0    *PtoP*   Up
P3             Gi0/0/0/1    *PtoP*   Up

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis database verbose PE6.00-00 | include Locator
  SRv6 Locator:   MT (IPv6 Unicast) fcbb:bb01:6::/48 D:0 Metric: 1 Algorithm: 128
! before the fault: a second line, fcbb:bb00:6::/48, Algorithm: 0

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48
The requested route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 was not found in the IS-IS CORE IPv6 Unicast Routing Table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
% Network not in table
  • Now we read all five layers of fault 2. On PE6, the locator MAIN is removed from IS-IS.
  • Layer 1: the adjacencies are up. PE1 still has its neighbors P2 and P3.
  • Layer 2: the LSP of PE6 has lost the locator. Only the Flex-Algo locator remains. Before the fault, the LSP also had fcbb:bb00:6::/48 in algorithm 0.
  • Layer 3: SPF has no prefix to calculate. The IS-IS route table does not contain the route.
  • Layer 4: the RIB has no route. Layer 5 follows: CEF drops the service, as the previous page showed.
  • The fault started at layer 2, on the far router. When the locator is added back, the route returns with metric 31, and the ping succeeds.

8.12 Fault 3: a filter on the way into the RIB

! PE1
ipv6 prefix-list BLOCK-PE6-LOCATOR
 10 deny fcbb:bb00:6::/48
 20 permit ::/0 le 128
!
router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  distribute-list prefix-list BLOCK-PE6-LOCATOR in
  • Fault 3 is the most difficult to see. On PE1, we add a filter between IS-IS and the RIB.
  • It is a prefix list. It denies only PE6's locator and permits all other prefixes.
  • We apply it with distribute-list in, under the IPv6 address family. It filters the routes that IS-IS installs. It does not stop the flooding of LSPs.

8.13 Fault 3: the layers disagree

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis database verbose PE6.00-00 | include Locator
  SRv6 Locator:   MT (IPv6 Unicast) fcbb:bb00:6::/48 D:0 Metric: 1 Algorithm: 0

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [31/115]

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
% Network not in table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6/32 detail
      valid, internal, best, group-best
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: inaccessible

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 2
Success rate is 0 percent (0/2)
  • Now read the five layers on PE1, from top to bottom.
  • Layer 2: PE6's locator is in the LSP. The filter did not change the flooding.
  • Layer 3: IS-IS still calculates the route, with metric 31.
  • Layer 4: the RIB does not have it. Network not in table.
  • BGP keeps the customer path as best, with the locator inaccessible, as in Episode 3.
  • The customer has no service. Layers 2 and 3 say yes, and layer 4 says no. This difference shows that there is a filter.

Ep09 · TI-LFA

9.1 Link P2 to P4, repaired by P2

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (link), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2 P3, Metric: 71
         P node: P3.00 [2001:db8:100::3], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:: uN (PSP/USD)
         Q node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:: uA (PSP/USD)

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
    next hop ..., Repair Node(s): 2001:db8:100::5
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:3:e005::}
  • Now the router. First, without node protection, the example that we drew.
  • P2 has a TI-LFA backup through P3. The metric after the repair is 71.
  • The P node is P3, the Q node is P5, and the adjacency SID e005 goes from P3 to P5. This agrees with our prediction.
  • In CEF, the repair is H.Insert.Red with one container, fcbb:bb00:3:e005::. P3's node SID and its adjacency to P5 are in one address.
  • On this platform, the repair inserts a routing header into the packet. It does not add a second outer header.

9.2 Link P4 to PE6, and link PE1 to P2

Router / tool: P4 and PE1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (link), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2 P5, Metric: 51
         P node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:5:: uN (PSP/USD)
         Q node: PE6.00 [2001:db8:100::6], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:5:e001:: uA (PSP/USD)
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:5:e001::}

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: LFA, via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1, P3, Metric: 71
  • Two more link examples.
  • P4 protects its link to PE6: go to P5, then use the adjacency from P5 to PE6, in one container. The metric is 51. This agrees with the prediction.
  • PE1 protects its link to P2. The backup is a normal LFA through P3, with no SIDs. Not every failure needs a segment list. This example proves it.

9.3 Asking for node protection

router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  fast-reroute per-prefix tiebreaker node-protecting index 100
  • Link protection expects that only the link failed. If the full neighbor router fails, a link-protecting backup can send traffic back to that router.
  • On this release, we had to request node protection with a tiebreaker. We added it on all six routers.

9.4 Node P2, repaired by PE1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (node), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1 P3, Metric: 101
         P node: P3.00 [2001:db8:100::3], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:: uN (PSP/USD)
         Q node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:: uA (PSP/USD)
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:3:e005::}
  • Now the node examples. First, P2 fails, as PE1 sees it.
  • PE1 now has a node-protecting backup through P3, with metric 101.
  • The list is one container: go to P3, then use the adjacency to P5. It is shorter than our manual calculation, which had three segments.
  • Why? P3 is PE1's direct neighbor, so the first hop needs no adjacency SID; the outgoing interface is sufficient. From P5, the normal path to PE6 goes through P4, not through P2. Thus PE6 needs no segment.
  • The router found the shortest list. Our manual calculation was correct, but not the shortest. Remember this difference when you check your predictions.

9.5 Node P4, repaired by P2

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (node), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2 P3, Metric: 91
         P node: P3.00 [2001:db8:100::3], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:: uN (PSP/USD)
         Q node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:: uA (PSP/USD)
         Q node: PE6.00 [2001:db8:100::6], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:5:e001:: uA (PSP/USD)
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::}
  • Now P4 fails, as P2 sees it.
  • There is a node-protecting backup through P3, with metric 91.
  • The repair has three parts: go to P3, use the adjacency from P3 to P5, then use the adjacency from P5 to PE6. This agrees with the manual calculation.
  • Look at the encoding: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::. The second adjacency, e001, is P5's adjacency. P5's node SID is not in front of it. After P3 shifts the address, P5 finds e001 as its own local SID.
  • Three instructions are in one container, and there is no routing header.

9.6 When node protection is impossible

Router / tool: P4

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
       Backup path: TI-LFA (link), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2 P5, Metric: 51
       TI-LFA Path Fallback Information:
         TI-LFA link: Path valid
         TI-LFA node: Path not found
  • One more example, which was not in the predictions. P4 protects traffic to PE6, with node protection requested.
  • P4 still uses a link-protecting backup.
  • P4 gives the reason: it did not find a node-protecting path. The destination, PE6, is the neighbor. You cannot protect traffic to a router against the failure of that router.

9.7 How much is protected

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute summary
IS-IS CORE IPv6 Unicast FRR summary
                          Critical   High       Medium     Low        Total
                          Priority   Priority   Priority   Priority
Prefixes reachable in L2
  All paths protected     0          0          5          10         15
  Some paths protected    0          0          0          0          0
  Unprotected             0          0          0          0          0
  Protection coverage     0.00%      0.00%      100.00%    100.00%    100.00%
  • One command shows if some prefixes have no protection. Use it on each router after a change.
  • On P2, all 15 IPv6 prefixes have a protected path.
  • No prefix is unprotected.
  • The coverage is 100 percent. Before, when two links had changed to one-way without a warning, P4 showed only 87 percent here. When this number decreases, the topology is often not what you think.

9.8 Failure test: the ping and the shutdown

Router / tool: PE1 and P4

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 4000 timeout 1
Sending 4000, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.30.6.6 timeout is 1 seconds:

# while the ping runs, on P4:
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4(config)#interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 shutdown
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4(config)#commit

# when the ping ends, on PE1:
Success rate is 100 percent (4000/4000), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/13 ms
  • Now the main test. We make a failure while traffic flows. First, in CML, we start captures on the core links.
  • Then, on PE1, we start a long GREEN ping: 4000 packets, with a timeout of 1 second.
  • While the ping runs, we shut the interface of P4 toward P2. This is the failure. P2 is the point of local repair.
  • When the ping ends, all 4000 packets got a reply. Next, we see what the routers recorded.

9.9 Failure test: what the routers saw

Router / tool: P2 and PE1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show logging last 12
%L2-BFD-6-SESSION_STATE_DOWN : BFD session to neighbor ... has gone down. Reason: Nbor signalled down
%ROUTING-ISIS-5-ADJCHANGE : ISIS (CORE): Adjacency to P4 (GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1) (L2) Down, BFD session DOWN

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [81/115] Label: None, low priority
     via fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, P2, SRGB Base: 16000, Weight: 0

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1
 1  2001:db8:200:12::1
 2  2001:db8:200:23::1
 3  2001:db8:200:35::1
 4  2001:db8:200:45::
 5  2001:db8:100::6
  • What did the routers record? First, the log of P2.
  • BFD on P2 reports that the session to P4 is down. Then IS-IS removes the adjacency to P4.
  • A few seconds later, PE1 has a new IS-IS route. The metric is 81, not 31. The next hop is still P2.
  • The traceroute shows the new path: P2, P3, P5, P4, and then PE6. It has five hops, not three.

9.10 A repair, caught on the wire

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r fail-P2-P3.pcap -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.routing.segleft -e ipv6.nxt | sort | uniq -c
   44  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::   1   43
   15  fcbb:bb00:3:e005::        1   43
 1481  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::     4

# time of the first packet of each group, in seconds
9.645  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::
9.749  fcbb:bb00:3:e005::
9.787  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::
  • Now the most important part: the packets on the link from P2 to P3. We count the echo requests by destination. The last two columns are Segments Left and the next header.
  • Phase 1: 44 packets. P2 inserted its node-protecting repair. The routing header has Segments Left 1, and the next header is 43.
  • Phase 2: 15 packets with a shorter list: P3 and the adjacency to P5, still with a routing header. We did not verify which router state caused this short phase.
  • Phase 3: 1481 packets with no routing header. The next header is 4. PE1 uses its new path, and P2 stopped the repair. Episode 10 explains this phase.
  • The times show how short the repair was. Phase 1 starts at 9.645 seconds, and phase 3 starts at 9.787. The repair carried traffic for about 0.14 seconds.

9.11 Following phase 1 to PE6

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.routing.segleft -e ipv6.nxt | sort | uniq -c
# P2 to P3
   44  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:e001::   1   43
# P3 to P5
   44  fcbb:bb00:e001::          1   43
 1496  fcbb:bb00:6:e008::            4
# P5 to PE6
   44  fcbb:bb00:6:e008::            4
  • Follow the 44 repaired packets to PE6. We read the capture of each link with the same command.
  • On the link P2 to P3, P2 inserted the repair in front of the service SID.
  • P3 did its adjacency instruction and shifted the address. The remaining instruction is e001, P5's adjacency to PE6.
  • P5 did e001 and sent the packet on the direct link to PE6. P5 is the penultimate endpoint, thus it removed the routing header. PE6 received only the service SID.
  • The other 1496 packets on the link P3 to P5 are the later traffic of phases 2 and 3. They have the same destination, and they have no routing header.
  • The functions from Episodes 4, 5 and 6 worked together in less than a quarter of a second.

9.12 Run it twice

# run 1
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 4000 timeout 1
Success rate is 100 percent (4000/4000), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/13 ms

# run 2, the same failure
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 6000 timeout 1
Success rate is 99 percent (5992/6000), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/17 ms
  • We did the same failure again, and we got a different result. You must see this too.
  • In the first test, the repair carried traffic for about 0.14 seconds, and no ping was lost.
  • In the second test, no repaired packet appeared, and 8 pings were lost. There were no packets on the wire for approximately one second. Then PE1's new path started.
