  • We did not verify why the two tests were different. This is a software forwarder in a virtual lab. It proves that the repair is there and shows its format. It cannot tell you the speed of protection. Measure the speed on hardware.

Ep10 · Microloops, BFD, and What a Virtual lab Cannot Time

10.1 The configuration and the delay

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show running-config router isis CORE address-family ipv6 unicast
  microloop avoidance segment-routing

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis protocol
        Microloop avoidance:       Enabled
          Configuration:           Type: Segment Routing, RIB update delay: 5000 msec
  • This is the configuration, and the router output.
  • There is one line under the IPv6 address family, on each router.
  • The router shows a RIB update delay of 5000 milliseconds. This is the Cisco default value. No RFC gives this value.

10.2 The failure test

Router / tool: P4 and P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4(config)#interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 shutdown
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4(config)#commit

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show logging last 12
03:46:34.253  %L2-BFD-6-SESSION_STATE_DOWN : BFD session to neighbor ... has gone down. Reason: Nbor signalled down
03:46:34.253  %ROUTING-ISIS-5-ADJCHANGE : ISIS (CORE): Adjacency to P4 (GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1) (L2) Down, BFD session DOWN
  • Now the test. As in Episode 9, we make the link between P2 and P4 fail while a GREEN ping runs from PE1. In CML, we start captures on the core links first.
  • On P4, we shut the interface toward P2, and we commit.
  • On P2, the log shows the BFD session to P4 going down, with the reason: the neighbor signalled down.
  • IS-IS removes the adjacency in the same millisecond. This is time zero for everything that follows.

10.3 P2, a fraction of a second later

Router / tool: P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [71/115]
   Installed Oct 03 03:46:34.354
     via fe80::5454:ff:fea8:d13a, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2, P3
     exp fe80::5454:ff:fea8:d13a, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2, P3
       P node: P3.00 [2001:db8:100::3], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:: uN (PSP/USD)
       Q node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:: uA (PSP/USD)
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:3:e005::}
  • We made the P2 to P4 link fail again, and we read the routers immediately after.
  • P2 installed its new route to PE6, with metric 71, at 34.354 seconds after the minute.
  • The new next hop is P3. There is a second line with the mark exp: an explicit path.
  • The explicit path is P3, then the adjacency to P5. These are the same segments as the repair. Thus packets get to P5 without the old table of P3.

10.4 PE1 does the same

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [81/115]
   Installed Oct 03 03:46:34.719
     via fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, P2
     exp fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, P2
       P node: P3.00 [2001:db8:100::3], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:: uN (PSP/USD)
       Q node: P5.00 [2001:db8:100::5], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:3:e005:: uA (PSP/USD)
  • PE1 is two hops from the failure, and it also changes.
  • PE1 installed its new route, with metric 81, at 34.719. This is a little more than one third of a second after P2.
  • PE1 also keeps an explicit path through P3 and the adjacency to P5. Its normal next hop is still P2.

10.5 PE1, a few seconds later

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [81/115]
   Installed Oct 03 03:46:40.219
     via fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, P2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
   via fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1/128, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, protected
   via fe80::5454:ff:fec1:58eb/128, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1, backup (Local-LFA)
  • This is PE1 again, some seconds later.
  • There is a new installation at 40.219. The explicit path is gone. Only the normal path through P2 is there.
  • CEF shows the route as protected again, with a new backup for the new topology. The network is stable.

10.6 The explicit path on the wire

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r fail2-P2-P3.pcap -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e ipv6.dst | sort | uniq -c
  979  fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::
 2621  fcbb:bb00:6:e008::

# first and last packet of the explicit path, in seconds
9.897   first   fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::
14.087  last    fcbb:bb00:3:e005:6:e008::
  • Now we can explain phase 3 from Episode 9. This capture is from the second test of that failure. We count the echo requests on the link P2 to P3 by destination.
  • Immediately after the failure, GREEN traffic is in one container: P3, the adjacency to P5, then PE6's service SID. This is the explicit path, with the service, in one address. There are 979 packets.
  • Later, the packets use only the service SID again. They follow the new shortest path through P2, P3, P5 and P4. There are 2621 packets.
  • The explicit path ran from 9.897 to 14.087 seconds, which is about 4.2 seconds. The router state showed 5.5 seconds. Use both numbers as approximate values, not as measurements.

10.7 Did anything loop?

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e eth.src -e ipv6.hlim | sort | uniq -c
# link P2 to P3, run 1
 1540  56:54:00:1c:70:f9  254
# link P2 to P3, run 2
 3600  56:54:00:1c:70:f9  254
  • A microloop leaves evidence on the wire. Thus we looked for it on the link between P2 and P3, the two routers from our manual example. We count the packets by source MAC address and hop limit.
  • In the first test, one source sent all 1540 packets, with hop limit 254. The source is P2.
  • The second test gave the same result: 3600 packets, one source, hop limit 254.
  • No packet came from P3. A looping packet would appear in the two directions, with a decreasing hop limit. With microloop avoidance on, we saw none.
  • We did not verify if a loop occurs with avoidance off. This is a good test for your lab.

10.8 BFD

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show running-config router isis CORE interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  bfd minimum-interval 100
  bfd multiplier 3
  bfd fast-detect ipv6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bfd ipv6 session
Gi0/0/0/0            fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1
No                   n/a             0s(0s*0)         300ms(100ms*3)   UP
  • Detection is the first step. This is how we made it fast.
  • BFD runs on each IS-IS interface, every 100 milliseconds. After 3 missed packets, BFD declares the session down.
  • Thus the detection time is 300 milliseconds, and the session is up. Without BFD, IS-IS waits for its hello holdtime, which is many seconds.
  • In our test, P4 shut its own interface, so P2 learned about the failure from BFD. Thus the BFD event and the adjacency event occurred in the same millisecond.

10.9 Restoration is an event too

Router / tool: P4, P2 and PE1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4(config)#no interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 shutdown
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4(config)#commit

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P2#show logging last 12
03:52:07.575  %L2-BFD-6-SESSION_STATE_UP : BFD session to neighbor ... on interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1 is up
03:52:14.102  %ROUTING-ISIS-5-ADJCHANGE : ISIS (CORE): Adjacency to P4 (GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1) (L2) Up, New adjacency

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 route fcbb:bb00:6::/48 detail
L2 fcbb:bb00:6::/48 [31/115] Label: None, low priority
   Installed Oct 03 03:52:20.122 for 00:00:04

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#ping vrf GREEN 10.30.6.6 source 10.30.1.1 count 6000 timeout 1
Success rate is 100 percent (6000/6000), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/12 ms
  • Then we restored the link while the pings continued. The restoration is also an event.
  • On P4, we remove the shutdown, and we commit.
  • BFD came up first, at 07.575 seconds after 03:52.
  • IS-IS brought the adjacency up at 14.102, six and a half seconds later.
  • PE1 changed its route back to metric 31 at 20.122, six seconds after that. This agrees with the same 5000-millisecond delay for an up event.
  • No ping was lost: 6000 of 6000. For the whole test, the traffic stayed on the detour. A repaired network changes back step by step, more than ten seconds later.

Ep11 · Flex-Algo

11.1 The configuration

! PE1: defines and advertises algorithm 128
router isis CORE
 flex-algo 128
  priority 200
  metric-type delay
  advertise-definition
!
! P3: takes part, does not advertise a definition
router isis CORE
 flex-algo 128
  metric-type delay
!
! every router: a locator in algorithm 128
segment-routing srv6 locators locator FA128
 prefix fcbb:bb01:1::/48
 algorithm 128
  • This is our configuration, in three parts.
  • PE1 defines algorithm 128 with the delay metric, at priority 200, and advertises the definition. PE6 does the same, at priority 100.
  • P3 participates, with the same metric type, but it does not advertise a definition. P2, P4 and P5 have the same configuration.
  • Each router has a second locator in the fcbb:bb01 block, for algorithm 128. In this lab, we use a separate block for Flex-Algo. This is our choice, not a rule of the RFC.

11.2 Who defines algorithm 128?

Router / tool: P3

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P3#show isis flex-algo 128
Flex-Algo 128:
  Level-2:
    Definition Priority: 200
    Definition Source: PE1.00
    Definition Equal to Local: Yes
    Definition Calculation Type: SPF
    Definition Metric Type: Delay
  Topologies supported:
    IPv6 Unicast
  Local Priority: 128
  • Two routers advertise a definition. Which definition does the network use? We ask P3, which advertises none.
  • The selected definition comes from PE1, at priority 200.
  • It is the same as P3's local configuration. If it were different, P3 would still use the selected definition, and this line would tell you to compare them.
  • The metric type is delay.
  • P3's local priority is 128, the default value, because P3 does not compete. RFC 9350 selects the highest priority. If two are equal, it selects the highest system ID.

11.3 The delays we advertise

! PE1
performance-measurement
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  delay-measurement
   advertise-delay 5000
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
  delay-measurement
   advertise-delay 1000
  • The delay values must come from a source. In a real network, the router measures them. In this lab, we advertise fixed values. Then you can build the same lab.
  • PE1 advertises 5000 microseconds for its upper link to P2.
  • It advertises 1000 for its lower link to P3. Each lower link has 1000. Each upper link and cross link has 5000. This is the opposite of the costs, on purpose.

11.4 Two routes, two paths

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb01:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 3001, SRv6-locator (algo 128), type level-2

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute fcbb:bb00:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1
 1  2001:db8:200:12::1
 2  2001:db8:200:24::1
 3  2001:db8:100::6
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute fcbb:bb01:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1
 1  2001:db8:200:13::1
 2  2001:db8:200:35::1
 3  2001:db8:100::6
  • The router gives the same result.
  • There are two routes to PE6, one for each locator. Algorithm 0 has metric 31. Algorithm 128 has metric 3001: 3000 microseconds plus 1 for the locator.
  • A traceroute to PE6's algorithm 0 SID goes through P2 and P4.
  • A traceroute to its algorithm 128 SID goes through P3 and P5. The routers and the links are the same, but there are two topologies. The destination address selects the topology.

11.5 Every algorithm has its own SIDs

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 sid
*** Locator: 'FA128' ***
fcbb:bb01:1::               uN (PSP/USD)      'default':1                       sidmgr
fcbb:bb01:1:e000::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/0, Link-Local]:128:P     isis-CORE
fcbb:bb01:1:e001::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/0, Link-Local]:128       isis-CORE
fcbb:bb01:1:e002::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/1, Link-Local]:128:P     isis-CORE
fcbb:bb01:1:e003::          uA (PSP/USD)      [Gi0/0/0/1, Link-Local]:128       isis-CORE
  • Each algorithm has its own SIDs. Episode 8 showed this in the LSP.
  • PE1 has a second node SID, fcbb:bb01:1::, in algorithm 128.
  • It also has a second pair of adjacency SIDs for each link, with the mark 128. A packet with these SIDs follows the algorithm 128 paths on each hop, not only on the first hop.

11.6 Protection stays inside the algorithm

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show isis ipv6 fast-reroute flex-algo 128 fcbb:bb01:6::/48 detail
     via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1, P3
       Backup path: TI-LFA (node), via ..., GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 P2, Metric: 15001
         P node: P4.00 [2001:db8:100::4], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb01:4:: uN (PSP/USD)

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb01:6::/48 detail
    SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb01:4::}
  • TI-LFA also works in each algorithm.
  • The primary path to PE6's algorithm 128 locator goes through P3. Its node-protecting backup goes through P2, with a delay metric of 15001.
  • The repair SID is P4's algorithm 128 node SID, fcbb:bb01:4::. The repair stays in the same topology as the traffic that it protects.

11.7 Putting a customer on algorithm 128

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show running-config router bgp 65000 vrf RED
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator FA128

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 sid | include RED
fcbb:bb01:6:e004::          uDT6              'RED'                             bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:6:e006::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000
  • Now the result. How do you put a customer on the low-delay topology? In SRv6, the simplest method is one line on the egress PE.
  • For RED IPv4, PE6 allocates its service SID from MAIN, algorithm 0.
  • For RED IPv6, PE6 allocates it from FA128, algorithm 128.
  • Thus RED IPv6's service SID is in the fcbb:bb01 block. Each packet that PE1 sends to it follows algorithm 128 automatically. No policy and no colour are necessary.

11.8 RED IPv6, both directions

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 3 2001:db8:c:206::2
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmpv6.type == 128 or icmpv6.type == 129" -T fields -e ipv6.dst
# PE1 to P3, CE-A to CE-B
fcbb:bb01:6:e004::     (outer destination, algorithm 128)
# PE1 to P2, CE-B to CE-A
fcbb:bb00:1:e007::     (outer destination, algorithm 0)
  • Now the result on the wire. We pinged from CE-A to CE-B in RED IPv6. We captured the two core links of PE1, and we read each file with tshark.
  • All three pings succeed.
  • To CE-B, the packets go out on the lower link, to the algorithm 128 service SID.
  • The replies come back on the upper link. PE1's own RED IPv6 SID is still in MAIN, so the return path uses algorithm 0. The two directions are different, because we configured only one end.
  • If you want low delay in the two directions, allocate from the algorithm 128 locator on the two PEs.

11.9 Experiment: make one link slow

! P3 and P5, the link between them
performance-measurement
 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1      ! on P5: GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
  delay-measurement
   advertise-delay 20000
  • Now a test. We increase the advertised delay of the P3 to P5 link from 1000 to 20000 microseconds, on the two ends. The costs do not change.
  • Predict the result before the next page. What occurs to each algorithm, and to RED IPv6?

11.10 One number changed

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb01:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 15001, SRv6-locator (algo 128), type level-2
    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1, from 2001:db8:100::6, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0, Protected

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#traceroute fcbb:bb01:6:: source 2001:db8:100::1
 1  2001:db8:200:12::1
 2  2001:db8:200:24::1
 3  2001:db8:100::6

CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 3 2001:db8:c:206::2
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

# captures after the change, from the same ping
PE1 to P2: fcbb:bb01:6:e004::  and  fcbb:bb00:1:e007::
PE1 to P3: no echo request
  • These are the results, after the delay of the P3 to P5 link became 20000. We start with the routes on PE1.
  • Algorithm 0 did not change. It has the same metric 31 and the same path. It does not use delay.
  • Algorithm 128 now has metric 15001, and the next hop is P2, the upper link. The lower path has a total of 22000 microseconds, and the upper path, at 15000, is better.
  • The traceroute to the algorithm 128 SID confirms this: P2, P4, then PE6.
  • The customer ping still works. The service did not change.
  • On the wire, the RED IPv6 traffic also moved. Both directions are now on the link PE1 to P2, and the link PE1 to P3 carries none. When we restored the delay, the traffic moved back.

Ep12 · L3VPN, Build BLUE and RED

12.1 The VRF

vrf BLUE
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  import route-target
   65000:100
  export route-target
   65000:100
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  import route-target
   65000:100
  export route-target
   65000:100
  • This is VRF BLUE on PE1.
  • There is one VRF with the name BLUE.
  • For IPv4, it imports and exports route target 65000:100.
  • IPv6 is the same. RED uses 65000:200. In this lab, these values are examples. Compare them with your own numbering plan.

12.2 The attachment

interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
 description TO-CE BLUE
 vrf BLUE
 ipv4 address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:c:101::1/64
  • This is the attachment to CE-A.
  • First, the interface goes into VRF BLUE. Then it gets an address.
  • Then it gets an IPv4 and an IPv6 address. RED has its own port and its own addresses.

12.3 BGP

router bgp 65000
 address-family vpnv4 unicast
 address-family vpnv6 unicast
 neighbor 2001:db8:100::6
  remote-as 65000
  update-source Loopback0
  address-family vpnv4 unicast
  address-family vpnv6 unicast
 vrf BLUE
  rd 65000:101
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
    alloc mode per-vrf
   redistribute connected
  • BGP connects all the parts.
  • One IPv6 session between the PE loopbacks carries VPNv4 and VPNv6. There is no IPv4 in this core.
  • Under the VRF, there is a route distinguisher: 65000:101 on PE1, and 65000:106 on PE6.
  • This is the SRv6 part. BGP allocates the service SID from locator MAIN, one for each VRF.
  • Redistribute connected advertises the CE subnet and the tenant loopback on the PE. In a real network, you also add static or eBGP routes to the CE.

12.4 The service SIDs

Router / tool: PE1 and PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing srv6 sid
fcbb:bb00:1:e004::          uDT4              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:1:e005::          uDT6              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:1:e006::          uDT6              'RED'                             bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:1:e007::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show segment-routing srv6 sid
fcbb:bb00:6:e004::          uDT4              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:6:e005::          uDT6              'BLUE'                            bgp-65000
fcbb:bb00:6:e006::          uDT4              'RED'                             bgp-65000
fcbb:bb01:6:e004::          uDT6              'RED'                             bgp-65000
  • These are the service SIDs on the two PEs.
  • On PE1, BLUE has a uDT4 and a uDT6. BGP owns both.
  • RED has its own pair. The function values, e004 to e007, come from the dynamic range, in the sequence of allocation.
  • PE6 has its own SIDs, with different values. On PE6, RED IPv6 is in the fcbb:bb01 block. This is the algorithm 128 setting from Episode 11. Do not write these values in your configuration. Read them.

12.5 BGP and the VRF table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast summary
Neighbor        Spk    AS MsgRcvd MsgSent       TblVer  InQ OutQ  Up/Down  St/PfxRcd
2001:db8:100::6   0 65000      31      21           70    0    0 00:02:51          5

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route vrf BLUE
C    10.1.1.0/24 is directly connected, 00:05:38, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
L    10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, 00:05:38, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
B    10.1.6.0/24 [200/0] via 2001:db8:100::6 (nexthop in vrf default), 00:01:13
L    10.100.1.1/32 is directly connected, 00:05:43, Loopback101
B    10.100.6.6/32 [200/0] via 2001:db8:100::6 (nexthop in vrf default), 00:01:13
  • Now the control plane.
  • The VPNv4 session to PE6 is up. It received five prefixes. The VPNv6 session shows four.
  • VRF BLUE on PE1 has the local CE subnet and the tenant loopback.
  • It also has two BGP routes from PE6. Their next hop is in the default table: PE6's loopback. The router resolves this next hop through PE6's locator and service SID. Episode 13 follows this chain step by step.

12.6 Tests from CE-A

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.2.1.2 10.2.6.2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 2001:db8:c:106::2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 2001:db8:c:206::2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -W 1 -I 10.1.1.2 10.2.6.2
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss
  • Now the important tests, from the customer side. On CE-A, the option -I sets the source address, and the source address selects the BLUE or RED port.
  • BLUE IPv4, site to site: both packets are answered.
  • RED IPv4: both packets are answered.
  • BLUE and RED IPv6: the pings are successful.
  • Now the negative test: from a BLUE source to a RED address, there is no reply. A test of reachability only is half a test. Always prove the isolation too.

12.7 Experiment: the same address in both customers

! PE6
interface Loopback199
 description BLUE overlap test
 vrf BLUE
 ipv4 address 10.99.0.6 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback299
 description RED overlap test
 vrf RED
 ipv4 address 10.99.0.6 255.255.255.255
  • Customers do not plan their addresses together. Thus we give the two customers the same address on PE6, on purpose.
  • 10.99.0.6 in BLUE.
  • 10.99.0.6 in RED. The same router has the same address two times.

12.8 Two routes for one address

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.99.0.6/32 detail
      Received Label 0xe0040
      Extended community: RT:65000:100
      Source Route Distinguisher: 65000:106

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf RED 10.99.0.6/32 detail
      Received Label 0xe0060
      Extended community: RT:65000:200
      Source Route Distinguisher: 65000:206
  • How does BGP keep them separate?
  • The BLUE route arrived with PE6's BLUE route distinguisher. The RED route arrived with RED's. Thus BGP has two different routes.
  • Each route has its own route target. Each VRF on PE1 imports only its own route.
  • Each route has a different service SID function: e004 for BLUE and e006 for RED. They are in the label field, as Episode 3 showed.

12.9 One address, two destinations

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.1.1.2 10.99.0.6
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.2.1.2 10.99.0.6
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss

# outer destination on PE1 to P2, from the capture
from 10.1.1.2, BLUE   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::
from 10.2.1.2, RED    fcbb:bb00:6:e006::
  • Now the wire. CE-A pings the same address, 10.99.0.6, with two different source addresses.
  • From its BLUE address, the ping is answered by the BLUE loopback.
  • From its RED address, the ping is answered by the RED loopback.
  • In the capture, PE1 sends the BLUE packet to PE6's BLUE service SID, e004. It sends the RED packet to the RED service SID, e006. The same address, two customers and two SIDs: the router does not mix them up.

12.10 Experiment: forget one import

! PE1
vrf BLUE
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  no import route-target 65000:100
  • One more test shows the function of route targets. On PE1, we remove only BLUE's IPv4 import route target. The export and IPv6 do not change.
  • Before the next page, predict what fails, and in which direction.

12.11 Half a VPN

Router / tool: PE1, PE6 and CE-A

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route vrf BLUE
C    10.1.1.0/24 is directly connected, 00:11:03, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
L    10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, 00:11:03, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
L    10.100.1.1/32 is directly connected, 00:11:07, Loopback101

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24
Paths: (0 available, no best path)

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show route vrf BLUE
B    10.1.1.0/24 [200/0] via 2001:db8:100::1 (nexthop in vrf default), 00:08:19
B    10.100.1.1/32 [200/0] via 2001:db8:100::1 (nexthop in vrf default), 00:08:19

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -W 1 -I 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 2 2001:db8:c:106::2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
  • These are the results from the two ends, after we removed the import of 65000:100 for BLUE IPv4 on PE1.
  • PE1's BLUE table lost all the IPv4 routes from PE6. Only the local routes are there.
  • BGP has no path for CE-B's subnet. PE1 did not keep PE6's route, because no VRF on PE1 imported that route target.
  • PE6 does not know about the problem. It still has PE1's routes, because PE1 still exports them. The VPN is broken in one direction only.
  • BLUE IPv4 pings fail.
  • But BLUE IPv6 still works, because we did not change the IPv6 import. When we restored the line, all the routes came back in some seconds.
  • When one address family of one customer fails, first examine the route targets of that address family on the two ends.

Ep13 · L3VPN, the Resolution Chain

13.1 Step 1: PE6 allocates and advertises

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
BGP routing table entry for 10.1.6.0/24, Route Distinguisher: 65000:106
    SRv6-VPN SID: fcbb:bb00:6:e004::/64
    Format: f3216
    Alloc Mode/Locator ID: per-vrf/2
  Advertised to peers (in unique update groups):
    2001:db8:100::1
      Origin incomplete, metric 0, localpref 100, weight 32768, valid, redistributed, best
      Extended community: RT:65000:100
  • Step 1, on PE6, where the prefix starts.
  • The route is in BLUE, with PE6's BLUE route distinguisher.
  • PE6 adds its BLUE service SID, fcbb:bb00:6:e004::. The SID comes from locator MAIN, with per-VRF allocation.
  • PE6 advertises the route to PE1.
  • The route target is 65000:100. Now we capture this advertisement on the wire.

13.2 Step 2: make PE6 send an update

Router / tool: PE6 and tshark

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6(config)#interface Loopback199 shutdown
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6(config)#commit
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6(config)#no interface Loopback199 shutdown
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6(config)#commit

$ tshark -r bgp-update-P4-PE6.pcap -Y "bgp.type == 2" -V
  • Step 2. To make PE6 send an update, we flap one of its BLUE loopbacks. In CML, we first start a capture on the link from PE6 to P4.
  • We shut the loopback, and PE6 withdraws its routes.
  • Then we remove the shutdown, and PE6 advertises the routes again. This is the update that we want.
  • We read the capture with tshark, in verbose mode, with a filter for BGP updates. Next, the decoded update.

13.3 Step 2: the update on the wire, part 1

Router / tool: capture

Border Gateway Protocol - UPDATE Message
    Path Attribute - MP_REACH_NLRI
        Address family identifier (AFI): IPv4 (1)
        Subsequent address family identifier (SAFI): Labeled VPN Unicast (128)
        Next hop:  RD=0:0 IPv6=2001:db8:100::6
        Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI)
            Label Stack: 917568 (bottom)
            Route Distinguisher: 65000:106
            MP Reach NLRI IPv4 prefix: 10.99.0.6
    Path Attribute - EXTENDED_COMMUNITIES
        Route Target: 65000:100
  • This update carries 10.99.0.6, the overlap address from Episode 12. CE-B's subnet uses the same format.
  • The address family is IPv4, labeled VPN unicast. MPLS VPNs use the same family.
  • The next hop is PE6's IPv6 loopback. It is not a SID.
  • The NLRI has a label, the route distinguisher and the prefix. The label is 917568. Remember this number.
  • The route target is an extended community.

13.4 Step 2: the update on the wire, part 2

Router / tool: capture

    Path Attribute - BGP Prefix-SID
        Type Code: BGP Prefix-SID (40)
        SRv6 L3 Service
            Type: SRv6 L3 Service (5)
            SRv6 Service Sub-TLV - SRv6 SID Information
                SRv6 SID Value: fcbb:bb00:6::
                SRv6 Endpoint Behavior: End.DT4 with NEXT-CSID (0x003f)
                SRv6 SID Structure
                    Locator Block Length: 32
                    Locator Node Length: 16
                    Function Length: 16
                    Argument Length: 0
                    Transposition Length: 16
                    Transposition Offset: 48
  • This is part 2 of the same update: the SRv6 information.
  • It is in the BGP Prefix-SID attribute, type 40, in an SRv6 L3 Service TLV, type 5. RFC 9252 defines them.
  • The SID value is only fcbb:bb00:6::, PE6's locator. The behavior code is End.DT4 with NEXT-CSID. This is uDT4 on IOS XR.
  • The structure is block 32, node 16, function 16, argument 0.
  • There are two more numbers: transposition length 16 and offset 48. The function is not in the SID value. These two numbers tell where it is.

13.5 Step 3: PE1's BGP path

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
BGP routing table entry for 10.1.6.0/24, Route Distinguisher: 65000:101
      Received Label 0xe0040
      Origin incomplete, metric 0, localpref 100, valid, internal, best, group-best, imported
      Extended community: RT:65000:100
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: 31
        T:1(Sid information), Sid:fcbb:bb00:6::(Transposed), Behavior:63
           Length [Loc-blk,Loc-node,Func,Arg]:[32,16,16,0], Tpose-len:16, Tpose-offset:48
      Source AFI: VPNv4 Unicast, Source VRF: default, Source Route Distinguisher: 65000:106
  • Step 3, on PE1.
  • PE1 imported the route into BLUE, from PE6's route distinguisher into PE1's own route distinguisher.
  • The received label is e0040. This is the same number as on the wire, in hexadecimal.
  • BGP checked the locator: it is reachable, with metric 31. In Episode 3, this line showed inaccessible.
  • This is the received transposed SID and its structure. PE1 now has all the information to build the full SID.

13.6 Step 4: the VRF route

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
Routing entry for 10.1.6.0/24
  Known via "bgp 65000", distance 200, metric 0, type internal
    2001:db8:100::6, from 2001:db8:100::6
      Nexthop in Vrf: "default", Table: "default", IPv6 Unicast
      Source RD attributes: 0x0000:65000:106
      SRv6 Headend: H.Encaps.Red [f3216], SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e004::}
  • Step 4, the VRF routing table.
  • The route is in BLUE. PE1 learned it from BGP.
  • Its next hop is PE6's loopback, in the default table. BGP next hops are loopbacks, as in MPLS VPNs.
  • This is the full SID, fcbb:bb00:6:e004::, with the instruction to encapsulate: reduced form, f3216. This line is all the SRv6 information in the route.

13.7 Step 5: CEF resolves through the locator

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
10.1.6.0/24, version 31, SRv6 Headend
   via fcbb:bb00:6::/128, 9 dependencies, recursive
    next hop fcbb:bb00:6::/128 via fcbb:bb00:6::/48
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e004::}
    0     Y   GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6::/48
  Known via "isis CORE", distance 115, metric 31, SRv6-locator, type level-2
  • Step 5, CEF.
  • The entry does not resolve through PE6's loopback. It resolves through PE6's locator, fcbb:bb00:6::/48. Thus the locator must be reachable, not the loopback.
  • This is the encapsulation instruction, to the service SID.
  • This is the outgoing interface, GigabitEthernet 0/0/0/0 to P2. It comes from the IS-IS route to the locator. The chain on PE1 ends here: VPN route, locator route, interface.

13.8 Step 6: the wire

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -I 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e frame.len -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.hlim
# CE-A to PE1       98
# PE1 to P2        138   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::   255
# P4 to PE6        138   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::   253
# PE6 to CE-B       98
  • Step 6, the packet. CE-A sends a ping, and we captured it at four locations.
  • Both pings are answered.
  • From CE-A, it is a normal 98-byte IPv4 ping.
  • When it leaves PE1, it is 40 bytes larger, with the service SID as destination and an outer hop limit of 255.
  • When it arrives at PE6, it is the same, but two routers decreased the outer hop limit.
  • On the link to CE-B, it is a normal packet again. The customer packet did not change in the tunnel.

13.9 Step 7: PE6 receives

Router / tool: PE6

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:6:e004::/64
fcbb:bb00:6:e004::/64, version 136, SRv6 Endpoint uDT4
    next hop VRF - 'BLUE', table - 0xe0000002
    0     Y   recursive                 Lookup in table

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show route vrf BLUE 10.1.6.2
Routing entry for 10.1.6.0/24
  Known via "connected", distance 0, metric 0 (connected)
    directly connected, via GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
  • Step 7, on PE6 again.
  • The destination agrees with PE6's uDT4 entry. Its action is a lookup of the inner packet in BLUE.
  • In BLUE, CE-B is directly connected. The chain is complete: it starts with an allocation on PE6, and it ends at a port of PE6.

13.10 TTL, hop limit and DSCP

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo traceroute -n -t 184 -s 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2 -w 1 -q 1 -m 5
 1  10.1.1.1
 2  10.46.0.1
 3  10.1.6.2

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "ip.dst == 10.1.6.2 and udp" -T fields \
    -e frame.len -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.hlim -e ipv6.tclass -e ip.dsfield.dscp -e ip.ttl
# CE-A to PE1   60                                 DSCP 46   TTL 1, 2, 3
# PE1 to P2    100   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::   hop limit 255   tclass 0x0   DSCP 46   TTL 1, 2
# P4 to PE6    100   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::   hop limit 253   tclass 0x0   DSCP 46   TTL 1, 2
  • Two header fields are important: the hop limit and the quality of service marking. We send traceroute probes from CE-A, with the DSCP mark EF, which is 46.
  • The traceroute shows PE1, then PE6, then CE-B. The customer cannot see P2 and P4. RFC 2983 calls this the pipe model.
  • On the access link, the probes have DSCP 46 and the TTL 1, 2 and 3.
  • In the core, PE1 sets the outer hop limit to 255. It does not copy the customer TTL. P2 and P4 decrease only the outer hop limit: it is 253 at PE6.
  • The inner TTL did not change. The inner DSCP is still 46, but the outer traffic class is 0. A core router that queues on the outer header sends this traffic as best effort.
  • On this platform, the traffic class propagation is configurable, as the manager showed in Episode 2. If your core queues on the outer header, configure it, and verify it with a capture.

Ep14 · EVPN, a Layer 2 Service

14.1 The configuration on PE1

interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4
 description TO-CE L2 attachment circuit
 l2transport
!
l2vpn
 xconnect group SRV6-VPWS
  p2p ELINE-300
   interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4
   neighbor evpn evi 300 service 300 segment-routing srv6
!
evpn
 segment-routing srv6
  locator MAIN
  • This is all the configuration on PE1. PE6 has the same configuration, in the opposite direction. The BGP sessions already carry the Layer 2 VPN EVPN family.
  • The customer port becomes a Layer 2 transport port. It has no IP address. PE1 does not route on this port.
  • A point-to-point cross-connect connects the port to one remote service.
  • This is EVPN instance 300, service 300, over SRv6. The service number must be the same on the two PEs.
  • EVPN allocates its SIDs from locator MAIN. We did not configure route targets. EVPN made 65000:300 from the AS number and the instance.

14.2 Route type 1 on the wire, part 1

Router / tool: capture

Border Gateway Protocol - UPDATE Message
    Path Attribute - MP_REACH_NLRI
        Address family identifier (AFI): Layer-2 VPN (25)
        Subsequent address family identifier (SAFI): EVPN (70)
        Next hop: 2001:db8:100::1
        EVPN NLRI: Ethernet AD Route
            Route Type: Ethernet AD Route (1)
            Route Distinguisher: 10.0.0.1:300
            ESI: 00:00:00:00:00:00:00:00:00:00
            Ethernet Tag ID: 300
            MPLS Label 1: 917680
    Path Attribute - EXTENDED_COMMUNITIES
        EVPN Layer 2 Attributes: flags: 0x0002, L2 MTU: 0
        Route Target: 65000:300
  • We captured on the core link of PE1 during the commit. In less than two seconds, PE1 sent this update.
  • The family is Layer 2 VPN EVPN. The next hop is the loopback of PE1.
  • The route is type 1, Ethernet auto-discovery. PE1 made the route distinguisher from its router ID and the instance.
  • The Ethernet segment identifier is zero, because the CE connects to one PE only. The Ethernet tag is 300, the service number. The remote PE uses it to match the two ends.
  • There is a label field again: 917680.
  • There are two extended communities. The first is Layer 2 attributes, with MTU zero. Zero means: do not check. The second is the route target.

14.3 Route type 1 on the wire, part 2

Router / tool: capture

    Path Attribute - BGP Prefix-SID
        SRv6 L2 Service
            Type: SRv6 L2 Service (6)
            SRv6 Service Sub-TLV - SRv6 SID Information
                SRv6 SID Value: fcbb:bb00:1::
                SRv6 Endpoint Behavior: End.DX2 with NEXT-CSID (0x0041)
                SRv6 SID Structure
                    Locator Block Length: 32
                    Locator Node Length: 16
                    Function Length: 16
                    Argument Length: 0
                    Transposition Length: 16
                    Transposition Offset: 48
  • Part 2 has the same Prefix-SID attribute as in Episode 13, with one difference.
  • The TLV is SRv6 L2 Service, type 6. In Episode 13, it was L3 Service, type 5.
  • The SID value is the locator of PE1. The behavior is End.DX2 with NEXT-CSID, code 65. On IOS XR, this is uDX2: remove the outer header and send the frame out of one port.
  • The transposition is the same: 16 bits at offset 48. Thus the function is in the label field again.

14.4 The cross-connect is up

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show l2vpn xconnect detail
Group SRV6-VPWS, XC ELINE-300, state is up; Interworking none
  AC: GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4, state is up
    MTU 1500; XC ID 0x2; interworking none
  EVPN: PW ID: evi 300, ac-id 300, state is up ( established )
    Encapsulation SRv6
      SRv6              Local                        Remote
      uDX2              fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::           fcbb:bb00:6:e007::
      AC ID             300                          300
      MTU               1514                         0
      Locator Resolved  Yes                          N/A
      SRv6 Headend      H.Encaps.L2.Red              N/A
  • Now the state on PE1.
  • The cross-connect is up. The customer port is also up.
  • The EVPN side is up. The local SID is e00b and the remote SID is e007. These are the SIDs that we built from the capture.
  • The service is 300 on the two ends. PE6 advertised MTU zero, thus there is no MTU check. Remember this. It is important later.
  • The headend behavior is H.Encaps.L2.Red: encapsulate a Layer 2 frame, reduced form.

14.5 BGP and CEF on PE1

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp l2vpn evpn rd 10.0.0.6:300 [1][0000.0000.0000.0000.0000][300]/120 detail
    2001:db8:100::6 (metric 30) from 2001:db8:100::6 (10.0.0.6)
      Received Label 0xe00700
      Extended community: EVPN L2 ATTRS:0x02:0 RT:65000:300
       SID Locator: fcbb:bb00:6::/48, RIB metric: 31
        T:1(Sid information), Sid:fcbb:bb00:6::(Transposed), Behavior:65

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::/64 detail
fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::/64, version 243, SRv6 Endpoint uDX2
   via ::/128, GigabitEthernet0/0/0/4, 2 dependencies, weight 0, class 0
    AC Interface: Gi0/0/0/4
    XConnect ID: 0x2
  • This is the same chain as for Layer 3, but the last step is different.
  • PE1 received the type 1 route of PE6. The label shows in its three-byte form.
  • This is the locator check, metric 31, and behavior 65. If the locator of PE6 is not reachable, this service fails. It is the same as fault A in Episode 3.
  • This is the SID of PE1 in CEF. For uDT4, the action was a lookup in a VRF. For uDX2, there is no lookup. The action is a port, Gi0/0/0/4.

14.6 From CE-A

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ip neigh flush dev eth2
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 172.16.30.6
64 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=0 ttl=64 time=2.686 ms
64 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=1 ttl=64 time=1.449 ms
64 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=2 ttl=64 time=1.362 ms
CE-A:~$ sudo ping6 -c 3 2001:db8:30::6
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ip neigh show dev eth2
172.16.30.6 lladdr 52:54:00:34:24:24 ref 1 used 0/0/0 probes 4 REACHABLE
2001:db8:30::6 lladdr 52:54:00:34:24:24 ref 1 used 0/0/0 probes 4 REACHABLE
  • Now we send traffic. First, we clear the neighbor table on CE-A. Then ARP must also go through the service.
  • The table is empty.
  • The IPv4 ping to CE-B gets three replies, with TTL 64. No router decreased it. For the customer, there is no router between the two CEs.
  • IPv6 also operates. The PEs have no IPv6 configuration for this service.
  • This shows that the service is Layer 2. CE-A learned the MAC address of CE-B, which ends in 24:24. In a Layer 3 VPN, CE-A learns only the MAC address of PE1.

14.7 The frames, captured at three points

Router / tool: tshark

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "arp or icmp or ipv6.nxt == 143" -T fields \
    -e frame.len -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.nxt -e ipv6.hlim
# CE-A to PE1
  42                                      ARP request
  60                                      ARP reply
  98                                      echo request
# PE1 to P2
 114   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   143   255     ARP request
 114   fcbb:bb00:1:e00b::   143   253     ARP reply
 152   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   143   255     echo request
# P4 to PE6
 114   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   143   253     ARP request
 152   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   143   253     echo request
  • We captured at three locations during the ping from CE-A, and we read each file with tshark.
  • On the access link, there are an ARP request of 42 bytes, an ARP reply of 60 bytes, and the 98-byte ping.
  • In the core, the ARP broadcast is unicast, to the SID of PE6, with the outer next header 143. A point-to-point service has only one destination for a broadcast.
  • The reply from CE-B comes back to the SID of PE1, e00b.
  • The 98-byte ping is 152 bytes in the core. The next header 143 identifies Ethernet. RFC 8986 defines this value.
  • On the link P4 to PE6, the frames are the same, and the outer hop limit is two lower, as for Layer 3.

14.8 Testing the edge

Router / tool: CE-A

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -s 1418 172.16.30.6
PING 172.16.30.6 (172.16.30.6): 1418 data bytes
1426 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=0 ttl=64 time=1.296 ms
1426 bytes from 172.16.30.6: seq=1 ttl=64 time=1.639 ms
2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss
CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -s 1419 172.16.30.6
PING 172.16.30.6 (172.16.30.6): 1419 data bytes
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss
  • A ping with 1418 bytes of data is a 1446-byte IP packet: 1418, plus 8 for ICMP, plus 20 for IPv4.
  • The 1446-byte packet goes through.
  • With one more byte, all pings are lost. CE-A gets no error message. It only waits.

14.9 Where the 1447-byte packet died

Router / tool: CE-A, tshark and routers

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 2 -s 1419 172.16.30.6
2 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "ipv6.fraghdr" -T fields -e frame.len -e ipv6.src -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.fraghdr.offset
# PE1 to P2
1510   2001:db8:100::1   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   0
  75   2001:db8:100::1   fcbb:bb00:6:e007::   181
# P4 to PE6: the same two fragments

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show ipv6 traffic
         2 fragmented into 4 fragments, 0 failed
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE6#show ipv6 traffic
         0 fragments, 0 total reassembled
  • Where did the packet go? We have four items of evidence. First, the ping with 1419 bytes of data.
  • All pings are lost, and CE-A receives no error.
  • PE1 did not drop the frame. It fragmented the outer IPv6 packet into two fragments: 1510 and 75 bytes on the wire.
  • The counters of PE1 agree: two packets, fragmented into four fragments. These are our two pings.
  • The two fragments went through the core and arrived at PE6.
  • But the IPv6 counters of PE6 show zero fragments. The forwarding plane matched the SID and discarded the fragments before reassembly. CE-B received nothing, and no device sent a message.
  • This is the worst type of failure: it is silent, and it occurs only for large packets.

Ep15 · SR Policy and Binding SID

15.1 The policy on PE1

segment-routing
 traffic-eng
  segment-lists
   segment-list VIA-P3-P5-UN
    srv6
     index 10 sid fcbb:bb00:3::
     index 20 sid fcbb:bb00:5::
     index 30 sid fcbb:bb00:6::
  policy BLUE-C100
   srv6
    locator MAIN binding-sid dynamic behavior ub6-insert-reduced
   color 100 end-point ipv6 2001:db8:100::6
   candidate-paths
    preference 100
     explicit segment-list VIA-P3-P5-UN
  • This is the policy on PE1. Our goal is to send BLUE traffic to PE6 on the lower links, through P3 and P5.
  • The segment list has three node SIDs: P3, P5 and PE6.
  • The Binding SID comes from locator MAIN. It is dynamic, with the insert-reduced behavior. Episode 4 showed that this platform gives only this form.
  • The color is 100. The endpoint is the loopback of PE6.
  • There is one candidate path, with preference 100. It uses this list.

15.2 The policy is up

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing traffic-eng policy color 100 detail
Color: 100, End-point: 2001:db8:100::6
    Admin: up  Operational: up for 00:35:12 (since Oct  3 07:46:12.843)
    Preference: 100 (configuration) (active)
      Explicit: segment-list VIA-P3-P5-UN (valid)
          SID[0]: fcbb:bb00:3::/48
          SID[1]: fcbb:bb00:5::/48
          SID[2]: fcbb:bb00:6::/48
        Binding SID behavior: uB6 (PSP/USD Insert.Red)
        Install Final Node SID: No
    Binding SID: fcbb:bb00:1:e008::
    Steering BGP disabled: no
    Invalidation drop enabled: no
  • This is the state on PE1.
  • The policy is up. The explicit path is active, and its list is valid.
  • Look at this line: install final node SID, no. The node SID of PE6 is in the list, but PE1 does not put it in the packet. The service SID already goes to PE6.
  • The Binding SID is fcbb:bb00:1:e008::. It is a SID on the locator of PE1.
  • BGP steering is permitted. Invalidation drop is off. If the policy fails, traffic goes back to the usual path. We test this at the end.

15.3 Colour on the egress

Router / tool: PE6

extcommunity-set opaque COLOR-100
  100
end-set
!
route-policy BLUE-EXPORT-C100
  set extcommunity color COLOR-100
end-policy
!
vrf BLUE
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  export route-policy BLUE-EXPORT-C100
  • Now the egress side. PE6 selects which of its routes use color 100.
  • A color is an opaque extended community. Here, its value is 100.
  • A route policy sets it.
  • The BLUE IPv4 export uses this policy. Only BLUE IPv4 gets the color. BLUE IPv6, RED and GREEN do not change.

15.4 The coloured update on the wire

Router / tool: capture

Border Gateway Protocol - UPDATE Message
    Path Attribute - MP_REACH_NLRI
        Next hop:  RD=0:0 IPv6=2001:db8:100::6
            Label Stack: 917568 (bottom)  RD 65000:106  10.99.0.6
            Label Stack: 917568 (bottom)  RD 65000:106  10.1.6.0
            Label Stack: 917568 (bottom)  RD 65000:106  10.100.6.6
    Path Attribute - EXTENDED_COMMUNITIES
        Color: 0x0000 0x0000 0x0064 [Transitive Opaque]
        Route Target: 65000:100
    Path Attribute - BGP Prefix-SID
        SRv6 SID Value: fcbb:bb00:6::
        SRv6 Endpoint Behavior: End.DT4 with NEXT-CSID (0x003f)
  • We captured on the link from PE6 to P4 during the commit. PE6 advertised BLUE again immediately.
  • One update carries three BLUE prefixes, with the same label. Episode 13 told about this: the prefixes use one set of attributes together.
  • This is the new attribute: color, value 0x64. This is 100 in decimal.
  • The service SID did not change. The color does not change what PE6 does with the packet. It changes the path that PE1 uses to PE6.

15.5 PE1 steers into the policy

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
    2001:db8:100::6 C:100 (bsid: fcbb:bb00:1:e008::) (metric 30) from 2001:db8:100::6
      Extended community: Color:100 RT:65000:100
      SR policy color 100, up, not-registered, bsid fcbb:bb00:1:e008::

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show route vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
    2001:db8:100::6, from 2001:db8:100::6 via srv6-sid fcbb:bb00:1:e008:: (resolution len 64)
      SRv6 Headend: H.Encaps.Red [f3216], SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e004::}

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
   via local-srv6-sid fcbb:bb00:1:e008::, 3 dependencies, recursive
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e004::}
      SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:3:5::}
    0     Y   GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1
  • On PE1, we look at the same three tables as in Episode 13. Each table shows something new.
  • First, BGP. The next hop now shows C 100 and the Binding SID. Color 100 and next hop PE6 match our policy, and the policy is up.
  • Next, the VRF route. The service SID is the same. But the route now resolves through the Binding SID, not through the locator of PE6.
  • CEF shows two steps. First, encapsulate with the service SID. Then, insert the list of the policy before it: fcbb:bb00:3:5::. This is the insert form of the Binding SID.
  • The first link is GigabitEthernet 0/0/0/0, to P2. It is not the link to P3. Remember this.

15.6 On the wire: every core link

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 -I 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8" -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.hlim | sort -u
# PE1 to P2       fcbb:bb00:3:5:6:e004::   255
# P2 to P3        fcbb:bb00:3:5:6:e004::   254
# P3 back to P2   fcbb:bb00:5:6:e004::     253
# P2 to P4        fcbb:bb00:5:6:e004::     252
# P4 to P5        fcbb:bb00:5:6:e004::     251
# P5 back to P4   fcbb:bb00:6:e004::       250
# P4 to PE6       fcbb:bb00:6:e004::       249
  • We captured on all eight core links while CE-A sent a ping to CE-B in BLUE. All three pings got a reply. We read each file with tshark. These are all the links that carried a request.
  • PE1 sends the packet to P2. It does not send it to P3.
  • P2 sends it to P3, with no change.
  • P3 removes its micro-SID, and the packet goes back to P2.
  • Then the packet goes to P4 and P5. P5 removes its micro-SID.
  • Then it goes back to P4, and then to PE6. This is seven hops, not three, with two U-turns. The packet did not use the lower links.
  • The hop limit shows this: it decreases from 255 to 249, one for each router.

15.7 A strict path, with adjacency SIDs

  segment-lists
   segment-list VIA-P3-P5-UA
    srv6
     index 10 sid fcbb:bb00:3:e005::
     index 20 sid fcbb:bb00:5:e003::
  policy BLUE-C100
   candidate-paths
    preference 200
     explicit segment-list VIA-P3-P5-UA

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e004::}
      SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:3:e005:5:e003::}
  • To use the lower links, we need adjacency SIDs, from Episode 4. Read them on P3 and P5 immediately before the test. Dynamic uA values can change after a reboot, or after an outage of more than three minutes.
  • The adjacency SID of P3 to P5 is e005.
  • The adjacency SID of P5 to PE6 is e003.
  • We add them as a second candidate path, with preference 200. It becomes active, and we do not delete the first path.
  • CEF now inserts fcbb:bb00:3:e005:5:e003::. The Binding SID did not change. Thus BGP and the VRF route also did not change.

15.8 Strict path on the wire

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 -I 10.1.1.2 10.1.6.2
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8 or icmp.type == 0" \
    -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.hlim -e icmp.type | sort -u
# PE1 to P2    fcbb:bb00:3:e005:5:e003:6:e004   255   request
# P2 to P3     fcbb:bb00:3:e005:5:e003:6:e004   254   request
# P3 to P5     fcbb:bb00:5:e003:6:e004::        253   request
# P5 to PE6    fcbb:bb00:6:e004::               252   request
# P4 to PE6    fcbb:bb00:1:e004::               255   reply
# P2 to P4     fcbb:bb00:1:e004::               254   reply
# PE1 to P2    fcbb:bb00:1:e004::               253   reply
  • These are the addresses on the wire, for the same ping.
  • One address has six micro-SIDs: P3, its adjacency, P5, its adjacency, PE6 and the service. The address is full, but there is no routing header. The size is still 138 bytes.
  • P2 forwards it with no change.
  • P3 removes two micro-SIDs: its node SID and its adjacency SID. Then it sends the packet on the link from P3 to P5.
  • P5 does the same, to PE6.
  • What about the replies? They went PE6, P4, P2, PE1, on the IGP path, to the BLUE SID of PE1. Only the export of PE6 adds a color. A policy steers one direction only. To steer both directions, add a color on the other side too.

15.9 When the policy goes down

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing traffic-eng policy color 100
    Admin: down  Operational: down for 00:00:08 (since Oct  3 08:23:46.018)
    Preference: 200 (configuration) (inactive) (shutdown)
    Preference: 100 (configuration) (inactive) (shutdown)

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
    2001:db8:100::6 (metric 30) from 2001:db8:100::6 (10.0.0.6)
      Extended community: Color:100 RT:65000:100

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf BLUE 10.1.6.0/24 detail
   via fcbb:bb00:6::/128, 11 dependencies, recursive
    next hop fcbb:bb00:6::/128 via fcbb:bb00:6::/48
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e004::}
  • This is the last test: what occurs when the policy fails? We shut it down.
  • The policy is admin down. The two candidate paths are down. PE1 releases the Binding SID.
  • The route still has color 100. But BGP does not point it to a policy now.
  • CEF goes back to the locator of PE6 and a plain encapsulation, as in Episode 13. The capture showed PE1, P2, P4, PE6, and all pings got a reply.
  • On this platform, this fallback is the default, because invalidation drop is off. If a service must always stay on its path, for example for separation, set invalidation drop on. Then test that it drops the traffic.
  • After no shutdown, the policy came back with the same Binding SID value. But the value is dynamic. Do not make a design that needs this number.

Ep16 · On-Demand Next Hop Needs a PCE

16.1 The template on PE1

segment-routing
 traffic-eng
  on-demand color 200
   srv6
    locator FA128 binding-sid dynamic behavior ub6-insert-reduced
   !
   dynamic
    metric
     type latency

extcommunity-set opaque COLOR-200
  200
end-set
vrf RED
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  export route-policy RED-EXPORT-C200
  • This is the template. First, there is no PCE.
  • The on-demand color is 200.
  • Its Binding SID comes from the Flex-Algo locator, FA128.
  • The intent is a dynamic path with the lowest latency.
  • On PE6, the RED IPv4 routes have color 200 in the export. Thus each RED IPv4 route now asks PE1 for a low-latency path.

16.2 Test A: the headend computes

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing traffic-eng policy color 200 detail
Color: 200, End-point: 2001:db8:100::6
    Admin: up  Operational: down for 00:00:48 (since Oct  3 08:34:41.702)
    Preference: 200 (BGP ODN) (inactive)
      Last error: SRv6 SIDs failed verification
      Dynamic (inactive)
      Last error: HE computation not supported for SRV6 policy
        Metric Type: LATENCY (IANA PCEP/IGP: 12/1), Path Accumulated Metric: 0
    Preference: 100 (BGP ODN) (inactive)
      Last error: SRv6 SIDs failed verification
  • Test A. There is no PCE. PE1 must calculate the path.
  • PE1 made the policy for PE6, but the policy is down.
  • The output gives the reason: Headend computation not supported for SRv6 policy.
  • A second candidate path, with preference 100, also fails. We explain its function later.

16.3 Test A: what the traffic does

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf RED 10.2.6.0/24 detail
    2001:db8:100::6 (metric 30) from 2001:db8:100::6 (10.0.0.6)
      Extended community: Color:200 RT:65000:200

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf RED 10.2.6.0/24 detail
   via fcbb:bb00:6::/128, 7 dependencies, recursive
    next hop fcbb:bb00:6::/128 via fcbb:bb00:6::/48
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e006::}
    0     Y   GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0    fe80::5454:ff:fe66:75e1

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 -I 10.2.1.2 10.2.6.2
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss
  • What occurs to the RED traffic?
  • The route still has color 200, but it has no policy.
  • CEF goes back to the locator of PE6 and the plain encapsulation, out to P2. The capture showed PE1, P2, P4, PE6. This is the lowest-cost path. In this lab, it is also the highest-latency path.
  • All pings get a reply. Nothing is broken, thus no person sees the problem. The customer pays for low latency, but gets high latency, and no device tells anyone.

16.4 A minimal PCE

Router / tool: P4

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4#show running-config pce
pce
 address ipv6 2001:db8:100::4

router isis CORE
 distribute link-state

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show running-config segment-routing traffic-eng pcc
  pcc
   source-address ipv6 2001:db8:100::1
   pce address ipv6 2001:db8:100::4

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4#show pce ipv6 peer
Peer address: 2001:db8:100::1
  State: Up
  Capabilities: Stateful, Segment-Routing, Update, Instantiation, SRv6, SR-P2MP
  • Thus we add a PCE. In a production network, it is a special server or router. Here, P4 is the PCE, with three lines of configuration.
  • P4 becomes a PCE on its loopback.
  • IS-IS gives its topology database to the PCE, with the delays and the SIDs.
  • On PE1, the client side tells PE1 the address of the PCE.
  • The session is up, and the two sides support SRv6.

16.5 Test B: the PCE computes

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show segment-routing traffic-eng policy color 200 detail
    Admin: up  Operational: up for 00:00:48 (since Oct  3 08:30:28.609)
    Preference: 200 (BGP ODN) (inactive) (shutdown)
    Preference: 100 (BGP ODN) (active)
      Dynamic (pce 2001:db8:100::4) (valid)
        Metric Type: LATENCY (IANA PCEP/IGP: 12/1), Path Accumulated Metric: 3000
          SID[0]: fcbb:bb00:1:e002::/64 Behavior: uA (PSP/USD) (57)
          SID[1]: fcbb:bb00:3:e004::/64 Behavior: uA (PSP/USD) (57)
          SID[2]: fcbb:bb00:5:e002::/64 Behavior: uA (PSP/USD) (57)
    Binding SID: fcbb:bb01:1:e004::
  • Test B. This is the same template, with pcep under dynamic.
  • The policy is up.
  • Now we see the function of the two candidate paths. Preference 200 is the calculation on the headend, and it is shut. Preference 100 is delegated to the PCE, and it is active.
  • The total latency is 3000 microseconds.
  • The path has three adjacency SIDs: PE1 to P3, P3 to P5 and P5 to PE6. All three are the protected type.
  • The Binding SID comes from the FA128 locator, as the template specifies.

16.6 Test B in CEF

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf RED 10.2.6.0/24 detail
    2001:db8:100::6 C:200 (bsid: fcbb:bb01:1:e004::) (metric 30) from 2001:db8:100::6
      SR policy color 200, up, registered, bsid fcbb:bb01:1:e004::

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:PE1#show cef vrf RED 10.2.6.0/24 detail
   via local-srv6-sid fcbb:bb01:1:e004::, 3 dependencies, recursive
    SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {fcbb:bb00:6:e006::}

    0     Y   GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1    fe80::5454:ff:fec1:58eb
  • The steering is the same as in Episode 15.
  • The RED route now points to the Binding SID of the ODN policy.
  • This is the RED service SID, e006, and the inserted list: fcbb:bb00:e004:e002::. There are only two micro-SIDs for three adjacencies, and there are no node numbers. We decode this now.
  • The first hop is GigabitEthernet 0/0/0/1, directly to P3.

16.7 Test B on the wire

Router / tool: CE-A and tshark

CE-A:~$ sudo ping -c 3 -I 10.2.1.2 10.2.6.2
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

$ tshark -r <capture file> -Y "icmp.type == 8 or icmp.type == 0" -T fields -e ipv6.dst -e ipv6.hlim -e icmp.type
# PE1 to P3     fcbb:bb00:e004:e002:6:e006::   255   request
# P3 to P5      fcbb:bb00:e002:6:e006::        254   request
# P5 to PE6     fcbb:bb00:6:e006::             253   request
# PE1 to P2     fcbb:bb00:1:e007::             253   reply
# P2 to P4      fcbb:bb00:1:e007::             254   reply
# P4 to PE6     fcbb:bb00:1:e007::             255   reply
  • Now the wire, while CE-A sends a ping to CE-B in RED. We read each capture with tshark.
  • All three pings are answered. From PE1 to P3, the address is full.
  • P3 removes e004 and sends the packet on its link to P5.
  • P5 removes e002 and sends the packet to PE6. This is three hops, on the low-latency path.
  • The upper links carried only the replies, on the IGP path. As in Episode 15, the color steers one direction only.

Router / tool: P4

RP/0/RP0/CPU0:P4#show pce lsp detail
PCC 2001:db8:100::1:
